# The Offline DSA Interview Handbook (Java)

**A complete, self-contained Data Structures & Algorithms curriculum for SDE-1 / Software Engineer / Java Backend / Full Stack / Fresher interviews.**

- One file. No internet needed. Open it in VS Code, GitHub, or any Markdown viewer.
- Built on top of **your existing baseline** (37 completed problems) - not a restart from zero.
- 306 globally numbered problems, pattern chapters, brute-force  - optimal reasoning, dry runs, complexity analysis, edge cases, interview scripts.
- Progression: **UNDERSTAND  - RECOGNIZE  - ATTEMPT  - BRUTE FORCE  - OPTIMIZE  - IMPLEMENT  - DRY RUN  - ANALYZE  - EDGE CASES  - EXPLAIN  - REVISE**

## 1. About This Handbook

This is a **personal DSA textbook + problem bank + interview preparation guide**, not a list of random questions.

**Who this is for**

| Target | How this handbook helps |
|---|---|
| SDE-1 interviews | Pattern recognition on medium problems, clean code under pressure |
| Software Engineer interviews | Brute force  - optimal reasoning you can verbalize |
| Java Backend Developer interviews | Idiomatic Java collections, complexity of `HashMap`/`PriorityQueue`/`ArrayDeque` |
| Full Stack Developer interviews | Enough depth to clear DSA rounds without competitive-programming tricks |
| Fresher / Campus interviews | Gradual Easy  - Medium ramp with heavy revision support |

**What this handbook optimizes for**

1. Pattern recognition
2. Problem solving and approach selection
3. Brute force  - optimal thinking
4. Clean Java implementation
5. Time and space complexity with **reasoning**, not just a letter
6. Dry-run ability (real state tables, not fake ones)
7. Edge-case handling
8. Interview explanation ability

**What it deliberately does NOT do**

- It does not restart beginner DSA. Your 37 baseline problems are treated as done.
- It does not chase question count. ~306 carefully selected problems, each teaching something distinct.
- It does not use LeetCode numbering, external links, or videos. Everything needed is inside this file.
- It does not hide difficulty. Every problem carries an honest `Difficulty` label; Hard problems are rare and placed at the end of phases.

**Difficulty labels used**

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Easy | Direct application of one pattern |
| Easy-Medium | One pattern + one small twist |
| Medium | Standard SDE-1 interview question |
| Medium-Hard | Two ideas combined, or tricky state handling |
| Hard | Rare in SDE-1; included only where it is a known classic |

The majority of this handbook is **Easy-Medium and Medium**, which is exactly where SDE-1 rounds live.

## 2. How to Use This Handbook

### 2.1 Question-First Study Mode

Every problem is ordered so you can **attempt before you read**:

```
PROBLEM STATEMENT  - INPUT  - OUTPUT  - CONSTRAINTS  - EXAMPLES
         -
   (you attempt it on paper / in an editor)
         -
PATTERN NAME  - RECOGNITION CLUES
         -
<details> BRUTE FORCE  - WHY IT FAILS  - OPTIMAL  - WHY IT WORKS  -
         STEPS  - JAVA  - EXPLANATION  - DRY RUN  - COMPLEXITY  -
         EDGE CASES  - MISTAKES  - INTERVIEW Q&A  - VARIATIONS  -
         60-SECOND INTERVIEW SCRIPT </details>
```

Collapse/expand blocks (`<details>`) hide the solution. If your viewer does not render `<details>`, the "Pattern" heading is still a hard visual separator - **stop there and attempt first**.

**Rule: never read section 10 (Optimal) before you have written at least the brute force yourself.**

### 2.2 The Progression Per Problem

```
UNDERSTAND   -  RECOGNIZE   -  ATTEMPT   -  BRUTE FORCE   -  OPTIMIZE
    -  IMPLEMENT   -  DRY RUN   -  ANALYZE COMPLEXITY   -  HANDLE EDGE CASES
    -  EXPLAIN IN INTERVIEW   -  REVISE
```

A problem is only "done" when you can say the **60-Second Interview Explanation** out loud without looking.

### 2.3 Daily 5-Problem System

Every day:

| Slot | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Problem 1 | New concept / new pattern |
| Problem 2 | Same pattern (reinforce recognition) |
| Problem 3 | Harder variation of the same pattern |
| Problem 4 | Revision - re-solve an old problem **without** looking at the solution |
| Problem 5 | Random interview-style problem (different pattern) |

**Total = exactly 5.**

Important: this handbook is a **reference**, not a gate. Do not block yourself from continuing to the next phase because you solved 4 instead of 5 one day. Track it in the templates below and keep moving.

### 2.4 Daily Study Template

```markdown
# Day X - [Date]

## Problem 1 - [Title] (new pattern)
Notes:

## Problem 2 - [Title] (same pattern)
Notes:

## Problem 3 - [Title] (variation)
Notes:

## Problem 4 - [Title] (revision)
Notes:

## Problem 5 - [Title] (interview)
Notes:

## Daily Review
- Problems attempted:
- Problems solved without hints:
- Problems solved with hints:
- Pattern I struggled with:
- Common mistake:
- Complexity mistake:
- What I learned:
```

### 2.5 Weekly Review Template

```markdown
# Weekly Review - Week X

- Problems attempted:
- Problems solved:
- Success rate: %
- Patterns covered:
- Strongest pattern:
- Weakest pattern:
- Most common mistake:
- Problems requiring revision (list by number):
- Next week's focus:
```

### 2.6 Suggested Pace

| Pace | Time to cover the handbook |
|---|---|
| Aggressive (5/day, 7 days/week) | ~14 weeks |
| Balanced (5/day, 5 days/week) | ~18 weeks |
| Revision-heavy (3 new + 2 revision/day) | ~22 weeks (best retention) |

Phases 1-4 are the highest-yield for SDE-1. If time is short, do Phases 1-4, 7, 9, 11, 13 thoroughly before the rest.

### 3.1 Common Mistake / Improvement Notes on Baseline Problems

Small upgrades only - your implementations of these are assumed working:

- **Binary Search / First / Last Occurrence** - never write `mid = (low + high) / 2` in Java for huge arrays (`low + high` can overflow `int`). Use `int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;`. Also decide one loop convention (`while (low <= high)`) and one boundary update style, and never mix them.
- **Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array** - the two-pointer write index (`slow`) pattern you used here is exactly the engine behind *Remove Duplicates II*, *Move Zeroes*, and *Sort Colors*. Reuse the shape, don't reinvent it.
- **Sort 0s, 1s and 2s** - if your solution used `Collections.sort` or two passes, upgrade to the single-pass three-pointer Dutch National Flag (Problem 048).
- **Frequency Using HashMap** - standardize on `map.getOrDefault(key, 0) + 1` instead of `containsKey`; it is shorter and one lookup instead of two.
- **Fibonacci Using Recursion** - the naive tree recomputes the same subproblems exponentially. Keep this memory: it is the entire motivation for Phase 13 (memoization).
- **Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K** - this is your fixed-window foundation. Phase 2 generalizes it to a *variable* window where the window size is discovered by the condition, not given.

## 5. How to Recognize DSA Patterns (Master Checklist)

This is the most important chapter in the handbook. Interview performance = **how fast you recognize the pattern**, not how many solutions you memorized.

For every pattern below:

1. **Clues** - words/phrases in the problem statement
2. **Typical input**
3. **Typical output**
4. **Constraint hint** - the number that gives the pattern away
5. **Common brute force**
6. **What the pattern buys you**
7. **Common traps**

---

### 5.1 Hashing (HashMap / HashSet)

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "pair that sums to¦", "frequency", "appeared before", "duplicate", "group", "anagram", "once", "complement" |
| Input | Array / string, unordered |
| Output | Indexes, count, groups, yes/no |
| Constraint hint | `n ‰¤ 10^5` + must run in ~O(n)  - hashing, not nested loops |
| Common brute force | Nested loops over all pairs  - O(n²) |
| Buys you | O(1) average lookup: turns "search for complement/frequency/previous occurrence" into one pass |
| Traps | Forgetting `getOrDefault`; assuming O(1) worst case; using a `TreeMap` (O(log n)) when a `HashMap` was asked |

**Recognition question:** *"Do I repeatedly need to know whether I have seen X before, how many times X occurred, or what complements X"* If yes  - hash.

### 5.2 Two Pointers

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "sorted array", "pair/triplet", "in-place", "reverse", "remove duplicates", "partition", "palindrome", "container" |
| Input | Sorted array/string, or data you are allowed to sort, or a linked structure |
| Output | Pair indices, in-place length, max/min over pairs |
| Constraint hint | O(n) or O(n log n) expected on a pair/triplet problem  - sort + two pointers |
| Common brute force | All pairs O(n²) / all triplets O(n³) |
| Buys you | Eliminates one full loop by proving one side can move safely |
| Traps | Moving both pointers with no monotone reason; forgetting to skip duplicates (3Sum); forgetting the array must be sorted |

**Recognition question:** *"Can controlled pointer movement replace a nested loop, given some monotone property (sum too big / too small / equal)"*

### 5.3 Sliding Window

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "contiguous subarray / substring", "longest/shortest such that¦", "at most / exactly K", "window of size K" |
| Input | Array or string |
| Output | Length of longest/shortest valid contiguous range, count, max/min over ranges |
| Constraint hint | `n ‰¤ 10^5` and the answer is about a *contiguous* range with a condition that gets invalid when you extend  - window |
| Common brute force | Enumerate all O(n²) subarrays, validate each O(n)  - O(n³) or O(n²) |
| Buys you | Each index enters and leaves the window at most once  - O(n) |
| Traps | Shrinking when you should expand (or vice versa); state not updated on both sides; using a window for *non*-contiguous requirements |

**Recognition question:** *"Is the range contiguous, and does validity degrade monotonically when I extend right"*

### 5.4 Prefix Sum

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "sum of range [l, r]", "subarray sum equals K", "equilibrium", "equal sums", count subarrays with property |
| Input | Array (often with negatives or arbitrary values)
| Output | Count of subarrays, a range sum, a target sum |
| Constraint hint | Many range/sum queries, or count subarrays with a sum  - prefix |
| Common brute force | Recompute each subarray sum  - O(n²) |
| Buys you | `sum(l..r) = pref[r] - pref[l-1]` in O(1); combined with HashMap  - O(n) counting |
| Traps | Off-by-one in prefix indexing; forgetting `prefix[0] = 0`; negatives break "window shrinks when sum grows" |

### 5.5 Binary Search

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "sorted", "first/last occurrence", "O(log n)", "search space", "monotonic" |
| Input | Sorted array, or any space where a property flips once from false to true |
| Output | Index, boundary, or an optimal value |
| Constraint hint | `n ‰¤ 10^6` + sorted/monotone  - O(log n) is expected |
| Common brute force | Linear scan O(n) (or O(n·X) for answer problems) |
| Buys you | Halving the search space each step |
| Traps | Wrong loop invariant; off-by-one bounds; `low + high` overflow; mid computed then bounds updated inconsistently |

### 5.6 Binary Search on Answer

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "minimum/maximum such that", "can we¦", "smallest capacity/time/speed", "at least/at most K" |
| Input | Array of values + a target feasibility condition |
| Output | A single number (capacity, days, speed, distance) |
| Constraint hint | Answer range is numeric (1¦10^9) and checking feasibility is O(n)  - search the answer, not the array |
| Common brute force | Try every candidate answer O(maxAnswer · n) |
| Buys you | O(log(maxAnswer) · check(n)) - turns a huge answer space into ~30 checks |
| Traps | Feasibility is not monotonic; wrong direction (minimize  - check `tooSmall`); wrong low/high bounds; mid overflow |

### 5.7 Stack

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "matching/parentheses", "most recent", "undo", "previous/next", "nested", "reverse", "expression" |
| Input | String / array with nesting or ordering |
| Output | Match validity, next/previous element, evaluated value |
| Constraint hint | "Nearest greater/smaller to the right/left"  - stack (monotonic variant) |
| Common brute force | For each element scan neighbours  - O(n²) |
| Buys you | Elements that can never be the answer for future positions get popped and forgotten  - O(n) |
| Traps | Using `java.util.Stack` (legacy, synchronized) instead of `ArrayDeque`; popping after pushing incorrectly; forgetting circular wrap |

### 5.8 Monotonic Stack

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "next greater/smaller element", "temperature wait days", "span", "histogram rectangle", "sum of subarray minimums" |
| Input | Array of comparable values |
| Output | Array of nearest-bigger/smaller values, max area, counts |
| Constraint hint | "For every index, find nearest ¦ in O(n)"  - monotonic stack |
| Common brute force | Nested loops O(n²) |
| Buys you | Stack keeps a decreasing/increasing chain of *still useful* candidates |
| Traps | Wrong monotonic direction; not popping *while* condition holds; losing index information (store index, not value, when distances matter) |

### 5.9 Queue / Deque

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "first in first out", "level by level", "sliding window maximum", "front of the line", "circular", "multi-source spread" |
| Input | Stream of items, graph, or window |
| Output | Order of processing, window max/min, shortest unweighted distance |
| Constraint hint | "Maximum/minimum in every window"  - monotonic **deque** |
| Common brute force | Recompute max per window O(n·k) |
| Buys you | Keeps only candidates that can still win for future positions |
| Traps | Using `LinkedList` (poor cache, no capacity) instead of `ArrayDeque`; forgetting to remove indices outside the window |

### 5.10 BFS

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "shortest path" (unweighted / unit steps), "level by level", "nearest", "flood fill", "minimum moves/steps" |
| Input | Graph, grid, tree, state space |
| Output | Shortest number of steps, level ordering, reachability |
| Constraint hint | Unit-cost edges + "minimum steps"  - BFS |
| Common brute force | DFS trying all paths  - exponential |
| Buys you | First time you reach a node in BFS = shortest unweighted path |
| Traps | Marking visited *after* enqueue (causes duplicates); mixing with weighted graphs (use Dijkstra); not handling multi-source starts |

### 5.11 DFS

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "connected component", "explore all paths", "cycle detection", "topological", "path exists", "fill region" |
| Input | Graph, grid, tree |
| Output | Component count, cycle yes/no, ordering, reachability |
| Constraint hint | "Count regions/components" or "is there a cycle"  - DFS/BFS |
| Common brute force | Repeated BFS per cell without shared visited  - O(V·E) |
| Buys you | One O(V+E) sweep marks entire component |
| Traps | Recursion depth on big graphs (use iterative stack); visited marking inconsistent between recursive and iterative forms; directed vs undirected cycle rules differ |

### 5.12 Heap (Priority Queue)

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "top K", "kth largest/smallest", "median from stream", "always need the smallest/largest next", "schedule/merge K lists" |
| Input | Stream or K sorted collections |
| Output | Kth element, top K, running median, merged order |
| Constraint hint | `n ‰¤ 10^5` + "top K"  - heap (n log n sort also works; heap is better for streams) |
| Common brute force | Sort every time (O(n² log n)) or keep full sorted list |
| Buys you | O(log n) insert/extract; keep only K elements  - O(n log K) |
| Traps | Default `PriorityQueue` is a **min** heap (use a `Comparator` or negation for max); `peek()` on empty queue; forgetting to remove stale entries |

### 5.13 Greedy

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "maximum profit", "minimum number of", "earliest", "non-overlapping", "locally best" |
| Input | Intervals, weighted choices, sorted items |
| Output | Max profit / min count / schedule |
| Constraint hint | Sorting + single pass gives the answer  - greedy |
| Common brute force | Try all subsets  - O(2¿) |
| Buys you | O(n log n) after sorting |
| Traps | Greedy without an exchange argument; picking a locally best choice fails when a later choice blocks a better global one (that's when you need DP) |

**Recognition question:** *"After sorting by some key, can I commit to a choice now without regretting it later"* If unsure, ask what counterexample would break it.

### 5.14 Backtracking

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "all subsets/permutations/combinations", "arrangements", "place¦so that no two¦", "restore", "valid configurations" |
| Input | Small set (`n ‰¤ 15-20` typical), board size ‰¤ 9 |
| Output | List of all valid configurations / count of them |
| Constraint hint | Output itself is exponential (all subsets)  - backtracking; "return *one* solution"  - often DFS with pruning |
| Common brute force | Generate all candidates then filter (works, but explores dead branches fully) |
| Buys you | Prune invalid branches early; `choose  - explore  - undo` avoids copying state |
| Traps | Forgetting to undo; duplicate results when input has duplicates (sort + skip); no base case; building the same state twice |

### 5.15 Dynamic Programming

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "minimum/maximum", "number of ways", "can it be done", repeated identical subproblems, "best" over choices |
| Input | Sequence, grid, set with capacity |
| Output | Optimal value or count of ways |
| Constraint hint | Brute force recursion is exponential *and* subproblems repeat  - DP; `n ‰¤ 1000` often means O(n²) DP is fine |
| Common brute force | Recursion exploring every branch (e.g., naive Fibonacci) |
| Buys you | Each subproblem solved once  - O(number of states - transitions) |
| Traps | Wrong state meaning; missing base case; wrong transition order in tabulation; not handling "no valid way" (e.g., return `Integer.MAX_VALUE` only where safe) |

### 5.16 Trie

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "prefix", "autocomplete/suggestions", "startsWith", "dictionary of words", "search with wildcards", "XOR maximum" |
| Input | Set of words / strings over a small alphabet |
| Output | Words with a prefix, boolean search, longest XOR |
| Constraint hint | Many prefix queries over a fixed word set  - trie beats repeated `startsWith` scans |
| Common brute force | Check every word for every query  - O(total length - queries) |
| Buys you | Prefix lookup costs O(prefix length), independent of dictionary size |
| Traps | Forgetting to share nodes; wildcard search needs recursion at a node; XOR tries must insert bits from **most significant** bit |

### 5.17 Linked List Fast/Slow Pointers

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Clues | "middle", "cycle", "palindrome in list", "remove nth from end", "reorder", "has intersection" |
| Input | Singly/doubly linked list |
| Output | Middle node, cycle start, reversed/rotated list |
| Constraint hint | O(1) extra space requested on a linked list  - fast/slow or iterative reversal |
| Common brute force | Convert to array / count length twice (O(n) space or two passes) |
| Buys you | One pass, O(1) space, cycle detection without a hash set |
| Traps | `slow`/`fast` start at different offsets; NPE when list has 1 node; losing the `next` pointer before re-linking |

## 6. Master Decision Tree: Approaching an Unfamiliar Problem

Use this **out loud** in an interview. Say what you are checking. Interviewers reward structured thinking.

```
START: read problem, restate it, confirm input/output & constraints
  "'
  "œ" Q1. What is the INPUT type
  "'    "œ" Array / String """"""""""""""-º go to Q2
  "'    "œ" Linked List """""""""""""""""-º two pointers reverse merge (Phase 6)
  "'    "œ" Stack-like (nested/matching/nearest) ""-º stack / monotonic stack (Phase 7)
  "'    "œ" Queue-like (level order / spread / first-come) ""-º BFS / deque (Phase 7, 11)
  "'    "œ" Tree """"""""""""""""""""""""-º DFS or BFS (Phase 9/10)
  "'    "œ" Graph """""""""""""""""""""""-º connected weighted acyclic (Phase 11)
  "'    "œ" Set of words / prefixes """""-º trie (Phase 12)
  "'    """ "ways / best / can it be done" over a sequence ""-º DP (Phase 13)
  "'
  "œ" Q2. Is it SORTED (or can I sort without changing the answer)
  "'    "œ" Yes + looking for a pair/target ""-º two pointers (Phase 3)
  "'    "œ" Yes + searching an index/value ""-º binary search (Phase 4)
  "'    """ No ""-º consider hashing first (O(n)), sorting second (O(n log n))
  "'
  "œ" Q3. Is it asking about a CONTIGUOUS range with a condition
  "'    "œ" Fixed size K """"""""""""""""-º fixed sliding window (revision, baseline #28)
  "'    "œ" Longest valid """""""""""""""-º expand right, shrink while invalid (Phase 2)
  "'    "œ" Shortest valid """"""""""""""-º expand right, shrink while still valid (Phase 2)
  "'    """ Not contiguous """"""""""""""-º not a window - use hashing/sorting/DP
  "'
  "œ" Q4. Is FREQUENCY / "seen before" involved
  "'    """ Yes ""-º HashMap/HashSet one-pass (Phase 1)

  "œ" Q6. Is there a MONOTONIC property

  "œ" Q7. Is there a TREE / GRAPH relationship (structure, not array)

  """ Q9. Quick sanity checks before coding
       "œ" Can a hash map remove a nested loop         (Phase 1)
       "œ" Can two pointers remove a nested loop       (Phase 3)
       "œ" Can a window remove an O(n²) scan           (Phase 2)
       "œ" Can binary search remove a linear/answer scan (Phase 4)
       "œ" Can a heap replace repeated full scans      (Phase 8)
       """ What are the edge cases What is my brute force
```

### 6.1 The 60-Second Pre-Code Ritual

1. Restate the problem in one sentence.
2. Ask at least two clarifying questions (duplicates negatives sorted empty input allowed).
3. State the **brute force** and its complexity out loud.
4. Name the **bottleneck line** in the brute force.
5. Name the pattern that removes that line.
6. Only then write code.

## 7. Complexity Cheat Sheet

### 7.1 Growth Rates (Big-O)

| Complexity | Name | Example problem | n = 10¶ feasible |
|---|---|---|---|
| O(1) | Constant | HashMap `get`, array index, stack `push/pop` | Yes |
| O(log n) | Logarithmic | Binary search, heap `sift`, balanced BST op | Yes (‰ˆ20 steps) |
| O(n) | Linear | Single pass, two pointers, sliding window, BFS/DFS | Yes |
| O(n log n) | Linearithmic | Sorting, heap-sorting n items, "sort then scan" | Yes (‰ˆ2·10· ops) |
| O(n²) | Quadratic | Nested loops, DP over 2D n-n table, naive pair search | n ‰¤ ~5,000 |
| O(n³) | Cubic | Floyd-Warshall, matrix chain, triple nested loops | n ‰¤ ~500 |
| O(2¿) | Exponential | All subsets, naive recursion over choices | n ‰¤ ~25 |
| O(n!) | Factorial | All permutations generated naively | n ‰¤ ~10 |

**Rules of thumb for constraint guessing:**

| Constraint on n | Usually implies |
|---|---|
| n ‰¤ 10-20 | O(2¿) / O(n!) backtracking is acceptable |
| n ‰¤ 500 | O(n³) may pass; O(n²) definitely passes |
| n ‰¤ 5,000 | O(n²) passes, O(n³) does not |
| n ‰¤ 10µ"10¶ | O(n log n) or O(n) required; O(n²) fails |
| n ‰¤ 10¸"10¹ in the *answer*, O(n) check | Binary search on answer (Phase 4) |

### 7.2 Complexity of Common Java Data Structures

| Structure | Access | Search | Insert | Delete | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `int[]` / `ArrayList` get | O(1) | O(n) | O(1) amortized (add at end) / O(n) mid | O(n) mid | Array-backed; `ArrayList` remove is O(n) because of shifting |
| `LinkedList` | O(n) | O(n) | O(1) *if you hold the node* | O(1) *if you hold the node* | Rarely useful; node access itself costs O(n) |
| `HashMap` | - | **O(1) average**, O(n) worst | O(1) average | O(1) average | Worst case = all keys collide (resize/load factor matters) |
| `HashSet` | - | O(1) average | O(1) average | O(1) average | Built on HashMap |
| `LinkedHashMap` | - | O(1) average | O(1) average | O(1) average | + insertion (or access) order; useful for LRU / first-non-repeating |
| `TreeMap` / `TreeSet` | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(log n) | Sorted, supports `floorKey`/`higherKey`/range views |
| `ArrayDeque` (stack/queue) | O(1) ends | O(n) | O(1) amortized ends | O(1) ends | **Use this for stack and queue in interviews** |
| `PriorityQueue` (heap) | peek O(1) | O(n) search | **O(log n)** add | O(log n) poll / O(n) remove(Object) | Not sorted; only the head is guaranteed |
| `java.util.Stack` | O(1) | O(n) | O(1) | O(1) | Legacy + synchronized - avoid, use `ArrayDeque` |

### 7.3 Algorithm Complexity You Must Know Cold

| Algorithm / pattern | Time | Space |
|---|---|---|
| Binary search | O(log n) | O(1) iterative |
| Two pointers (sorted) | O(n) after O(n log n) sort | O(1) |
| Sliding window (variable) | O(n) | O(1) or O(k) for a char map |
| Prefix sum + HashMap | O(n) | O(n) |
| Kadane's algorithm | O(n) | O(1) |
| Monotonic stack | O(n) | O(n) |
| Monotonic deque (window max) | O(n) | O(k) |
| Sorting-based solutions | O(n log n) | O(n) or O(1) |
| Heap top-K from n items | O(n log k) | O(k) |
| Merge K sorted lists via heap | O(N log k), N = total nodes | O(k) |
| BFS / DFS on graph | O(V + E) | O(V) |
| Dijkstra with binary heap | O((V + E) log V) | O(V) |

## 8. Java DSA Reference

Everything you need from Java for this handbook. No external documentation required.

### 8.1 Arrays

```java
int[] a = new int[n];            // all zeros
int[] a = {1, 2, 3};             // literal
int x = a[i]; a[i] = x;          // O(1)
int n = a.length;                // fixed size - no add/remove
Arrays.sort(a);                  // primitive: dual-pivot quicksort, O(n log n)
Arrays.sort(objects);            // objects: TimSort, O(n log n), stable
Arrays.fill(a, -1);
Arrays.copyOf(a, n);
int idx = Arrays.binarySearch(a, key);  // valid only if sorted; may return -(insertion point)-1
```

**Interview mistakes**
- Forgetting arrays are 0-indexed in range math (`sum(l..r)` with prefix needs care).
- Assuming `Arrays.binarySearch` works on unsorted arrays.
- Returning `a.length` where a *length of result* was asked (off-by-one).

### 8.2 ArrayList

```java
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(5);                 // O(1) amortized
list.get(0);                 // O(1)
list.set(0, 9);              // O(1)
list.remove(list.size()-1);  // O(1) - MUST remove by index, not by int value
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(5)); // O(n) removes the object with value 5
list.size();                 // O(1)
```

**Interview mistakes**
- `list.remove(0)` on `ArrayList<Integer>` actually removes **index 0** (fine), but `list.remove(someIntegerObject)` removes by value - mixing them is a classic bug.
- Auto-boxing: `List<Integer>` cannot hold `int`; `list.get(i)` returns `Integer` (NPE if a null sneaks in).

### 8.3 HashMap

```java
Map<String, Integer> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("a", 1);
map.get("a");                      // null if absent
map.getOrDefault("a", 0);          //   use this for frequency counting
map.containsKey("a");
map.remove("a");
for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : map.entrySet()) {
    String k = e.getKey(); int v = e.getValue();
}
map.keySet(); map.values();
```

**Frequency template (memorize this)**
```java
Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
for (int x : nums) freq.put(x, freq.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1);
```

**Interview mistakes**
- Two lookups (`containsKey` + `get`) where one `getOrDefault` suffices.
- Using `HashMap` order-dependent logic - **HashMap has no order**. Need order `LinkedHashMap`.
- Assuming O(1) *worst case*; mention honestly: O(1) average, O(n) worst.
- Integer key hashing: `map.get(1)` with an `int` autoboxes correctly, but be consistent.

### 8.4 HashSet

```java
Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
seen.add(x); seen.contains(x); seen.remove(x);
set.size();
Set<Integer> a = new HashSet<>(listA);
a.retainAll(listB);   // intersection
a.addAll(listB);      // union
```

**Use when** you only need *presence*, not counts. Presence-only lookups are faster and simpler than a map.

### 8.5 LinkedHashMap

```java
Map<Character, Integer> map = new LinkedHashMap<>();  // insertion order preserved
```

**Use when** you need "first non-repeating character" (your baseline #16) or any "first seen order" iteration. `removeEldestEntry` also implements LRU in one line.

### 8.6 TreeMap / TreeSet

```java
Map<Integer, Integer> tm = new TreeMap<>();
SortedMap<Integer, Integer> sm = tm.headMap(key);   // < key
tm.floorKey(key);   // greatest key <= key
tm.ceilingKey(key); // smallest key >= key

Set<Integer> ts = new TreeSet<>();
ts.floor(x); ts.ceiling(x); ts.higher(x); ts.lower(x);
```

**Use when** you need sorted order, predecessor/successor, or range queries. Cost: O(log n) instead of O(1).

### 8.7 Stack - use ArrayDeque

```java
Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
stack.push(x);        // addFirst
stack.pop();          // removeFirst  (throws if empty - check isEmpty() first)
stack.peek();         // peekFirst
stack.isEmpty();
```

**Do not use `java.util.Stack`** in interviews: it extends `Vector` (synchronized, slower) and is considered legacy. One line of explanation impresses interviewers: *"I'll use ArrayDeque since Stack is legacy and synchronized."*

### 8.8 Queue and Deque - ArrayDeque

```java
Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
q.offer(x);   // enqueue (returns false if capacity-restricted; ArrayDeque never is)
q.poll();     // dequeue, null if empty
q.peek();     // head, null if empty
q.isEmpty(); q.size();

Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
dq.offerFirst(x); dq.offerLast(x);
dq.pollFirst();   dq.pollLast();
dq.peekFirst();   dq.peekLast();
```

**Interview mistake:** choosing `LinkedList` for queues - correct but slow and verbose; `ArrayDeque` is the idiomatic choice.

### 8.9 PriorityQueue (the heap - read this carefully)

```java
// MIN-HEAP by default (smallest on top)
PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();
minHeap.offer(5);
int top = minHeap.peek();   // O(1), smallest, does NOT remove
int x = minHeap.poll();     // O(log n), removes smallest

// MAX-HEAP (largest on top)
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> b - a);
PriorityQueue<Integer> maxHeap2 = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());

// objects
PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);      // by first column
PriorityQueue<int[]> pq2 = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0]));

// Kth largest: keep a min-heap of size K, then peek
PriorityQueue<Integer> kLargest = new PriorityQueue<>();
for (int x : nums) {
    kLargest.offer(x);
    if (kLargest.size() > k) kLargest.poll();   // drop the smallest of the K
}
int answer = kLargest.peek();
```

**Critical facts**
1. Default order = **min heap**. Max heap needs an explicit comparator.
2. `poll()` on empty throws `NoSuchElementException` (not `null`) - guard it.
3. A `PriorityQueue` is **not sorted internally** - only the head is guaranteed. If you iterate it you get arbitrary order.
4. `remove(Object)` is O(n) because it must search; `poll()` is O(log n).
5. `size()` is O(1).

**Min-heap vs max-heap rule**
- Kth **largest**  - min-heap of size K (evict smallest, head = Kth largest).
- Kth **smallest**  - max-heap of size K (evict largest, head = Kth smallest).
- Two heaps for a running median  - max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half.

**When a heap beats sorting:** you need the top K of a **stream**, or you repeatedly extract min/max while still receiving elements. If the whole array is present and you sort once, `Arrays.sort` at O(n log n) is just as good and simpler - say that out loud in an interview.

### 8.10 String and StringBuilder

```java
String s = "abc";            // immutable - every + creates a new String (O(n) each)
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append('a'); sb.length(); sb.charAt(0);
String res = sb.toString();

s.charAt(i); s.length(); s.substring(1, 3);   // [1,3) - copies
s.toCharArray();
s.equals(other);                 // content equality
s.compareTo(other);              // lexicographic
s.toLowerCase(); s.split("\\s+");
```

**Interview mistakes**
- Building strings with `+=` in a loop  - O(n²). Use `StringBuilder`.
- `substring` in Java 7+ copies - calling it inside a loop is O(n) each time.
- Comparing with `==` (reference equality) instead of `.equals()`.

### 8.11 Comparable vs Comparator

```java
class Point implements Comparable<Point> {
    int x, y;
    public int compareTo(Point o) { return Integer.compare(this.x, o.x); }
}
Collections.sort(points);                       // natural order from Comparable

Comparator<Point> byY = (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.y, b.y);
points.sort(byY.thenComparingInt(p -> p.x));     // multi-key sort
Collections.sort(points, Comparator.reversed());
Arrays.sort(arr, (a, b) -> b - a);               // int[] needs an Integer[] for a comparator
```

**Rule:** `Comparable` = the object's *own* natural order (one implementation). `Comparator` = an *external* order (many possible). Sorting intervals, custom tuples, or "by frequency then value" all use `Comparator`.

# Phase 1 - Arrays + Hashing

**Goal:** turn O(n²) nested-loop instincts into O(n) hashing/prefix-scan instincts, and learn to *name* why.

**Prerequisites (your baseline):** #1"#10 (array traversal), #29 (Frequency Using HashMap), #30 (First Repeated), #31 (Common Elements), #26"#28 (two pointers, fixed window).

## Pattern Chapter - Arrays + Hashing

### P1.1 What this phase is really about

Almost every Phase 1 problem is a variation of one sentence:

> **"Instead of searching for something inside the array again, remember it in a hash table, or express it as a prefix quantity you have already computed."**

Two engines power this whole phase:

1. **Remember (hashing):** "have I seen the complement / the frequency / the previous occurrence"  - O(1) lookup kills a nested loop.
2. **Prefix (cumulative):** `sum(l..r) = prefix[r] - prefix[l-1]`  - recomputing a range becomes O(1), and *counting subarrays with a target sum* becomes a single scan with a HashMap.

### P1.2 The patterns in this phase

| Pattern | One-line idea | Problems |
|---|---|---|
| HashMap lookup | Store what you need to find later; look it up once | 001, 007 |
| Frequency counting | `freq.put(x, freq.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1)` | 002, 003 |
| HashSet presence | Fast duplicate / membership test | 018 |
| Prefix sum | Range sums in O(1) | 009, 010 |
| Prefix sum + HashMap | Count subarrays whose sum = K (handles negatives) | 008, 009 |
| Kadane (running best) | Extend the running sum, drop it when negative | 005, 006 |
| Prefix + suffix arrays | "Product except self" without division | 011 |
| In-place manipulation | Write-index / reversal / rotation by hand | 012, 014, 015 |
| Sorting + scanning | Sort brings order  - adjacent/group comparisons | 007 (alt), 016 |
| Intervals | Sort by start, merge overlapping | 016 |
| Greedy commit | Locally optimal choice is globally safe | 017 |

### P1.3 Fixed-window foundation  - what changes now

You already solved *Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K* (baseline #28). That is the fixed window:

```java
int windowSum = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) windowSum += nums[i];
int best = windowSum;
for (int i = k; i < n; i++) {
    windowSum += nums[i] - nums[i - k];   // slide: add right, drop left
    best = Math.max(best, windowSum);
}
```

Phase 1 problems that ask for a **subarray** but have *no fixed K* are **not** windows - they are prefix-sum/Kadane problems, because negatives or "exact sum" break the shrink-while-invalid trick. Learning to tell them apart is the point of Phases 1-2.

### P1.4 Recognition checklist for this phase

- "Find a **pair/triplet** with a target sum"  - HashMap (unsorted) or two pointers (sorted, Phase 3).
- "**How many** subarrays have sum = K"  - prefix sum + HashMap (Phase 1); "**longest** subarray with sum = K"  - prefix + HashMap tracking first index, or two pointers if all positive.
- "**Contiguous** range + condition + all non-negative"  - sliding window (Phase 2).
- "Best **so far** while scanning, reset when it hurts"  - Kadane.
- "**Merge / overlap / combine** ranges"  - sort by start, sweep.
- "Without using **division**"  - prefix + suffix.
- "**In-place / O(1) extra space**"  - write pointer, reversal tricks.

### P1.5 Phase 1 common traps

1. Using `HashMap<Integer, Integer>` and forgetting `getOrDefault`  - two lookups and possible NPE.
2. Computing prefix sums in a separate array when you only need one running value  - wasted O(n) space (fine, but say why).
3. `sum = target - sum` overflow for `int` extremes  - use `long` where the problem says sums can be large.
4. Kadane with all-negative input if you initialize `maxSoFar = 0`  - wrong answer; initialize to the first element (or `Integer.MIN_VALUE`).
5. Sorting an array when the problem asked to return the original *indices*  - store `(value, index)` pairs first.
6. Merging intervals after sorting but forgetting that the merged result's end must be `max(currentEnd, nextEnd)`, not `nextEnd`.

---

### Problem 001 - Two Sum

**Category:** Arrays + Hashing | **Difficulty:** Easy-Medium | **Pattern:** HashMap

#### 1. Problem Statement

Given an array of integers and a target value, find **two different elements** whose sum equals the target. Return the indices of those two elements. Exactly one valid answer exists; you may return the indices in any order.

#### 2. Input

- `int[] nums` - the array of integers (may contain negatives and duplicates).
- `int target` - the required sum.

#### 3. Output

- `int[2]` containing the two indices `i` and `j` (`i != j`) such that `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`.

#### 4. Constraints

- `2 <= nums.length <= 10^5` (this is the real constraint that decides the approach)
- `-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9`
- `-10^9 <= target <= 10^9`
- Exactly one solution exists (if the statement guarantees it).

#### 5. Examples

**Example 1**
```
Input:
  nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9
Output:
  [0, 1]
Explanation:
  nums[0] + nums[1] = 2 + 7 = 9
```

**Example 2**
```
Input:
  nums = [3, 2, 4], target = 6
Output:
  [1, 2]
Explanation:
  3 is at index 0, but 3 + 3 would need the same element twice.
  The pair (2, 4) at indices 1 and 2 sums to 6.
```

**Edge case**
```
Input:
  nums = [3, 3], target = 6
Output:
  [0, 1]
Explanation:
  Duplicate values are fine as long as they are at different indices.
```

#### 6. Pattern

**HashMap (one-pass complement lookup).**

#### 7. How to Recognize This Pattern

- The problem asks for a **pair** with a given sum.
- The array is **not sorted**, so two pointers would require sorting (which destroys original indices).
- The constraint `n <= 10^5` forbids checking every pair.
- Clue phrases: *"two elements that sum to"*, *"pair with target"*, *"return their indices"*.
- The moment you notice the brute force needs `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`, ask: *"for element `nums[i]`, what exactly am I searching for The value `target - nums[i]`. Have I seen it"* That question **is** the HashMap.

<details>
<summary><b>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</b></summary>

#### 8. Brute Force Approach

**Idea:** try every possible pair.

**Algorithm:** for each `i` from 0 to n-1, for each `j` from `i+1` to n-1, if `nums[i] + nums[j] == target` return `[i, j]`.

**Why it works:** every pair is checked, so the answer cannot be missed.

**Time:** O(n²) - n·(n-1)/2 pair checks. **Space:** O(1).

#### 9. Why Brute Force Is Not Ideal

The bottleneck is the **inner loop**: for each `i` you re-scan the entire right side of the array looking for `target - nums[i]`. That is a *search* being done n times by scanning - exactly what a hash table does in O(1). With `n = 10^5`, O(n²) ‰ˆ 10^10 operations: several seconds. The interviewer expects O(n).

#### 10. Optimal Approach

Walk the array once, left to right. For each element `x = nums[i]`:

1. Compute `need = target - x`.
2. Ask the map: *have I already seen `need`*
3. If yes  - we found the pair: return `[map.get(need), i]`.
4. If no  - store `x  - i` in the map and move on.

We store **before** we could ever pair an element with itself, because we only look up elements from earlier indices.

#### 11. Why the Optimal Approach Works

**Why is it safe** The answer is some pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`. When the scan reaches `j`, the element `nums[i]` (at the earlier index) has already been inserted into the map. So at step `j` the lookup `need = target - nums[j] = nums[i]` succeeds and we return.

**Why don't we miss the answer** Every index is processed exactly once, and each index is inserted after its lookup. So every *ordered* pair (earlier, later) is implicitly tested - the same coverage as the double loop, minus the redundant rescans.

**Why can't an element pair with itself** Because we only look up values inserted at *strictly smaller* indices. That's why `[3, 3], target = 6` works: the second 3 finds the first 3.

#### 12. Algorithm / Steps

1. Create `Map<Integer, Integer> seen` mapping value  - index.
2. For `i` in `0..n-1`:
   1. `need = target - nums[i]`
   2. If `seen.containsKey(need)`  - return `{seen.get(need), i}`
   3. `seen.put(nums[i], i)`
4. (If guaranteed) return an empty/placeholder array.

#### 13. Java Solution

```java
class Solution {
    public int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int need = target - nums[i];
            if (seen.containsKey(need)) {
                return new int[] { seen.get(need), i };
            }
            seen.put(nums[i], i);
        }
        return new int[] {};
    }
}
```

#### 14. Code Explanation

- `seen.put(nums[i], i)` happens **after** the lookup - this is what prevents pairing an element with itself while still covering every earlier element.
- We store the *index*, not just the value, because the output needs indices.
- `containsKey` + `get` is two lookups; in a tight loop you may combine them, but clarity wins in an interview. Note: storing the *earliest* index (skip overwriting) is irrelevant here since any valid pair is accepted.

#### 15. Detailed Dry Run

`nums = [2, 7, 11, 15]`, `target = 9`

| Step | i | nums[i] | need = 9 - nums[i] | seen (before) | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 2 | 7 | {} | 7 not found  - store {2 '0} |
| 2 | 1 | 7 | 2 | {2 '0} | **2 found at index 0**  - return [0, 1] |

Verification: `nums[0] + nums[1] = 2 + 7 = 9`. œ"

Second run, `nums = [3, 3]`, `target = 6`:

| Step | i | nums[i] | need | seen (before) | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 3 | 3 | {} | not found  - store {3 '0} |
| 2 | 1 | 3 | 3 | {3 '0} | found  - return [0, 1] œ" |

#### 16. Complexity Analysis

- **Time: O(n)** - exactly one pass; each iteration performs a constant number of hash operations, each O(1) *on average*.
- **Space: O(n)** - in the worst case (no pair found early) the map holds every element. Auxiliary space beyond the input is O(n).
- Why not O(1) Because we deliberately trade memory for time. If the interviewer asks for O(1) extra space, the honest answer is: you'd need sorting + two pointers (O(n log n), and it loses original indices) or an O(n²) scan - there is no known O(n) time / O(1) space solution for arbitrary unsorted data with duplicates.

#### 17. Edge Cases

- **Duplicate values** (`[3,3]`, target 6): handled because lookup happens before insert.
- **Negatives** (`[-1, -2, -3, -4]`, target -4): arithmetic is sign-safe.
- **Same element twice** must be rejected: guaranteed by insert-after-lookup order.
- **Large values:** `target - nums[i]` can overflow only if you use types smaller than the inputs; `int` arithmetic with `int` inputs matching `target`'s type is safe, but if constraints reach ±10^9 the sum itself fits `int` - however `need` computed as `int` is fine. Mention: if constraints were ±10^18 you'd use `long`.
- **No solution:** return an empty array; don't index into an empty map.

#### 18. Common Mistakes

1. Inserting into the map **before** the lookup  - `[3,3], target = 6` wrongly returns `[0,0]` or `[1,1]`.
2. Returning the *values* instead of the *indices*.
3. Storing only `i` and not the value (map value  - index, not index  - index).
4. Using `HashMap` but writing `if (map.get(need) != null)` when `0` is a valid stored index - `Integer` boxing makes `null` checks correct here, but `getOrDefault` + `containsKey` is clearer.
5. Reverting to O(n²) when the interviewer says the array *is* sorted - then two pointers is better (see Phase 3).

#### 19. Interview Questions

**Q1. Why HashMap**
> Because for each element I need to know in O(1) whether its complement `target - x` has already appeared. A HashMap turns the inner loop of the O(n²) solution into a constant-time lookup.

**Q2. Can you do it without extra space**
> In O(n) time, no. I could sort and use two pointers in O(1) space, but that's O(n log n) and I lose the original indices unless I sort (value, index) pairs first.

**Q3. What happens with duplicates**
> They work fine - `[3,3]` with target 6 returns `[0,1]` because I insert index 0 before I ever query for index 1.

**Q4. What is the worst-case complexity**
> Hash operations are O(1) average, O(n) worst if every key collides - practically with a good hash function we treat it as O(n).

**Q5. What if there were four numbers (4Sum)**
> Fix two numbers, then apply this exact two-sum inside the remainder - or sort and use two pointers around them (Phase 3).

#### 20. Variations

1. **Two Sum - sorted input:** use two pointers moving inward (O(1) space) - see Phase 3.
2. **Return all unique pairs (Two Sum II with duplicates):** sort, two pointers, and skip equal values on both sides.
3. **Count all pairs with a given sum:** same one-pass map, but instead of returning immediately, add `freq[need]` to a counter and increment `freq[x]`.
4. **Three Sum:** sort first, fix one value, then run this two-sum on the rest while skipping duplicates.

#### 21. Related Problems

Problem 044 (3Sum), Problem 045 (3Sum Closest), Problem 055 (Pair With Given Difference), Problem 169-ish (Two Sum data-structure design - see Phase 8 practice).

#### 22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds

> "I'd solve this in one pass with a HashMap that stores each value and its index. For every element I compute the complement `target - x` and check whether I've already seen it. If yes, those two indices are my answer; if not, I store the current element and move on. Because I only look up values that were inserted at earlier indices, an element can never pair with itself, which handles duplicates like `[3,3]`. This is O(n) time and O(n) space - it's essentially trading memory for the O(n²) inner loop."

</details>

### Problem 002 - Majority Element

**Category:** Arrays + Hashing | **Difficulty:** Easy-Medium | **Pattern:** Frequency counting (HashMap)  - Boyer"Moore optimization

#### 1. Problem Statement

Given an array of size n, find the element that appears **more than ŒŠn/2Œ‹ times** (the *majority element*). You may assume the majority element always exists.

#### 2. Input

- `int[] nums` - array of length n. It may be unsorted and may contain duplicates.

#### 3. Output

- The value that occurs strictly more than `n/2` times.

#### 4. Constraints

- `1 <= nums.length <= 5 * 10^4`
- `-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9`
- It is guaranteed that a majority element exists (state this assumption out loud).

#### 5. Examples

**Example 1**
```
Input:
  nums = [3, 2, 3]
Output:
  3
Explanation:
  n = 3, so we need more than 1 occurrence. 3 appears 2 times. œ"
```

**Example 2**
```
Input:
  nums = [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
Output:
  2
Explanation:
  n = 7, need > 3.5, i.e. at least 4. 2 appears 4 times, 1 appears 3 times.
```

**Edge case**
```
Input:
  nums = [1]
Output:
  1
Explanation:
  n = 1, need > 0.5  - 1 occurrence is enough.
```

#### 6. Pattern

**Frequency counting (HashMap)** - with the **Boyer"Moore Voting** O(1)-space optimization as the interview upgrade.

#### 7. How to Recognize This Pattern

- The phrase *"appears more than n/2 times"* (or *"more than n/3 times"*) is a frequency problem.
- Constraint `n ‰¤ 5 * 10^4` allows O(n) with a map; if it said *O(1) extra space*, it forces Boyer"Moore.
- General rule: **"element that appears most often / more than k times"**  - count frequencies.
- If the statement also says *"can you solve it with constant space"*  - the majority element is the only candidate that can survive pairwise cancellation  - Boyer"Moore.

<details>
<summary><b>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</b></summary>

#### 8. Brute Force Approach

**Idea:** for each distinct value, count how many times it appears by scanning the whole array.

**Algorithm:** for every element `x`, scan the array counting occurrences of `x`; if count > n/2 return `x`.

**Why it works:** exhaustive counting cannot miss the majority element.

**Time:** O(n²). **Space:** O(1).

#### 9. Why Brute Force Is Not Ideal

The bottleneck is **re-scanning the entire array for each candidate**. Information is thrown away after every scan: your counts from the previous candidate are useless. With n = 50,000, O(n²) ‰ˆ 2.5 billion operations. Also, sorting first and counting runs is O(n log n) - better, but still not linear, and it destroys the input order (usually allowed, but unnecessary).

#### 10. Optimal Approach

**Version A - HashMap (the clear interview starter):** one pass, count every value with `getOrDefault`. If any count > n/2, return it. O(n) time, O(n) space.

**Version B - Boyer"Moore Voting (the interview win):** maintain a `candidate` and a `counter`.

1. Counter is 0  - adopt the current element as `candidate`.
2. Same element as candidate  - `counter++`.
3. Different element  - `counter--` (cancel one pair).
4. When counter hits 0, the prefix so far has no strict majority - reset and continue.
5. At the end, `candidate` is the only possible majority element.

#### 11. Why the Optimal Approach Works

**Intuition (pairwise cancellation):** every *non-majority* element can cancel at most one *majority* element, because there are fewer of them than there are majority elements. Think of each non-majority vote as "spending" itself to eliminate one majority vote. Since majority votes outnumber all others combined, some majority votes survive every possible cancellation - and the algorithm's `candidate` is exactly a survivor.

**Why don't we miss the answer** The algorithm never claims `candidate` is the majority during the scan - it only guarantees that *if* a majority exists, the surviving candidate must be it. That's why the problem statement's guarantee matters; you should state this dependency in the interview. A second O(n) verification pass (count occurrences of the candidate) makes it correct even without the guarantee.

#### 12. Algorithm / Steps (Boyer"Moore)

1. `candidate = 0`, `count = 0`.
2. For each `x` in nums:
   1. If `count == 0`  - `candidate = x`, `count = 1`.
   2. Else if `x == candidate`  - `count++`.
   3. Else  - `count--`.
3. Return `candidate` (optionally verify with one more pass).

#### 13. Java Solution

```java
class Solution {
    public int majorityElement(int[] nums) {
        int candidate = 0, count = 0;
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (count == 0) {
                candidate = x;
                count = 1;
            } else if (x == candidate) {
                count++;
            } else {
                count--;
            }
        }
        return candidate;
    }
}
```

HashMap version (if asked for the straightforward one):

```java
class SolutionMap {
    public int majorityElement(int[] nums) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        for (int x : nums) freq.put(x, freq.getOrDefault(x, 0) + 1);
        for (Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> e : freq.entrySet()) {
            if (e.getValue() > nums.length / 2) return e.getKey();
        }
        return -1; // unreachable when a majority is guaranteed
    }
}
```

#### 14. Code Explanation

- `count == 0` resets the candidate: at that point all previously seen elements can be partitioned into equal-opposing pairs, so no element has a strict majority among them - a fresh start loses nothing.
- `candidate` is initialized to `0` only because the `count == 0` branch always assigns it before it is ever returned (on a non-empty array, count becomes 1 at index 0).
- The `count--` branch does **not** change the candidate - cancellation is symmetric; only the *end* of the chain picks a new one.

#### 15. Detailed Dry Run

`nums = [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]`

| Step | x | count before | Action | candidate | count after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | 0 | adopt | 2 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 1 | same  - ++ | 2 | 2 |
| 3 | 1 | 2 | diff  - -- | 2 | 1 |
| 4 | 1 | 1 | diff  - -- | 2 | 0 |
| 5 | 1 | 0 | adopt | 1 | 1 |
| 6 | 2 | 1 | diff  - -- | 1 | 0 |
| 7 | 2 | 0 | adopt | 2 | 1 |

Final candidate = **2**. Occurrences of 2 = 4 > ŒŠ7/2Œ‹ = 3. œ"

#### 16. Complexity Analysis

- **Time: O(n)** - one pass over the array; each element does O(1) work. (HashMap version: O(n) for counting + O(distinct) for the check = O(n).)
- **Space: O(1)** for Boyer"Moore - only `candidate` and `count`. HashMap version: **O(n)** auxiliary in the worst case (all distinct, though then no majority exists).
- Input space: the array itself is O(n) and given; we don't count it as auxiliary.

#### 17. Edge Cases

- **n = 1:** candidate adopted immediately.
- **All elements identical:** count grows, candidate never changes.
- **Majority element appears exactly ŒŠn/2Œ‹ + 1 times:** still correct because the comparison is `> n/2` (integer division already floors).
- **Negative and extreme values:** `candidate` stores values, not counts - no arithmetic on values, no overflow.
- **No majority exists (if the guarantee were removed):** Boyer"Moore returns an arbitrary survivor  - always run the verification pass.
- **Even n with two elements each at n/2:** no strict majority  - relies on the statement's guarantee.

#### 18. Common Mistakes

1. Using `>= n/2` instead of `> n/2` - wrong when two elements tie at exactly half.
2. Returning `candidate` without noting the existence guarantee (or without a verification pass).
3. Resetting `candidate = x` **and** `count = 1` when `count > 0` but `x != candidate` - cancellation must not adopt the new element.
4. Assuming sorted order is needed - the problem says nothing about order.

#### 19. Interview Questions

**Q1. Why does the majority element always win the cancellation game**
> Because non-majority elements are strictly fewer than majority elements, every cancellation pairs a non-majority with a majority; at least one majority vote can never be cancelled.

**Q2. Solve it with O(1) space.**
> Boyer"Moore: candidate + counter, as above.

**Q3. What if the threshold were n/3 instead of n/2**
> At most two candidates can exceed n/3, so keep two candidates and two counters (Majority Element II) - see Problem 003.

**Q4. Can you do it in one pass with a HashMap**
> Yes for counting, but you must check after (or during) counting; the one-pass HashMap version needs a final scan of the map - still O(n).

**Q5. Is sorting better**
> Sorting gives O(n log n) and then the middle element of a sorted majority array is the answer - correct but slower than O(n).

#### 20. Variations

1. **Majority Element II (appears > n/3):** keep at most two candidates, then verify both.
2. **Verify a claimed majority (no guarantee):** one extra counting pass, O(n)/O(1).
3. **Majority element in a stream:** same algorithm with periodic verification checkpoints.

#### 21. Related Problems

Problem 003 (Majority Element II), Problem 018 (First Missing Positive), Problem 162 (Top K Frequent Elements).

#### 22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds

> "The straightforward approach is a HashMap frequency count in O(n) time and O(n) space. Since the element appears more than half the time, I can do better: Boyer"Moore voting keeps a candidate and a counter - same element increments, different element decrements, counter zero adopts a new candidate. Because every non-majority element can cancel at most one majority element, a majority element always survives. That gives O(n) time and O(1) space. The statement guarantees a majority exists; otherwise I'd add one verification pass."

</details>

### Problem 003 - Majority Element II

**Category:** Arrays + Hashing | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Frequency counting (Boyer"Moore generalization)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an array of size n, find **all** elements that appear **more than ŒŠn/3Œ‹ times**. At most two such elements can exist; return them in any order.

#### 2. Input
- `int[] nums`, length n, unsorted, may contain negatives and duplicates.

#### 3. Output
- `List<Integer>` of every value occurring **strictly more than n/3** times (possibly empty).

#### 4. Constraints
- `1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4`
- `-10^9 <= nums[i] <= 10^9`
- **No guarantee** that such an element exists  - verification is required.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [3, 2, 3]
Output: [3]
Explanation: n = 3  - threshold = 3/3 = 1, need > 1. 3 appears 2 times. œ"

Input:  nums = [1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 3]
Output: [1, 3]
Explanation: n = 8  - threshold = 8/3 = 2 (integer division), need > 2.
             1 appears 3 times, 3 appears 4 times, 2 appears 2 times (not > 2).

Edge case:
Input:  nums = [1, 2]
Output: [1, 2]
Explanation: n = 2  - threshold = 2/3 = 0, need > 0  - any element that occurs qualifies.
             Saying this out loud in an interview shows you check integer division.
```

#### 6. Pattern
**Frequency counting**, or Boyer"Moore voting generalized to two candidates.

#### 7. How to Recognize This Pattern
- *"appears more than n/k times"*  - by the pigeonhole principle at most `k - 1` values can qualify.
- `n/2` (Problem 002) is the special case k = 2; `n/3` means two candidate slots.
- If the problem asks for O(1) space  - two-slot voting. Otherwise a HashMap is simpler and easier to defend.

<details>
<summary><b>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</b></summary>

#### 8-10. Brute Force  - Why It Fails  - Optimal
**Brute:** for each distinct value, scan and count  - **O(n²) time, O(1) space**.
**Bottleneck:** re-scanning the whole array per candidate; counts from earlier scans are thrown away.
**Optimal (HashMap):** one pass to build frequencies, then collect keys above the threshold  - **O(n) time, O(n) space**.
**Optimal (O(1) space):** keep two candidates `c1, c2` and counters `k1, k2`:
1. `x == c1`  - `k1++`; else `x == c2`  - `k2++`.
2. Else if `k1 == 0`  - adopt: `c1 = x, k1 = 1`.
3. Else if `k2 == 0`  - adopt: `c2 = x, k2 = 1`.
4. Else  - `k1--, k2--` (cancel one occurrence from each).
5. **Verify** both candidates with a counting pass and keep those above threshold.

#### 11. Why It Works
At most two elements can strictly exceed n/3 (three values each above n/3 would sum to more than n occurrences). Voting is a two-slot cancellation game: a third distinct value decrements both candidates, so a value that keeps winning against everything must be one of the two heavy hitters. But since **existence is not guaranteed**, survivors can be impostors - the verification pass is not optional; it's what makes the algorithm correct in general.

#### 12-13. Steps & Java
```java
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> majorityElement(int[] nums) {
        int c1 = 0, c2 = 0, k1 = 0, k2 = 0;
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (x == c1) k1++;
            else if (x == c2) k2++;
            else if (k1 == 0) { c1 = x; k1 = 1; }
            else if (k2 == 0) { c2 = x; k2 = 1; }
            else { k1--; k2--; }
        }
        k1 = 0; k2 = 0;
        for (int x : nums) {
            if (x == c1) k1++;
            else if (x == c2) k2++;
        }
        List<Integer> res = new ArrayList<>();
        if (k1 > nums.length / 3) res.add(c1);
        if (c2 != c1 && k2 > nums.length / 3) res.add(c2);
        return res;
    }
}
```

#### 14. Code Explanation
- The `c2 != c1` guard exists because if the second slot was never adopted, `c2` still holds its initial value `0`, which might be a legitimate value elsewhere in the array - we'd double-count or add a phantom.
- Comparisons happen **before** adoption, so a value matching an existing candidate never wastes a slot.
- Verification reuses the same comparison chain with fresh counters - clean, no extra structures.

#### 15. Dry Run
`nums = [1, 1, 1, 3, 3, 2, 2, 3]`, threshold = 8/3 = 2 (need ‰¥ 3)

| Step | x | Action | (c1, k1) | (c2, k2) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | k1 == 0  - adopt | (1, 1) | (0, 0) |
| 2 | 1 | match c1 | (1, 2) | (0, 0) |
| 3 | 1 | match c1 | (1, 3) | (0, 0) |
| 4 | 3 | k2 == 0  - adopt | (1, 3) | (3, 1) |
| 5 | 3 | match c2 | (1, 3) | (3, 2) |
| 6 | 2 | neither, both > 0  - cancel | (1, 2) | (3, 1) |
| 7 | 2 | neither, both > 0  - cancel | (1, 1) | (3, 0) |
| 8 | 3 | k2 == 0  - adopt | (1, 1) | (3, 1) |

Verification pass: count(1) = 3 > 2 œ", count(3) = 4 > 2 œ"  - `[1, 3]`.

#### 16. Complexity
**Time O(n)**: voting pass + verification pass = 2n steps. **Space O(1)**: two candidates, two counters. HashMap alternative: O(n) time (nearly one pass) and O(n) space for distinct values.

#### 17. Edge Cases
- n = 1: threshold 0  - the single element qualifies.
- All identical: only `c1` ever adopted  - output must contain one element, not duplicates.
- No value clears the threshold  - empty list.
- Negative values / `Integer.MIN_VALUE`: only comparisons are performed, no arithmetic on values.
- Exact ties at n/3 (e.g., 3 values each at exactly n/3)  - must **not** be reported (strictly greater).
- Element 0 with `c2` never adopted  - the `c2 != c1` guard.

#### 18. Common Mistakes
1. Skipping verification when existence is not guaranteed.
2. Using `>= n/3` instead of `> n/3`.
3. Pushing `c2` unconditionally  - phantom `0` in the answer.
4. Forgetting that the output order doesn't matter (don't sort unnecessarily).

#### 19. Interview Questions
**Q: Why can there be at most two such elements**  - Three values each strictly above n/3 would total more than n occurrences - impossible.
**Q: HashMap or voting**  - HashMap is O(n)/O(n) and clearer; voting is O(n)/O(1). I'd give HashMap first, then optimize when space is requested.
**Q: What changes for n/4**  - Three candidate slots, same structure, then verify each.
**Q: Why must I verify here but not in Majority Element**  - The first problem guarantees a majority exists; this one does not, so voting can end with impostors.

#### 20. Variations
1. General `n/k` with `k - 1` slots.
2. "Return the element with frequency > n/3 in a stream"  - periodic re-verification.
3. "Count occurrences of every element"  - plain HashMap frequency (baseline #29).

#### 21. Related Problems
Problem 002, Problem 162 (Top K Frequent Elements), Problem 173-ish (Leaderboard patterns in Phase 8).

#### 22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds
> "Because only two values can appear more than n/3 of the time, I keep two candidates with counters - the Boyer"Moore idea with two slots. A match increments, an unclaimed value adopts an empty slot, and a third distinct value cancels one count from each candidate. Since this problem doesn't guarantee that such an element exists, I finish with a counting pass and only keep candidates that actually beat the threshold. O(n) time, O(1) space."

</details>

---

### Problem 004 - Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

**Category:** Arrays + Hashing | **Difficulty:** Easy | **Pattern:** Running minimum (one-pass greedy)

#### 1. Problem Statement
You are given the price of a stock on each day. Choose one day to buy and a **later** day to sell to maximize profit. Return the maximum profit; if no profitable trade exists, return 0.

#### 2. Input
- `int[] prices` - prices[i] is the price on day i (`n >= 1`).

#### 3. Output
- `int` - maximum profit, or 0 when every buy/sell pair loses money.

#### 4. Constraints
- `1 <= prices.length <= 10^5`
- `0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4`
- The buy day must be strictly before the sell day.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]
Output: 5
Explanation: Buy day 2 (price 1), sell day 5 (price 6)  - profit 5.

Input:  prices = [7, 6, 4, 3, 1]
Output: 0
Explanation: Prices only fall  - do nothing  - profit 0.

Edge case:
Input:  prices = [5]
Output: 0
Explanation: Only one day - you could buy but never sell.
```

#### 6. Pattern
**One-pass running minimum** (greedy). Not a sliding window - you only need the cheapest price seen so far.

#### 7. How to Recognize This Pattern
- Clue: *"one transaction"* + *"buy before sell"*.
- The shape is: for each j, best value ending at j = `prices[j] - min(prices[0..j-1])`.
- Recurring family: **"max of (current value ˆ' best value before it)"**  - scan while tracking the best so far. Same skeleton appears in Kadane (Problem 005), Container With Most Water (Problem 046), and stock-with-fee variants.

<details>
<summary><b>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</b></summary>

#### 8-10. Brute Force  - Why It Fails  - Optimal
**Brute:** try every pair `(i, j)` with `i < j`, keep the max of `prices[j] - prices[i]`  - **O(n²) time, O(1) space**.
**Bottleneck:** for each sell day you re-scan the entire prefix looking for the cheapest buy - recomputing "minimum of the prefix" n times.
**Optimal:** single pass with `minSoFar` and `best`. For each price: first `best = max(best, price - minSoFar)`, then `minSoFar = min(minSoFar, price)`.

#### 11. Why It Works
The answer is some pair (buy day i, sell day j) with i < j. For the optimal j, the optimal i is exactly the minimum price in the prefix before j - which `minSoFar` holds when we reach j. So each sell day is evaluated against its best possible buy, and every candidate pair's sell day is visited  - the optimum is covered. Computing profit **before** updating `minSoFar` guarantees the buy is strictly earlier.

#### 12-13. Steps & Java
1. `minSoFar = prices[0]`, `best = 0`.
2. For each price p: `best = max(best, p - minSoFar)`; then `minSoFar = min(minSoFar, p)`.
3. Return `best`.

```java
class Solution {
    public int maxProfit(int[] prices) {
        int minSoFar = prices[0];
        int best = 0;
        for (int price : prices) {
            best = Math.max(best, price - minSoFar);
            minSoFar = Math.min(minSoFar, price);
        }
        return best;
    }
}
```

#### 14. Code Explanation
- `best = 0` at the start encodes "not trading is always allowed".
- The body's line order is the whole algorithm: *evaluate against the past, then absorb today into the past*.
- No array is allocated: the state is two integers.

#### 15. Dry Run
`prices = [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]`

| Step | price | minSoFar before | price - minSoFar | best after | minSoFar after |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 7 | 7 | 0 | 0 | 7 |
| 2 | 1 | 7 | -6 | 0 | 1 |
| 3 | 5 | 1 | 4 | 4 | 1 |
| 4 | 3 | 1 | 2 | 4 | 1 |
| 5 | 6 | 1 | 5 | **5** | 1 |
| 6 | 4 | 1 | 3 | 5 | 1 |

Result: **5** œ" (buy at 1, sell at 6)

#### 16. Complexity
**Time O(n)** - one constant-time operation per day. With n up to 10^5, O(n²) would be 10^10 operations and would time out, which is how you *justify* the approach rather than just asserting it.
**Space O(1)** - only `minSoFar` and `best`; the input array is given and not counted as auxiliary space.

#### 17. Edge Cases
- Strictly decreasing prices  - `best` stays 0.
- Single element  - 0.
- All equal prices  - 0.
- Minimum price on the last day  - never becomes a profitable sell, `best` unaffected.
- Maximum on the first day  - still fine; other days compare against it.
- Empty input (if allowed by the variant)  - return 0 without reading `prices[0]`.

#### 18. Common Mistakes
1. Updating `minSoFar` before computing profit  - allows same-day buy/sell.
2. Initializing `best = Integer.MIN_VALUE` and returning a negative number for decreasing arrays (answer must be 0).
3. Starting the loop at index 1 while initializing `minSoFar = Integer.MAX_VALUE` - then the first price is skipped incorrectly.
4. Solving it with Kadane's full reset logic - unnecessary here (and Kadane's reset changes the meaning).

#### 19. Interview Questions
**Q: Why not sort the prices**  - Sorting destroys chronology; the constraint "buy before sell" is about days, not values.
**Q: Why is this greedy correct**  - For every candidate sell day we pair with the true prefix minimum, so no pair can be better than one we evaluated.
**Q: What if there were at most 2 transactions**  - Two-pass DP (left-to-right best, right-to-left best), O(n)/O(n), or a state machine.
**Q: What about cooldown/fees**  - State-machine DP with hold/sold/rest states - see Problem 296.
**Q: Space optimizable**  - Already O(1).

#### 20. Variations
1. **Stock II (unlimited trades):** sum every positive consecutive rise.
2. **Stock with cooldown (Problem 296):** three-state DP.
3. **Stock IV (at most k trades):** DP with transaction counter, O(n·k).
4. **"Max difference with j > i"** on arbitrary arrays: identical algorithm.

#### 21. Related Problems
Problem 005 (Kadane - same running-best skeleton), Problem 046 (Container With Most Water), Problem 296 (DP state machine).

#### 22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds
> "I scan left to right keeping two values: the cheapest price seen so far and the best profit so far. For each day, the best trade ending that day is today's price minus the cheapest earlier price - I update the answer first, then fold today's price into the minimum, which keeps the buy strictly before the sell. Every possible sell day is paired with its optimal buy, so nothing is missed: O(n) time, O(1) space. If prices only fall, the answer stays zero, meaning I don't trade."

</details>

### Problem 005 - Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm)

**Category:** Arrays + Hashing | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Kadane (running best with reset)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array, find the **contiguous** subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. The subarray must contain at least one element.

#### 2. Input
- `int[] nums` - length n ‰¥ 1; values may be negative, zero, or positive.

#### 3. Output
- `int` - the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays.

#### 4. Constraints
- `1 <= nums.length <= 10^5`
- `-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4`
(The 10^5 length rules out O(n²) enumeration of all subarrays.)

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]
Output: 6
Explanation: The subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] sums to 6.

Input:  nums = [-3, -1, -7]
Output: -1
Explanation: All elements are negative  - the answer is the largest single element (-1).
             This is the classic trap: an answer of 0 would be wrong.

Edge case:
Input:  nums = [5]
Output: 5
Explanation: Only one element.
```

#### 6. Pattern
**Kadane's algorithm** - a dynamic-programming scan written as two lines.

#### 7. How to Recognize This Pattern
- The problem asks for a **contiguous** range and an **optimal sum** (max/min), with **negatives allowed**.
- Constraint `n ‰¤ 10^5`  - you cannot enumerate all O(n²) subarrays.
- Clues: *"largest sum subarray"*, *"maximum profit over a range"*, *"most balanced"* (via sums).
- Key discriminator vs sliding window: a window needs a condition that lets you shrink safely; with negatives, "sum is bad" doesn't mean "shrink" - instead you **restart**. That restart is Kadane.

<details>
<summary><b>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</b></summary>

#### 8. Brute Force Approach
**Idea:** compute the sum of every possible subarray and keep the maximum.
**Algorithm:** for each start i, running = 0; for each end j ‰¥ i: running += nums[j]; best = max(best, running).
**Why it works:** every subarray is enumerated.
**Time O(n²)** (or O(n³) if you re-sum naively). **Space O(1)**.

#### 9. Why Brute Force Is Not Ideal
The inner loop **recomputes a running sum that shares almost everything with the previous one**: the sum from i to j+1 differs from i to j by exactly `nums[j+1]`. Worse, each starting point i re-derives sums that a single left-to-right pass could produce incrementally. At n = 10^5, O(n²) ‰ˆ 10^10 operations  - timeout.

#### 10. Optimal Approach
Define two quantities while scanning:
- `bestEndingHere` = the maximum sum of a subarray that **ends exactly at the current index**.
- `bestOverall` = the max of those across the scan.

Transition for each element x:
1. Either extend the previous ending subarray: `bestEndingHere + x`
2. Or start fresh at x: `x`
3. `bestEndingHere = max(x, bestEndingHere + x)`
4. `bestOverall = max(bestOverall, bestEndingHere)`

#### 11. Why the Optimal Approach Works
**Why is the recurrence right** Any subarray ending at index i either (a) contains index i-1, in which case its sum = (best subarray ending at i-1) + nums[i], or (b) consists of nums[i] alone. Taking the max of those two covers every subarray ending at i - no others exist.

**Why is resetting safe** If `bestEndingHere` is negative, carrying it forward can only make the sum worse. Starting fresh at the current element discards a harmful prefix. This is why Kadane *drops* a losing prefix instead of shrinking a window.

**Why don't we miss the answer** `bestOverall` is the max over *all* end positions of *the best subarray ending there* - and every subarray has an end position. So the global optimum is included.

**Connection to DP:** `bestEndingHere` is the memoized value of `f(i) = max subarray sum ending at i`; `f(i) = max(nums[i], f(i-1) + nums[i])`. Kadane is memoization in O(1) space - worth saying, it impresses interviewers and links to Phase 13.

#### 12. Algorithm / Steps
1. `bestEndingHere = nums[0]`, `bestOverall = nums[0]`.
2. For i from 1 to n-1: `bestEndingHere = max(nums[i], bestEndingHere + nums[i])`; `bestOverall = max(bestOverall, bestEndingHere)`.
3. Return `bestOverall`.

#### 13. Java Solution
```java
class Solution {
    public int maxSubArray(int[] nums) {
        int bestEndingHere = nums[0];
        int bestOverall = nums[0];
        for (int i = 1; i < nums.length; i++) {
            bestEndingHere = Math.max(nums[i], bestEndingHere + nums[i]);
            bestOverall = Math.max(bestOverall, bestEndingHere);
        }
        return bestOverall;
    }
}
```

#### 14. Code Explanation
- Both variables start at `nums[0]`, **not** 0 - this is what makes all-negative arrays work.
- `Math.max(nums[i], bestEndingHere + nums[i])` is the entire recurrence; the second line is bookkeeping for the answer.
- Note the order: compute the new `bestEndingHere` before comparing to `bestOverall`.

#### 15. Detailed Dry Run
`nums = [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]`

| Step | i | nums[i] | bestEndingHere + nums[i] | bestEndingHere (after) | bestOverall (after) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| init | 0 | -2 | - | -2 | -2 |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | -2 + 1 = -1 | max(1, -1) = 1 | max(-2, 1) = 1 |
| 2 | 2 | -3 | 1 + (-3) = -2 | max(-3, -2) = -2 | 1 |
| 3 | 3 | 4 | -2 + 4 = 2 | max(4, 2) = 4 | 4 |
| 4 | 4 | -1 | 4 + (-1) = 3 | 3 | 4 |
| 5 | 5 | 2 | 3 + 2 = 5 | 5 | 5 |
| 6 | 6 | 1 | 5 + 1 = 6 | 6 | **6** |
| 7 | 7 | -5 | 6 + (-5) = 1 | 1 | 6 |
| 8 | 8 | 4 | 1 + 4 = 5 | 5 | 6 |

Answer: **6** from subarray [4, -1, 2, 1].

Second run `nums = [-3, -1, -7]`: bestEndingHere: -3  - max(-1, -3-1) = -1  - max(-7, -1-7) = -7; bestOverall: -3  - -1  - -1. Answer **-1** œ"

#### 16. Complexity Analysis
**Time: O(n)** - exactly one pass, constant work per element. The recurrence reuses the previous ending-sum instead of recomputing subarray sums, which is what removes the O(n²) loop.
**Space: O(1)** auxiliary - two integers. If you wrote the DP as `dp[i]` for each index you'd use O(n) space; the observation that `dp[i]` depends only on `dp[i-1]` lets you keep one variable. Input space is O(n) (given).

#### 17. Edge Cases
- **All negative:** answer is the largest single element (initializing to 0 gives a wrong 0).
- **Single element:** returns it.
- **All zeros:** returns 0 - valid since elements must be non-empty.
- **Alternating signs:** reset behavior picks the largest positive single value if extending hurts.
- **Integer overflow:** n ‰¤ 10^5 with |nums[i]| ‰¤ 10^4  - max |sum| ‰¤ 10^9, fits `int`; for larger constraints say you'd use `long`.
- **Empty array:** not allowed by constraints (return 0 defensively if asked).

#### 18. Common Mistakes
1. Initializing `best = 0`  - wrong for all-negative arrays.
2. Returning `bestEndingHere` instead of `bestOverall` (that's only the best *ending at the last index*).
3. Forgetting to include the current element in the comparison (`max(0, ...)` variants that drop negatives).
4. Confusing this with a sliding window: you cannot "shrink while sum > K" here - there's no K.
5. Solving a *return the subarray* variant but returning only the sum's indices without tracking them (start/end need extra bookkeeping).

#### 19. Interview Questions
**Q: Why start both variables at `nums[0]` rather than 0**  - Because at least one element must be chosen; with all negatives, 0 would represent an empty subarray.
**Q: Isn't this just DP**  - Yes: `f(i) = max(nums[i], f(i-1) + nums[i])` is the recurrence, and Kadane stores only the last value  - O(1) space.
**Q: Can you return the subarray itself**  - Track a `start`/`end`: reset `start = i` whenever `bestEndingHere = nums[i]`, and update `end = i` when `bestOverall` improves.
**Q: What if the array can be rotated**  - Either try each rotation (expensive) or note that the max subarray of a rotated array is either a wrap-around sum of a min-subarray complement or a normal Kadane result.
**Q: Minimum subarray sum**  - Same code with `min` instead of `max` (or negate the array).

#### 20. Variations
1. **Return the subarray indices too**  - track start/end as above.
2. **Maximum product subarray**  - different state (keep min and max, because a negative - negative can become large) - Problem 006.
3. **Circular maximum subarray**  - max(Kadane, totalSum - minSubarray).
4. **Subarray sum ‰¥ / = K**  - prefix sum + HashMap, Problems 008-010.
5. **Divide array into k parts to maximize the minimum part sum**  - binary search on answer (Phase 4).

#### 21. Related Problems
Problem 006 (Maximum Product Subarray), Problem 008 (Subarray Sum Equals K), Problem 011 (Product of Array Except Self); the Kadane-as-DP connection is made explicit in Phase 13 (`f(i) = max(nums[i], f(i-1) + f(i))` with `f(i)` = best sum ending at i).

#### 22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds
> "I use Kadane's algorithm. I keep the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index: either I extend the previous one or I start fresh at the current element - I take the max of those two. If the accumulated sum so far is negative it can only hurt, so I drop that prefix. Along the way I track the overall maximum of those ending sums. Every subarray has an ending index, so the global best is covered. It's O(n) time and O(1) space, and I initialize both variables to the first element so all-negative arrays are handled correctly."

</details>
