### Problem 031 - Minimum Window Substring

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium-Hard | **Pattern:** Shortest window containing all characters of a pattern

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given strings `s` and `t`, return the **smallest window** of `s` that contains **every character of `t`**, including duplicates (if `t` has two `a`'s, the window must contain at least two `a`'s). If no such window exists, return `""`.

#### 2. Input
- `String s` (text), `String t` (pattern); `t` may contain characters absent from `s`.

#### 3. Output
- `String` - the minimum-length window of `s` covering all of `t`, or `""`.

#### 4. Constraints
- `1 <= s.length, t.length <= 10^4`
- `s` and `t` consist of English letters (uppercase/lowercase distinguishable).

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  s = "ADOBECODEBANC", t = "ABC"
Output: "BANC"
Explanation: Windows "ADOBEC" (6) and "CODEBA" (6) also cover A,B,C - but "BANC" has length 4.

Input:  s = "a", t = "a"
Output: "a"

Edge case:
Input:  s = "a", t = "aa"
Output: ""
Explanation: t needs two 'a's but s has one  - impossible.
```

#### 6. Pattern
**Shortest valid window** with a *"satisfied requirements"* counter (the most general form of the window template).

#### 7. How to Recognize This Pattern
- *"minimum/shortest substring that contains/covers all of¦"*  - expand until satisfied, then shrink while still satisfied, recording inside the loop.
- Requirements with duplicates  - counts, not sets; the *"formed"* counter tracks how many requirement-letters currently meet their quota.
- This problem is the capstone of Phase 2: it combines fixed-window counting (024), the shortest-shrink rule (028), and an incremental "satisfaction" flag.

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - for every start i, scan forward accumulating counts until the window covers `t`, record length; O(n² - k) worst case (or O(n²) with incremental counts and a check loop).
**9. Why It Fails** - each start re-derives coverage already computed for its neighbours; worst case quadratic, and the coverage check itself can be O(alphabet) per window.
**10. Optimal Approach** - two counts plus one counter:
1. `need[c]` = required count of character c from `t`; `have[c]` = count in the current window.
2. `formed` = number of distinct characters whose `have[c] >= need[c]`; `required` = number of distinct characters in `t`.
3. Expand `right`. When a character reaches its quota, `formed++`.
4. **While `formed == required`**: record `best = (right-left+1, left)` if smaller, then remove `s[left]`; if that drops a count below its quota, `formed--`; `left++`.

**11. Why It Works** - `formed == required` is an exact, O(1) encoding of "window covers t" (each requirement class counted once, duplicates handled by the `have >= need` test). Shrinking while still fully covered finds the **shortest** window for this right edge; stopping the moment coverage breaks guarantees we never discard a viable window. Every valid window has a right edge, so the min over all right edges is the global minimum. Coverage is monotone in a useful direction: extending can only *add* coverage (never remove it), shrinking can only *remove* it - which is precisely what lets both loops be linear.

**12. Steps** - build `need`, `formed = 0`, `required = distinct in t`  - expand; update `formed` when a quota is met  - while fully formed: try updating the best window, evict left (adjusting `formed` when a quota breaks)  - return the best slice (or `""`).

**13. Java Solution**
```java
class Solution {
    public String minWindow(String s, String t) {
        if (t.length() > s.length()) return "";
        Map<Character, Integer> need = new HashMap<>();
        for (char c : t.toCharArray()) need.put(c, need.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
        Map<Character, Integer> have = new HashMap<>();
        int required = need.size(), formed = 0;
        int left = 0, bestLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE, bestStart = 0;

        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            char c = s.charAt(right);
            have.put(c, have.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
            if (need.containsKey(c) && have.get(c).equals(need.get(c))) formed++;

            while (formed == required && left <= right) {
                if (right - left + 1 < bestLen) {
                    bestLen = right - left + 1;
                    bestStart = left;
                }
                char d = s.charAt(left);
                have.put(d, have.get(d) - 1);
                if (need.containsKey(d) && have.get(d) < need.get(d)) formed--;
                left++;
            }
        }
        return bestLen == Integer.MAX_VALUE  "" : s.substring(bestStart, bestStart + bestLen);
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `formed` increments only when a count **reaches exactly** its quota (so it counts each requirement class once, not once per occurrence) and decrements only when a count **drops below** its quota - this exact-pairing is what keeps `formed == required` equivalent to "fully covered". `bestLen` starts at MAX_VALUE so an uncovered string naturally returns `""`.

**15. Dry Run** - `s = "ADOBECODEBANC"`, `t = "ABC"` (need: A:1, B:1, C:1; required = 3)

| right | char | formed after add | shrink loop (while formed == 3) | left after | best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | A | 1 | none | 0 | - |
| 1 | D | 1 | none | 0 | - |
| 2 | O | 1 | none | 0 | - |
| 3 | B | 2 | none | 0 | - |
| 4 | E | 2 | none | 0 | - |
| 5 | C | 3 | record [0..5] len 6  - best 6@0; evict A  - formed 2 | 1 | 6 @0 |
| 6 | O | 2 | none | 1 | 6 |
| 7 | D | 2 | none | 1 | 6 |
| 8 | E | 2 | none | 1 | 6 |
| 9 | B | 2 (B:2 ‰  need 1  - no change) | none | 1 | 6 |
| 10 | A | 3 | window [1..10] len 10 (not better); evict D, O, B, E (all still formed); at [5..10] len 6 not < 6; evict C  - formed 2 | 6 | 6 @0 |
| 11 | N | 2 | none | 6 | 6 |
| 12 | C | 3 | [6..12] len 7 (no); evict O  - still formed; evict D  - [8..12] len 5  - best 5@8; evict E  - [9..12] len 4  - **best 4@9**; evict B  - formed 2 | 10 | **4 @9** |

Result: `s.substring(9, 13)` = **`"BANC"`** œ" (covers A@10, B@9, C@12).

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n)**: `right` moves n times, `left` moves at most n times total; map operations are O(1) average. **Space O(1)** in practice (‰¤ 52 keys for letters) - O(k) where k is the number of distinct characters in `t`.

**17. Edge Cases** - `t` longer than `s`  - `""`; characters in `t` missing from `s`  - `""`; `s` equal to `t` (window is the whole string); duplicates in `t` (the `have >= need` test); overlapping windows; case sensitivity; a window that must extend to the very end of `s`; `t` with one unique character repeated ("aaa" in "aa"  - empty).

**18. Common Mistakes** - using a set instead of counts (duplicates break it); incrementing `formed` every time a count is ‰¥ quota (should be only on the crossing); recording the window **after** shrinking out of validity; forgetting to check `t` characters that don't exist in `s`; returning the length when the substring was asked (or vice versa).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why a `formed` counter instead of comparing maps**  - Comparing maps is O(alphabet) per step; `formed` makes each check O(1) - the interviewer wants to see that you know this.
**Q: What's the invariant**  - After the inner loop, the window `[left, right]` is the shortest fully-covering window ending at `right` (or is not fully covering).
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n) time, O(alphabet) space - each index moves across the boundary at most once.
**Q: What if `t` had no duplicates**  - Same algorithm; the quota test degenerates to presence (count ‰¥ 1).

**20. Variations** - Minimum window **sequence** containing a subsequence (harder, greedy matching); smallest window covering characters of a pattern with wildcards (Problem 031 with ``); permutation in string (030, fixed size); count windows covering all pattern chars (at-most difference trick).

**21. Related Problems** - Problem 024, 028, 030, 032.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I keep two histograms: what the pattern requires, and what's currently in the window. I also keep a counter of how many character classes have met their quota - that lets me test coverage in O(1) instead of comparing maps. I expand right until the window is fully covered, then shrink from the left while it stays covered, recording the best window each time it's still valid. Every index moves in or out once, so O(n) time and constant space."

</details>

### Problem 032 - Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Variable window + frequency map + distinct counter

#### 1. Problem Statement
Find the length of the **longest contiguous substring** of `s` that contains **at most `k` distinct characters**.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `String s`, `int k`.
- **Output:** `int` - maximum substring length with ‰¤ k distinct characters (0 if `k == 0` or `s` empty).
- **Constraints:** `0 <= s.length <= 5 * 10^4`, `0 <= k <= 50` (varies; up to `s.length`), `s` = letters/digits/symbols.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  s = "eceba", k = 2
Output: 3        ("ece")

Input:  s = "aa", k = 1
Output: 2

Edge case: k = 0  - 0 ; s = "abc" with k = 3  - 3
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** variable window with a **distinct-count** constraint (the K-generalization of Fruit Into Baskets).

**Recognition:** "longest substring with *at most k different/unique kinds*"  - frequency map + `distinct` counter + shrink while `distinct > k`. If the statement said *exactly k*, use the at-most difference trick (Problem 033).

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - try every O(n²) substring, count distinct with a set  - O(n²) or O(n³).
**9. Why It Fails** - distinct counts for overlapping windows are recomputed from scratch; n = 5-10^4  - 2.5-10^9.
**10. Optimal Approach** - expand `right`, increment `count[c]` (if it becomes 1, `distinct++`); while `distinct > k`, decrement `count[s[left]]` (if it hits 0, `distinct--`) and `left++`; record `max(right-left+1)`.

**11. Why It Works** - after the shrink the window is legal (‰¤ k distinct), so it is a candidate; any longer window ending at `right` would need a smaller `left`, which the loop proves impossible (it stopped only when legality was restored). Since validity degrades monotonically as you extend, no legal window is skipped, and `left`/`right` each move n times  - O(n).

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int lengthOfLongestSubstringKDistinct(String s, int k) {
        if (k == 0) return 0;
        Map<Character, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
        int left = 0, distinct = 0, best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            char c = s.charAt(right);
            count.put(c, count.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
            if (count.get(c) == 1) distinct++;
            while (distinct > k) {
                char d = s.charAt(left++);
                count.put(d, count.get(d) - 1);
                if (count.get(d) == 0) distinct--;
            }
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        return best;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `distinct` changes only at count 1 (birth) and 0 (death) of a key; using `map.size()` would also work **only if** dead keys are removed (this code keeps dead keys at 0 - hence the explicit counter, which is the safer habit).

**15. Dry Run** - `s = "eceba"`, `k = 2`

| right | char | counts | distinct | shrink | left | best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | e | e:1 | 1 | no | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | c | e:1,c:1 | 2 | no | 0 | 2 |
| 2 | e | e:2,c:1 | 2 | no | 0 | 3 |
| 3 | b | e:2,c:1,b:1 | 3 | evict s[0]='e'  - e:1 (alive  - still 3); evict s[1]='c'  - c:0  - distinct 2  - stop | 2 | 3 |
| 4 | a | e:1,b:1,a:1 | 3 | evict s[2]='e'  - e:0  - distinct 2  - stop | 3 | 3 |

Result **3** ("ece") œ"

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n)**: each index enters/leaves once, O(1) map ops. **Space O(k)**: at most k+1 keys are alive in the window (plus dead keys if you don't remove them - remove them or use the counter).

**17. Edge Cases** - `k = 0`  - 0; `k ‰¥` number of distinct chars  - n; empty string; all identical (answer n); k = 1 (longest equal run); duplicate keys left at count 0 (affects `map.size()`).

**18. Common Mistakes** - using `map.size()` while leaving dead entries; recording the answer before shrinking; handling `k = 0` (infinite loop risk if `distinct > 0` never drops below... it drops fine, but `best` must start at 0).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Exactly k instead of at most**  - `atMost(k) - atMost(k-1)`, one helper called twice (Problem 033).
**Q: Return the substring**  - Track `bestLeft`.
**Q: Difference from Fruit Into Baskets**  - Identical algorithm with `k` generalized to 2.

**20. Variations** - Fruit Into Baskets (029, k=2); exactly K distinct (033); longest with at most k *replacements* (027).

**21. Related Problems** - 025, 027, 029, 033.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Same window skeleton as before: expand right, track a frequency map and how many distinct characters are currently alive, and shrink from the left whenever a third (or (k+1)-th) character appears. Each shrink step removes one character from the window, so every index crosses the boundary at most once - O(n) time. The window is always legal when I record it, so the maximum length is the answer."

</details>

### Problem 033 - Subarrays with K Different Integers

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium-Hard | **Pattern:** At-most trick: `exactly(k) = atMost(k) ˆ' atMost(kˆ'1)`

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of **contiguous subarrays** that contain **exactly `k` distinct integers**.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums`, `int k`.
- **Output:** `int` - count of subarrays with exactly k distinct values.
- **Constraints:** `1 <= nums.length <= 2 * 10^4`, `1 <= k <= nums.length`, values up to 10^9 (so a **map**, not an array).

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [1,2,1,2,3], k = 2
Output: 9
Explanation: (0,1) (0,2) (0,3) (1,2) (1,3) (1,4) (2,3) (2,4) (3,4)  - 9 subarrays.

Input:  nums = [1,1,1], k = 1
Output: 6        (every subarray: 3 singles + 2 pairs + 1 triple)

Edge case: k > number of distinct values in nums  - 0.
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** sliding window **at-most counting** + subtraction trick.

**Recognition:** *"exactly k distinct"* over contiguous subarrays. Directly counting "exactly" is hard because a window with k distinct can't safely shrink (removing an element may keep it at k, so the loop has no monotone exit). The fix: count windows with **at most** k (easy, monotone) and subtract **at most** kˆ'1.

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - enumerate all O(n²) subarrays, count distinct in each with a set  - O(n²) time (O(n³) if rebuilt naively), O(k) space.
**9. Why It Fails** - distinct counts are recomputed for every range; n = 2-10^4  - 4-10^8+ operations. More importantly it ignores the structural insight that "exactly" is a *difference* of two "at most" counts.
**10. Optimal Approach** - define `atMost(k)` = number of subarrays with **‰¤ k** distinct: expand right; while `distinct > k` shrink left (monotone!); every time the window is legal, **add `right - left + 1`** - because all subarrays ending at `right` that start at ‰¥ `left` are legal (shorter suffixes of a legal window are also legal since removing elements can't increase distinct count). Then `exactly(k) = atMost(k) - atMost(k-1)`.

**11. Why It Works** - for "at most", once the window `[left..right]` is legal, **every** suffix window `[i..right]` with `i ‰¥ left` is also legal (distinct count only decreases as the start moves right)  - that's `right - left + 1` valid subarrays ending at `right`, and the shrink loop guarantees we stop exactly before the first illegal start. Summing over `right` counts each legal subarray once.

For "exactly": every subarray with ‰¤ k distinct either has ‰¤ kˆ'1 or exactly k (disjoint cases)  - subtraction isolates exactly-k. Note that direct shrinking on "exactly k" fails: a window can stay at k after a shrink or drop below it, so validity is not monotone - this is the crux of the problem and the thing interviewers want you to articulate.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int subarraysWithKDistinct(int[] nums, int k) {
        return atMost(nums, k) - atMost(nums, k - 1);
    }
    private int atMost(int[] nums, int k) {
        if (k < 0) return 0;
        Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
        int left = 0, distinct = 0;
        long ans = 0;                 // count can exceed int for large n
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            if (count.getOrDefault(nums[right], 0) == 0) distinct++;
            count.put(nums[right], count.getOrDefault(nums[right], 0) + 1);
            while (distinct > k) {
                int x = nums[left++];
                count.put(x, count.get(x) - 1);
                if (count.get(x) == 0) distinct--;
            }
            ans += right - left + 1;
        }
        return (int) ans;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - the crucial line is `ans += right - left + 1` **inside** the loop (counting all legal endings) rather than `best = max(...)` (which would only measure length). `k < 1`  - `atMost(0) = 0` is guarded; the `k < 0` guard makes `exactly(0)` calls safe.

**15. Dry Run** - `nums = [1,2,1,2,3]`, computing `atMost(2)`

| right | value | distinct after | shrink | left | legal suffixes added (`right-left+1`) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 1 | none | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 2 | 2 | none | 0 | 2  - total 3 |
| 2 | 1 | 2 | none | 0 | 3  - total 6 |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | none | 0 | 4  - total 10 |
| 4 | 3 | 3 | evict 1 (idx0)  - 1:0  - distinct 2 | 1 | 4  - total 14 |

`atMost(2) = 14`. Now `atMost(1)`: windows with ‰¤1 distinct are the runs of equal values - `[1],[2],[1],[2],[3]`  - 5 (each single-element window plus no longer run since values alternate).

Cross-check `atMost(1)` with the same loop: r0  - +1 (left0); r1 (value 2, distinct 2 > 1)  - evict 1  - distinct 1, left 1  - +1 (total 2); r2 (1, distinct 2)  - evict 2  - left 2  - +1 (3); r3 (2, distinct 2)  - evict 1  - left 3  - +1 (4); r4 (3, distinct 2)  - evict 2  - left 4  - +1 (5). **atMost(1) = 5** œ"

`exactly(2) = 14 ˆ' 5 = 9` œ" matches the example.

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n)** per `atMost` call  - **O(n)** total (two passes). **Space O(k)** for the map.

**17. Edge Cases** - `k = 1` (count runs of equal values: each run of length L contributes L(L+1)/2); `k` greater than the number of distinct values (0 - `atMost` returns all n(n+1)/2 and the difference cancels); all elements identical; `k = 0` (0, guarded); very large counts (n = 2-10^4  - up to ~2-10^8 subarrays - fits `int`, but say you'd use `long` for larger n).

**18. Common Mistakes** - trying to shrink on the "exactly k" condition directly (not monotone  - wrong); forgetting `atMost(k-1)` needs `k-1 = 0  - 0` handling; adding `right-left+1` only when `distinct == k` (undercounts windows with fewer distinct); using arrays when values can be up to 10^9.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why not count directly**  - "Exactly k" isn't monotone: shrinking can keep k or reduce it, so the loop can't decide when to stop. "At most k" is monotone.
**Q: Why add `right-left+1`**  - Every suffix of a legal window is legal (fewer elements  - no more distinct values).
**Q: Complexity**  - Two linear passes, O(n) time, O(k) space.
**Q: Generalize**  - This trick appears for "exactly k zeros", "exactly k odds" (Problem 035), "at most k distinct in a stream", etc.

**20. Variations** - Count nice subarrays (035, exactly k odds); count subarrays with exactly k zeros; number of subarrays with at most k distinct (one `atMost` call only).

**21. Related Problems** - 029, 032, 035, 008 (prefix version for sums).

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Counting 'exactly k distinct' directly is unsafe because shrinking a window doesn't move the distinct count monotonically. So I count 'at most k' instead - which is monotone and easy: shrink while distinct exceeds k, then add right-left+1 to the answer because every suffix of that window is also legal. Then exactly-k is just atMost(k) minus atMost(k-1). Two linear passes, O(n) time, O(k) space."

</details>

### Problem 034 - Maximum Sum of Distinct Size K Subarrays

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Fixed window + distinctness check

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an array of integers and `k`, find the maximum sum of a **contiguous subarray of length exactly k** whose elements are **all distinct**. Return 0 if no such subarray exists.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums`, `int k`.
- **Output:** `int` - maximum sum of a length-k window with all distinct values (0 if none).
- **Constraints:** `1 <= nums.length <= 10^5`, `1 <= k <= nums.length`, values up to 10^5.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [4,4,4,3,1,2,3], k = 3
Output: 8
Explanation: [4,3,1] (indices 2,3,4) - all distinct, sum 8.
             [4,4,4] and [4,4,3] have duplicates  - rejected.

Input:  nums = [1,1,1], k = 2
Output: 0        (no length-2 window has distinct elements)
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** fixed window + **Set** of the window's elements.

**Recognition:** fixed length k + "all different/distinct/unique" + an aggregate (sum/max)  - window whose state includes a set (or a frequency map with a `distinct` counter).

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - build a set for every length-k window and sum it if all distinct  - O(n·k).
**9. Why It Fails** - the set and the sum are rebuilt per window although windows overlap by kˆ'1 elements.
**10. Optimal Approach** - one window: maintain a running `sum` and a `Set`. Add `nums[right]`; if the set size would exceed k (i.e., a duplicate entered), evict from the left until the duplicate is gone, subtracting evicted values from `sum`. When the window has exactly k elements, update `best`.

**11. Why It Works** - the window is always either (a) shorter than k while a duplicate is being evicted, or (b) of size k with all elements distinct - exactly the legal state. The invariant "set size == window length" is what *defines* all-distinct: if a duplicate were present, size < length. Evicting from the left until the offending value disappears guarantees the duplicate is removed (the set contains it, so we keep popping until we've passed its last occurrence).

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public long maxSubarrayDistinct(int[] nums, int k) {
        Set<Integer> window = new HashSet<>();
        long sum = 0, best = 0;
        int left = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            while (window.contains(nums[right])) {
                window.remove(nums[left]);
                sum -= nums[left++];
            }
            window.add(nums[right]);
            sum += nums[right];
            if (right - left + 1 == k) {
                best = Math.max(best, sum);
                window.remove(nums[left]);
                sum -= nums[left++];
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - two exits: (1) a duplicate entered  - pop until it's gone; (2) the window reached size k  - record the sum, then slide by one to make room for the next element. `sum` as `long` avoids overflow when values are large (10^5 - 10^5 = 10^10 > `int`).

**15. Dry Run** - `nums = [4,4,4,3,1,2,3]`, `k = 3`

| right | value | action | window after | sum | best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 4 | add | [4] | 4 | 0 |
| 1 | 4 | duplicate  - evict 4 (idx0)  - add | [4] | 4 | 0 |
| 2 | 4 | duplicate  - evict 4 (idx1)  - add | [4] | 4 | 0 |
| 3 | 3 | add, size 2 | [4,3] | 7 | 0 |
| 4 | 1 | add, size 3  - record | [4,3,1] | 8 | 8; then slide  - [3,1] |
| 5 | 2 | add, size 3  - record | [3,1,2] | 6 | 8; then slide  - [1,2] |
| 6 | 3 | add, size 3  - record | [1,2,3] | 6 | 8; slide |

Result **8** œ" (window `[4,3,1]` at indices 2..4).

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n):** each index is added once and removed once (the inner while moves `left` forward only). **Space O(k):** at most k elements live in the set.

**17. Edge Cases** - no valid window (all duplicates  - 0); k = 1 (max single element if all windows valid - always valid  - max element); k = n (check whole array); negative values (sum bookkeeping still fine); large sums (use `long`).

**18. Common Mistakes** - recording when size **‰¥** k instead of **==** k; forgetting to subtract evicted values from `sum`; using a set without a sum (or vice versa); not handling the duplicate-eviction loop (only evicting one element when the duplicate is deeper).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why a set instead of a map**  - We only need presence; a map would be needed if we counted frequencies.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n) amortized, O(k) space.
**Q: Variant: longest window with all distinct**  - Problem 026.

**20. Variations** - Max sum of size-k window (baseline #28, no distinctness); longest distinct substring (026); count windows with distinct elements (at-most trick).

**21. Related Problems** - 026, 028, baseline #28.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I keep a fixed-size window with a running sum and a HashSet of its elements. When a duplicate enters, I pop from the left until that value is gone; when the window reaches size k with no duplicates, I update the best sum and slide the window forward by one. Because left only advances, each element is added and removed once - O(n) time, O(k) space."

</details>

### Problem 035 - Count Nice Subarrays

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** At-most trick on "number of odd elements"

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, count the number of **contiguous subarrays** containing **exactly `k` odd numbers**.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums`, `int k`.
- **Output:** `int` - number of subarrays with exactly k odds.
- **Constraints:** `1 <= nums.length <= 5 * 10^4`, `1 <= k <= nums.length`.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [1,1,2,1,1], k = 2
Output: 5
Explanation: (0,1) (0,2) (1,3) (2,4) (3,4)  - each contains exactly two odds.

Input:  nums = [2,2,2,1,2,2,1,2,2], k = 2
Output: 16        (classic example from the standard problem set)

Edge case: k larger than the total number of odds  - 0.
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** sliding window counting with the **at-most subtraction** (`exactly(k) = atMost(k) ˆ' atMost(kˆ'1)`).

**Recognition:** "exactly k ¦ elements with a property" over contiguous subarrays  - the property count is monotone under shrinking (adding elements never decreases the count), so "at most k" is a legal window condition while "exactly k" is not  - subtract. Same reasoning as Problem 033 with "distinct integers" replaced by "odd numbers".

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - all O(n²) subarrays, count odds in each  - O(n²).
**9. Why It Fails** - overlapping subarrays re-count the same odds; also it misses the structural trick.
**10. Optimal Approach** - convert odds to 1 and evens to 0, then count subarrays with sum exactly k  - the prefix-sum + HashMap method (Problem 008) also works. The window method: `atMost(k)` = expand right; while `oddCount > k` shrink; add `right - left + 1`; then subtract `atMost(k-1)`.

**11. Why It Works** - for a fixed right, if `[left..right]` has ‰¤ k odds, every suffix `[i..right]` (i ‰¥ left) also has ‰¤ k odds (removing elements can only reduce the odd count)  - `right-left+1` subarrays are legal, and the shrink loop stops at the first index that would break the limit. Difference of two at-most counts isolates exactly-k because subarrays with ‰¤ kˆ'1 odds and those with exactly k odds are disjoint and together make ‰¤ k.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int numberOfSubarrays(int[] nums, int k) {
        return atMost(nums, k) - atMost(nums, k - 1);
    }
    private int atMost(int[] nums, int k) {
        if (k < 0) return 0;
        int left = 0, odds = 0;
        long ans = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            if (nums[right] % 2 != 0) odds++;
            while (odds > k) {
                if (nums[left] % 2 != 0) odds--;
                left++;
            }
            ans += right - left + 1;
        }
        return (int) ans;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - identical structure to Problem 033; only the window state changes (an odd counter instead of a distinct counter). The `ans += right - left + 1` line is the counting engine.

**15. Dry Run** - `nums = [1,1,2,1,1]`, `k = 2`

| right | value | odds after | shrink | left | added (rightˆ'left+1) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 1 | none | 0 | 1 |
| 1 | 1 | 2 | none | 0 | 2  - total 3 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | none | 0 | 3  - total 6 |
| 3 | 1 | 3 | evict idx0 (odd  - 2) | 1 | 3  - total 9 |
| 4 | 1 | 3 | evict idx1 (odd  - 2) | 2 | 3  - total 12 |

`atMost(2) = 12`.

`atMost(1)`:

- r0: odds 1  - +1  - 1
- r1: odds 2  - evict idx0 (odd  - 1), left = 1  - +1  - 2
- r2: even, odds 1  - +2  - 4
- r3: odds 2  - evict idx1 (odd  - 1), left = 2  - +2  - 6
- r4: odds 2  - evict idx2 (even, left 3, odds still 2)  - evict idx3 (odd  - 1), left = 4  - +1  - 7

`atMost(1) = 7`  - `exactly(2) = 12 ˆ' 7 = 5` œ" - matching the enumerated subarrays (0,1), (0,2), (1,3), (2,4), (3,4).

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n)** for two passes. **Space O(1).**

**17. Edge Cases** - no odds at all (0); k > total odds (0); k = 1 (counts runs of isolated odds - think about prefixes before/after each odd); all odds (atMost(k) = n(n+1)/2 differences); single element.

**18. Common Mistakes** - shrinking on "exactly k" (not monotone); forgetting the `k-1` guard; wrong arithmetic when adding `right-left+1` only for `oddCount == k` (undercounts); `nums[i] % 2` for negatives (in Java, `-3 % 2 == -1` ‰  0 - still correctly odd, but `== 1` would fail; use `!= 0`).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Alternative solution**  - Map odd-count to 1/0 and use prefix sums with a HashMap (Problem 008) - O(n)/O(n).
**Q: Why does the at-most trick work**  - "‰¤ k" decomposes into "‰¤ kˆ'1" or "exactly k", disjoint  - subtraction isolates exactly k.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n) time, O(1) space with the window version.

**20. Variations** - Subarrays with exactly K distinct (033); count subarrays with sum exactly K (008); "nice" subarrays with even counts (identical code).

**21. Related Problems** - 008, 033, 010.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Exactly k isn't a safe window condition - shrinking can leave the count at k or drop it below - so I count 'at most k' subarrays instead, which is monotone: shrink while the odd count exceeds k, then add rightˆ'left+1 because every suffix of the window is also legal. Then exactly-k is atMost(k) minus atMost(kˆ'1). Two linear passes, O(n) time, constant space."

</details>

### Problem 036 - Maximum Vowels in a Substring of Given Length

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Easy-Medium | **Pattern:** Fixed window + O(1) predicate counter

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given a string `s` and an integer `k`, return the **maximum number of vowel characters** in any substring of `s` with length `k`.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `String s`, `int k` (1 ‰¤ k ‰¤ s.length).
- **Output:** `int` - max vowel count in a length-k window.
- **Constraints:** `1 <= s.length <= 10^5`, `s` lowercase letters; vowels = a, e, i, o, u.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  s = "abciiidef", k = 3
Output: 3        ("iii")

Input:  s = "leetcode", k = 3
Output: 2        ("lee" or "eet" or "ode")

Edge case: k = s.length  - count vowels in the whole string.
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** fixed sliding window with a cheap membership predicate.

**Recognition:** fixed length k + "count/max of elements satisfying a property"  - build a window counter; add on entry, subtract on exit. This is the *easiest* window shape (baseline #28 with a predicate instead of a sum) and often appears as the warm-up in a real interview.

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - count vowels in every length-k substring  - O(n·k).
**9. Why It Fails** - consecutive windows share kˆ'1 characters; recounting them wastes work (n = 10^5, k large  - too slow).
**10. Optimal Approach** - count vowels in the first window; for each step right, add 1 if `s[right]` is a vowel, subtract 1 if `s[right-k]` leaves; track the max.

**11. Why It Works** - the window always has exactly k characters, and the incremental update keeps its vowel count exact: `newCount = oldCount + in ˆ' out`. Since every candidate window appears exactly once as the window slides, the max over those positions is the answer. Same argument as baseline #28 - the only change is what "contributes 1" means.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int maxVowels(String s, int k) {
        int count = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) if (isVowel(s.charAt(i))) count++;
        int best = count;
        for (int right = k; right < s.length(); right++) {
            if (isVowel(s.charAt(right))) count++;
            if (isVowel(s.charAt(right - k))) count--;
            best = Math.max(best, count);
        }
        return best;
    }
    private boolean isVowel(char c) {
        return c == 'a' || c == 'e' || c == 'i' || c == 'o' || c == 'u';
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - two phases: seed the first window, then slide. `right - k` is the element falling out of the window (valid because `right >= k` in the second loop). The helper keeps the main loop readable.

**15. Dry Run** - `s = "abciiidef"`, `k = 3`

| Step | window | in (vowel) | out (vowel) | count | best |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| seed | abc | a,b,c  - 1 | - | 1 | 1 |
| right=3 | bci | i œ" +1 | a œ" ˆ'1 | 1 | 1 |
| right=4 | cii | i œ" +1 | b œ- | 2 | 2 |
| right=5 | iii | i œ" +1 | c œ- | 3 | **3** |
| right=6 | iie | e œ" +1 | i œ" ˆ'1 | 3 | 3 |
| right=7 | ied | d œ- | i œ" ˆ'1 | 2 | 3 |
| right=8 | def | f œ- | e œ" ˆ'1 | 1 | 3 |

Result **3** œ"

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n)**: one pass, O(1) per step. **Space O(1)**.

**17. Edge Cases** - no vowels at all (0); k = 1 (max vowel indicator); k = n (whole string); string entirely vowels (k); vowels at window boundaries (the in/out logic must handle both in the same step).

**18. Common Mistakes** - recomputing counts per window (O(n·k)); forgetting the out-subtraction (count only grows); off-by-one in `right - k`; hard-coding vowels in a way that breaks case sensitivity.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why fixed window**  - The length is given; there's nothing to shrink.
**Q: Harder version**  - "Longest substring with at least k vowels"  - variable window with shrink-while-invalid.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n) time, O(1) space.

**20. Variations** - Max sum of size-k window (baseline #28); longest substring with ‰¥ k vowels (variable window); count windows with ‰¥ k vowels (at-most trick).

**21. Related Problems** - baseline #28, 024, 025.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I count vowels in the first k characters, then slide: each step adds the incoming character if it's a vowel and subtracts the outgoing one if it was, keeping the count exact in O(1). I track the maximum over all positions. O(n) time, O(1) space - essentially your fixed-window template with a predicate instead of a sum."

</details>

### Problem 037 - Subarray Product Less Than K

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Shortest/all-valid window counting with a product budget

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an array of positive integers `nums` and a positive integer `k`, return the **number of contiguous subarrays** whose product is **strictly less than `k`**.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums` (all > 0), `int k` (> 0).
- **Output:** `int` - number of subarrays with product < k.
- **Constraints:** `1 <= nums.length <= 3 * 10^4`, `1 <= nums[i] <= 1000`, `1 <= k <= 10^6`.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [10,5,2,6], k = 100
Output: 8
Explanation: [10],[5],[2],[6], [10,5], [5,2], [2,6], [5,2,6]  - all products < 100.
             [10,5,2] = 100 is NOT < 100  - excluded.

Edge case: k = 1  - 0 (all values ‰¥ 1, product ‰¥ 1).
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** sliding window **counting** (all suffixes of a valid window are valid).

**Recognition:** positive numbers + "product less/greater than a budget" + "count subarrays"  - window with a running product. Positivity makes the product monotone (extending never decreases it), so shrinking restores validity - same reasoning as Problem 028 but counting instead of minimizing.

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - all O(n²) subarrays, multiply each  - O(n²) (or O(n³) naive).
**9. Why It Fails** - products of overlapping ranges are recomputed; also multiplication of many elements can overflow if not careful.
**10. Optimal Approach** - expand `right`, multiply `product *= nums[right]`; while `product >= k`, divide out `nums[left]` and `left++`; then add `right - left + 1` (every suffix of the now-valid window has product < k).

**11. Why It Works** - all values are positive, so dividing out the left element strictly decreases the product and the shrink loop terminates with `product < k`. For a fixed `right`, the window `[left..right]` is valid, and **any suffix** `[i..right]` (i ‰¥ left) multiplies a subset of the same positive numbers  - product ‰¤ current product < k  - also valid. So exactly `right - left + 1` subarrays end at `right` legally, and no illegal one is counted (a window starting before `left` had product ‰¥ k when it was evicted, and adding elements only grows it).

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int numSubarrayProductLessThanK(int[] nums, int k) {
        if (k <= 1) return 0;
        int product = 1, left = 0, ans = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
            product *= nums[right];
            while (product >= k) product /= nums[left++];
            ans += right - left + 1;
        }
        return ans;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `k <= 1` shortcut: since every value ‰¥ 1, no product can be < 1. The `while` (not `if`) matters when several small values must be evicted. `ans += right-left+1` counts suffixes - this is the same counting engine as Problems 033/035.

**15. Dry Run** - `nums = [10,5,2,6]`, `k = 100`

| right | value | product after | shrink (while ‰¥ 100) | left | added | ans |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 10 | 10 | none | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 5 | 50 | none | 0 | 2 | 3 |
| 2 | 2 | 100 | 100 ‰¥ 100  - ·10  - 10, left 1; 10 < 100  - stop | 1 | 2 | 5 |
| 3 | 6 | 60 | none | 1 | 3 | **8** |

Result **8** œ"

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n):** each index multiplies in once and divides out once. **Space O(1).**

**17. Edge Cases** - `k = 1`  - 0; all ones (count = n(n+1)/2); a single element ‰¥ k (that element contributes 0); overflow: product of up to 3-10^4 values ‰¤ 1000 would overflow `int` - but the shrink loop keeps the product < k ‰¤ 10^6, so it stays bounded (say this out loud - it shows you checked); empty array.

**18. Common Mistakes** - using `<= k` instead of `< k`; dividing only once instead of a `while`; not guarding `k ‰¤ 1`; dividing by zero if values can be 0 (not allowed here - if they could, you'd need a different approach: count zeros as separators).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why does division work here**  - Positivity makes the product reversible; with zeros or negatives you couldn't divide your way back.
**Q: "At most k" vs "less than k"**  - Same code with `>`/`>=` flipped appropriately.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n) time, O(1) space via the two-pointer argument.

**20. Variations** - Product less than K (this); product greater than K (shrink while ‰¤ threshold and count differently); subarray sum less than K with negatives  - prefix sums with a sorted structure (harder).

**21. Related Problems** - 028, 033, 008.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "With all-positive values, the product grows monotonically as I extend the window, so I can shrink from the left (dividing out) until the product drops below k. At that point every suffix of the window also multiplies to less than k - fewer positive factors can only make it smaller - so I add rightˆ'left+1 to the answer. Each element is multiplied in and divided out once: O(n) time, O(1) space."

</details>

### Problem 038 - Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Complement window (sum of ends = total ˆ' middle window)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Several cards lie in a row, each with a point value. You may take **exactly `k` cards**, but only from **either end** of the row (front or back) on each pick. Return the maximum score you can obtain.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] cardPoints`, `int k`.
- **Output:** `int` - maximum sum obtainable by taking k cards from the ends.
- **Constraints:** `1 <= cardPoints.length <= 10^5`, `1 <= k <= cardPoints.length`, values up to 10^4.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  cardPoints = [1,2,3,4,5,6,1], k = 3
Output: 12
Explanation: Take 1 (front) + 6 + 1 (back) = 8 - check all splits:
  take 0 from front / 3 from back  - 5+6+1 = 12   max
  take 1/2  - 1 + 6 + 1 = 8;  take 2/1  - 1+2+1 = 4;  take 3/0  - 1+2+3 = 6.

Edge case: k = cardPoints.length  - sum of the whole array.
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** window on the **complement** (maximum of ends = total ˆ' minimum middle window).

**Recognition:** "pick from the ends" + a fixed count k  - the complement (the elements you *leave*) is a **contiguous window of length n ˆ' k** in the middle. So maximize ends ‡" minimize the untouched middle ‡" a fixed-window minimum.

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - try all splits: take i from the front and kˆ'i from the back, for i = 0..k  - O(k) with prefix sums (or O(n·k) if recomputing sums). A wrong "brute force" many give: enumerate all combinations of k cards  - exponential.
**9. Why It Fails** - recomputing sums per split is fine at O(k), but without the complement insight you may try to enumerate subsets (C(n,k)) - hopeless. The real insight needed is structural.
**10. Optimal Approach** - compute `total`. The cards NOT taken form a contiguous window of length `n ˆ' k`. Slide that window, track its minimum sum, and answer `total ˆ' minWindowSum`.

**11. Why It Works** - taking k cards from the ends means the untaken cards are never split across both ends: they must be a single middle segment (if you take i from the front and kˆ'i from the back, the untouched part is indices `i .. n-1-(k-i)`, a window of length nˆ'k). Every choice of i corresponds to exactly one such window and vice versa - a bijection. So maximizing the taken sum ‡" minimizing the untouched sum, and the minimum fixed-size window is a one-pass scan.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int maxScore(int[] cardPoints, int k) {
        int n = cardPoints.length;
        int total = 0;
        for (int x : cardPoints) total += x;
        int windowLen = n - k;
        if (windowLen == 0) return total;
        int window = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < windowLen; i++) window += cardPoints[i];
        int minWindow = window;
        for (int i = windowLen; i < n; i++) {
            window += cardPoints[i] - cardPoints[i - windowLen];
            minWindow = Math.min(minWindow, window);
        }
        return total - minWindow;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - the `windowLen == 0` shortcut handles k = n (nothing is left in the middle). The second loop is your baseline #28 fixed-window slide, applied to the *untaken* segment.

**15. Dry Run** - `cardPoints = [1,2,3,4,5,6,1]`, `k = 3`, `windowLen = 4`, `total = 22`

| Step | window (untaken) | window sum | minWindow |
|---|---|---|---|
| seed | [1,2,3,4] | 10 | 10 |
| i=4 | [2,3,4,5] | 14 | 10 |
| i=5 | [3,4,5,6] | 18 | 10 |
| i=6 | [4,5,6,1] | 16 | 10 |

Answer = `22 ˆ' 10` = **12** œ" (untake [1,2,3,4]  - take [5,6,1] from the back).

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n):** one pass for the total, one pass for the sliding minimum. **Space O(1).**

**17. Edge Cases** - k = n (return total); k = 1 (max of first and last element); all equal values; negative values (fine - min-window logic doesn't need positivity); n = 1.

**18. Common Mistakes** - trying to DP over "take from front or back" (overkill - the complement insight is O(n)); forgetting `total` includes everything; off-by-one in window length (`n - k` vs `n - k + 1`); handling k = n (empty middle window  - guard).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why think about the complement**  - "Take from both ends" is awkward to enumerate; "leave a contiguous middle" is a standard fixed window.
**Q: Related trick**  - Maximum subarray after removing one element, circular Kadane, and "minimum window to remove" problems all use the same complement idea.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n) time, O(1) space.

**20. Variations** - Circular maximum subarray (max(Kadane, total ˆ' minSubarray)); best time to buy/sell with at most k from ends (prefix/suffix sums); "take from both ends" variants with different constraints  - prefix sums.

**21. Related Problems** - baseline #28, 005 (circular Kadane), 028.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Rather than enumerating which cards I take from each end, I look at the cards I leave behind: if I take k cards from the ends, the untouched cards always form one contiguous block of length nˆ'k in the middle. So maximizing what I take is the same as minimizing that middle block - a fixed-size window minimum I can compute in one pass. Total minus that minimum is the answer: O(n) time, O(1) space."

</details>

### Problem 039 - Shortest Errand Segment

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
A delivery route has `n` stops with positive toll costs. Find the length of the **shortest contiguous stretch of stops** whose total toll is **at least** `target`. Return 0 if impossible.

- **Input:** `int[] tolls` (all > 0), `int target`; `1 <= n <= 10^5`, `1 <= target <= 10^9`.
- **Output:** `int` - minimum window length with sum ‰¥ target, else 0.

```
Input:  tolls = [2,3,1,2,4,3], target = 7  - 2     ([4,3])
Input:  tolls = [1,1,1,1],    target = 7  - 0
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** shortest valid window (Problem 028). Positives make the sum monotone  - shrink **while still valid**, recording inside the loop.

**Java:**
```java
class Solution {
    public int shortest(int[] t, int target) {
        int left = 0, sum = 0, best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int right = 0; right < t.length; right++) {
            sum += t[right];
            while (sum >= target) {
                best = Math.min(best, right - left + 1);
                sum -= t[left++];
            }
        }
        return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE  0 : best;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(n) time (each index enters/leaves the sum once), O(1) space.
**Mistakes:** recording after the loop (invalid window); applying to negative values (needs prefixes).
**60 seconds:** "All values are positive, so the sum is monotone - I expand until the target is met, then shrink while it stays met, recording each legal length. The last length I record for this right edge is the shortest valid one ending there."

</details>

---

### Problem 040 - Unique Characters Run

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
Find the length of the longest contiguous section of a sensor stream in which **no reading value repeats**.

- **Input:** `String stream` (any printable characters), `0 <= length <= 5*10^4`.
- **Output:** `int` - longest substring with all distinct characters.

```
Input:  "pwwkew"  - 3       ("wke"; "pwke" is not contiguous)
Input:  "bbbbb"   - 1
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** variable window + last-seen index map (Problem 026).

**Java:**
```java
class Solution {
    public int longest(String s) {
        Map<Character, Integer> last = new HashMap<>();
        int left = 0, best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            char c = s.charAt(right);
            if (last.containsKey(c) && last.get(c) >= left) left = last.get(c) + 1;
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
            last.put(c, right);
        }
        return best;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(n) time, O(distinct) space.
**Mistakes:** moving `left` without `max(left, last+1)`; recording before adjusting `left`.
**60 seconds:** "I keep a window of distinct characters and remember each character's last index. If the new character's last occurrence lies inside the window, I jump the left edge just past it. Left never moves backwards, so every character is processed once - O(n)."

</details>

---

### Problem 041 - Window with Two Kinds

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
A warehouse shelf holds boxes of different types in a row. You may fill **two crates**, each crate holding only one type. Choose a **consecutive** shelf segment that fits this rule and maximize the number of boxes collected.

- **Input:** `int[] shelf` (type ids), `1 <= length <= 10^5`.
- **Output:** `int` - longest contiguous segment containing at most 2 distinct values.

```
Input:  shelf = [1,2,3,2,2]  - 4     ([2,3,2,2])
Input:  shelf = [1,1,1]       - 3
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** at-most-K-distinct window with K = 2 (Problem 029).

**Java:**
```java
class Solution {
    public int pick(int[] s) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> count = new HashMap<>();
        int left = 0, distinct = 0, best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length; right++) {
            int v = s[right];
            count.put(v, count.getOrDefault(v, 0) + 1);
            if (count.get(v) == 1) distinct++;
            while (distinct > 2) {
                int w = s[left++];
                count.put(w, count.get(w) - 1);
                if (count.get(w) == 0) distinct--;
            }
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        return best;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(n) time, O(1) space in practice (‰¤ 3 live keys).
**Mistakes:** forgetting to drop the `distinct` counter when a count hits 0; recording before shrinking.
**60 seconds:** "It's the longest window with at most two distinct types: expand, and whenever a third type shows up, pop from the left until one type disappears. The window is legal whenever I record it, and each box enters and leaves once - O(n)."

</details>

---

### Problem 042 - Repeating Letter Budget

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
You may change at most `k` characters of a capital-letter string to any other capital letter. What is the length of the longest uniform (single-letter) substring you can obtain

- **Input:** `String s`, `int k`; `1 <= s.length <= 10^4`, `0 <= k <= s.length`.
- **Output:** `int` - maximum achievable uniform substring length.

```
Input:  s = "ABAB", k = 2  - 4
Input:  s = "AABABBA", k = 1  - 4
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** window with `size ˆ' maxFrequency ‰¤ k` (Problem 027).

**Java:**
```java
class Solution {
    public int uniform(String s, int k) {
        int[] cnt = new int[26];
        int left = 0, maxFreq = 0, best = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, ++cnt[s.charAt(right) - 'A']);
            while (right - left + 1 - maxFreq > k) cnt[s.charAt(left++) - 'A']--;
            best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1);
        }
        return best;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(n) time, O(1) space.
**Mistakes:** wrong replacement formula (it's size ˆ' maxFreq); recording before shrinking.
**60 seconds:** "To make a window uniform I'd keep its most frequent letter and convert the rest, so the cost is size minus that letter's count. I expand until the cost exceeds k, shrink until it fits, then record. Linear time, constant space."

</details>

### Problem 043 - Covering the Task

**Category:** Sliding Window | **Difficulty:** Medium-Hard | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
A checklist string `task` lists required items (duplicates matter). Find the **shortest window** of the schedule `sched` that contains **every required item with the right multiplicity**; return `""` if impossible.

- **Input:** `String sched`, `String task`; `1 <= both length <= 10^4`.
- **Output:** `String` - the minimum covering window, or `""`.

```
Input:  sched = "ADOBECODEBANC", task = "ABC"  - "BANC"
Input:  sched = "a", task = "aa"  - ""
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** shortest covering window with a `formed` counter (Problem 031).

**Java:**
```java
class Solution {
    public String cover(String s, String t) {
        Map<Character, Integer> need = new HashMap<>();
        for (char c : t.toCharArray()) need.put(c, need.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
        Map<Character, Integer> have = new HashMap<>();
        int formed = 0, required = need.size();
        int left = 0, bestLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE, bestStart = 0;
        for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
            char c = s.charAt(right);
            have.put(c, have.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
            if (need.containsKey(c) && have.get(c).equals(need.get(c))) formed++;
            while (formed == required && left <= right) {
                if (right - left + 1 < bestLen) { bestLen = right - left + 1; bestStart = left; }
                char d = s.charAt(left++);
                have.put(d, have.get(d) - 1);
                if (need.containsKey(d) && have.get(d) < need.get(d)) formed--;
            }
        }
        return bestLen == Integer.MAX_VALUE  "" : s.substring(bestStart, bestStart + bestLen);
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(n) time, O(alphabet) space.
**Mistakes:** sets instead of counts; `formed` incremented per occurrence rather than on the quota crossing; recording after coverage breaks.
**60 seconds:** "Two histograms - required vs in-window - plus a counter of how many requirements are satisfied, so coverage is an O(1) test. Expand until covered, shrink while still covered recording the best window each time. Each index moves once: linear."

</details>

## Common Mistakes From Phase 2

1. **Wrong shrink rule:** longest  - shrink while *invalid*, record after; shortest  - shrink while *valid*, record inside.
2. **Recording before restoring validity**  - counts an illegal window.
3. **`if` instead of `while`**  - only one violation fixed; the window stays broken.
4. **Forgetting to remove the left element's contribution** (count/sum/product drift).
5. **Off-by-one length:** `right - left + 1`, not `right - left`.
6. **Using a window with negatives + target sum**  - prefix sums instead (Phase 1).
7. **"Exactly K" shrunk directly**  - not monotone; use `atMost(k) - atMost(k-1)`.
8. **`map.size()` for distinct** while dead keys stay in the map  - keep an explicit counter.
9. **Never justifying O(n):** say *"left only moves forward, so total shrinks ‰¤ n"*.
10. **Set instead of frequency map** when duplicates matter (anagrams, counts).
11. **Ignoring the fixed window's seed phase** (first window built before sliding).
12. **Wrong vowel/parity test for negatives:** `-3 % 2 == -1`, so test `!= 0`, not `== 1`.

# Phase 3 - Two Pointers

**Goal:** learn to *prove* why a pointer may move - not just apply a trick.

**Prerequisites (your baseline):** #4 Reverse an Array, #6 Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array, #7 Move Zeroes, #26 Two Sum in Sorted Array, #27 Reverse Using Two Pointers, #25 Sort 0s/1s/2s.

## Pattern Chapter - Two Pointers

### P3.1 What Two Pointers Really Is

Two indices move through the data with a **maintained invariant**. The power comes from making the *inner loop* of a brute force unnecessary: instead of checking every pair `(i, j)`, one pointer advances only when the current pair tells you it is safe to do so.

The whole pattern rests on one question:

> **"What monotone property lets me move this pointer without missing the answer"**

If you cannot answer that, you are guessing - and interviewers will ask exactly this.

### P3.2 The Five Variants

| Variant | Direction | Typical use | Your baseline / phase problems |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Opposite direction** | `left`  ', `right`   | Sorted pair/triplet with a target sum | #26, 044, 045, 046, 054 |
| **Same direction (sliding/compaction)** | both  ', `slow` ‰¤ `fast` | In-place removal, partition, compaction | #6, #7, 047, 048, 056 |
| **Fast/slow** | different speeds | Cycle detection, middle of list, palindrome list | Phase 6: 114, 115, 119 |
| **Partition pointers** | `left`  ', `right`  , `cur`  - | Dutch National Flag, quicksort partition | #25, 048 |
| **Multiple pointers** | 3+ independent indices | 3Sum/4Sum, merge, K-way merge | 044, 054, 013 |

### P3.3 Why Is Moving a Pointer Valid (the proof habit)

**Opposite pointers on sorted data (target sum):**

```
sum = a[left] + a[right]
sum == target   - record, then BOTH sides move (any pair with these values is used;
                 moving both is safe because a[left] can't pair with a[right] again)
sum <  target   - left++    (array sorted ascending  - smallest untried sum needs a bigger left)
sum >  target   - right--   (need a smaller sum  - the largest element must go)
```

The invariant: **every answer pair with the current left has already been considered or is impossible.** That's why we never skip a solution.

**Same-direction (compaction):** `slow` marks "everything before here is final". You only write to positions you have already finished reading.

**The red flags that break validity:**
- Pointers on an **unsorted** array (the monotone argument collapses - sort first, or use a HashMap).
- Moving a pointer because "it feels right" without a comparison driving it.
- Moving both pointers on equality *and* skipping duplicates incorrectly (the 3Sum duplicate rule).

### P3.4 Recognition Checklist

1. Sorted (or sortable without losing meaning) **and** looking for a pair/triplet  - opposite pointers.
2. "In-place", "remove/replace/move without extra memory"  - same-direction compaction.
3. "Partition into groups"  - partition pointers (Dutch flag).
4. "Middle", "cycle", "is it a palindrome" (list)  - fast/slow.
5. Container/volume/area maximized with two ends  - opposite pointers with a *different* move rule (move the shorter side).
6. n ‰¤ 1000 + "all triplets"  - sort first (O(n²) is then expected).

### P3.5 Java Templates

**Opposite direction:**
```java
Arrays.sort(a);
int left = 0, right = a.length - 1;
while (left < right) {
    long sum = (long) a[left] + a[right];   // long avoids overflow
    if (sum == target) { /* record; left++; right--; */ }
    else if (sum < target) left++;
    else right--;
}
```

**Same-direction compaction:**
```java
int slow = 0;
for (int fast = 0; fast < n; fast++) {
    if (keep(a[fast])) a[slow++] = a[fast];
}
// new logical length = slow
```

### P3.6 Common Mistakes

1. Forgetting that opposite pointers **require sorting** - and that sorting destroys original indices (store pairs first).
2. Not skipping duplicates after a match (infinite work or duplicate answers in 3Sum).
3. On equality, moving only one pointer  - possible infinite loop or duplicate outputs.
4. `while (left <= right)` in a problem where pointers cross at equality  - re-counts or loops.
5. Overflow: `(long) a[i] + a[j]` when values reach ±10^9.
6. In Container-with-water style problems, moving the wrong pointer (always move the shorter side - proved in Problem 046).

---

### Problem 044 - 3Sum

**Category:** Two Pointers | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Sort + fix one + two pointers (with duplicate skipping)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array `nums`, return all **unique triplets** `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i < j < k` and their sum is **0**. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.

#### 2. Input
- `int[] nums`, length n.

#### 3. Output
- `List<List<Integer>>` - all unique triplets summing to 0 (order inside a triplet may vary; the set must be unique).

#### 4. Constraints
- `3 <= nums.length <= 2000` (some versions up to 10^3-10^4)
- `-10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5`

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]
Output: [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
Explanation: (-1) + (-1) + 2 = 0 and (-1) + 0 + 1 = 0. Duplicates in the input
             must not produce duplicate triplets.

Edge case:
Input:  nums = [0, 0, 0, 0]
Output: [[0, 0, 0]]
Explanation: Only one distinct triplet exists despite four zeros.

Input:  nums = [1, 2]  - [] (fewer than 3 elements)
```

#### 6. Pattern
**Sorting + fix one element + opposite-direction two pointers** (multiple-pointer variant), with duplicate skipping.

#### 7. How to Recognize This Pattern
- "Find **all triplets** with a target sum" + duplicates must not repeat  - sorting is what makes duplicate control possible (equal values become adjacent).
- n around 10^3-10^4 with an O(n²) expectation  - sort first, then a linear inner scan.
- If only *one* pair with a given sum were needed and indices mattered  - HashMap (Problem 001). If the array is already sorted  - two pointers directly (baseline #26).

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - three nested loops over all i < j < k  - **O(n³)** time, then a set to deduplicate  - O(n³) time plus O(n³) space for the set of triplets.
**9. Why It Fails** - for every i you re-scan pairs that the previous i already scanned, and there is no way to stop early without order. With n = 2000, n³ = 8-10^9. A set-based dedup also hides the fact that duplicates come from *equal values*, which sorting would make adjacent and easy to skip.
**10. Optimal Approach**
1. Sort the array - O(n log n).
2. For each index `i` from 0 to n-3 (as the first element):
   - **Skip duplicates:** if `i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i-1]`, continue (the same first element was already used).
   - Set `left = i + 1`, `right = n - 1`, `target = -nums[i]`.
   - While `left < right`: compute `sum = nums[left] + nums[right]`:
     - `sum == target`  - record `[nums[i], nums[left], nums[right]]`, then advance **both** and skip equal values at the left and right.
     - `sum < target`  - `left++` (need a bigger sum).
     - `sum > target`  - `right--` (need a smaller sum).

**11. Why the Optimal Approach Works**
- **Why does fixing `i` and using two pointers cover everything** For a fixed first element, the remaining problem is exactly Two Sum on a sorted subarray - and Problem 026/#26 proved that the opposite-direction scan visits the correct pair in O(n) without missing any.
- **Why is the pointer movement safe** The array is sorted: if the sum is too small, no pair using the *current* left with any right can be bigger by moving right inward - so the left must advance; symmetric for right.
- **Why skip duplicates** All equal values are adjacent after sorting, so "skip while equal" eliminates every duplicate triplet *before* it is generated - no HashSet of results needed. Skipping at all three levels (i, left, right) is what makes output unique.
- **Why only n-3 for i** The last valid triplet needs two elements after i  - `i <= n - 3`.

**12. Algorithm / Steps**
1. Sort `nums`.
2. For `i` in `0..n-3`: skip if equal to previous; `lo = i+1`, `hi = n-1`, `want = -nums[i]`.
3. While `lo < hi`: sum & compare; on match, add to result, then `lo++`/`hi--` with duplicate skips; on `<` `lo++`; on `>` `hi--`.
4. Return the list.

**13. Java Solution**
```java
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
        int n = nums.length;
        for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) {
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;      // skip equal first elements
            if (nums[i] > 0) break;                             // sorted  - sum can't reach 0
            int lo = i + 1, hi = n - 1, want = -nums[i];
            while (lo < hi) {
                int sum = nums[lo] + nums[hi];
                if (sum == want) {
                    res.add(Arrays.asList(nums[i], nums[lo], nums[hi]));
                    lo++;
                    hi--;
                    while (lo < hi && nums[lo] == nums[lo - 1]) lo++;   // skip dup left
                    while (lo < hi && nums[hi] == nums[hi + 1]) hi--;   // skip dup right
                } else if (sum < want) {
                    lo++;
                } else {
                    hi--;
                }
            }
        }
        return res;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation**
- `if (nums[i] > 0) break;` - once the smallest possible first element is positive, every sum is positive  - impossible to reach 0. A cheap but valuable early exit (say it in the interview).
- Duplicate skips at `i`, `lo`, and `hi` each prevent a distinct class of duplicate triplets.
- The inner `while` loops compare against `nums[lo-1]`/`nums[hi+1]` **after** the increment, so the just-recorded value is the one being skipped.

**15. Detailed Dry Run** - `nums = [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]`  - sorted `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`

| i | nums[i] | want | lo / hi | sum | action | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | -4 | 4 | 1 / 5 | -1+2 = 1 < 4 | lo++ | [] |
| 0 | -4 | 4 | 2 / 5 | -1+2 = 1 < 4 | lo++ | [] |
| 0 | -4 | 4 | 3 / 5 | 0+2 = 2 < 4 | lo++ | [] |
| 0 | -4 | 4 | 4 / 5 | 1+2 = 3 < 4 | lo++  - lo=5=hi  - inner ends | [] |
| 1 | -1 | 1 | 2 / 5 | -1+2 = 1 = 1 | **record [-1,-1,2]**; lo=3, hi=4; skip dups (none) | [[-1,-1,2]] |
| 1 | -1 | 1 | 3 / 4 | 0+1 = 1 = 1 | **record [-1,0,1]**; lo=4, hi=3  - inner ends | [[-1,-1,2],[-1,0,1]] |
| 2 | -1 | 1 | - | - | `nums[2] == nums[1]`  - skip | unchanged |
| 3 | 0 | 0 | 4 / 5 | 1+2 = 3 > 0 | hi--  - hi=4=lo  - ends | unchanged |
| 4 | 1 | - | - | - | `nums[4] > 0`  - break | unchanged |

Result `[[-1,-1,2], [-1,0,1]]` œ"

**16. Complexity Analysis**
- **Time: O(n²)** - sorting is O(n log n); the outer loop runs n times and the inner two-pointer scan moves `lo`/`hi` across the array once per `i`  - n - O(n) = O(n²).
- **Space: O(log n)** for the sort's recursion stack (or O(1) for an in-place primitive sort), plus O(1) for the two pointers and the output list (which is required, so usually not counted).

**17. Edge Cases**
- Fewer than 3 elements  - empty list.
- All zeros  - exactly one triplet `[0,0,0]`.
- All positive / all negative  - no triplet (the `> 0` break and the scan handle it).
- Heavy duplicates (`[-2,0,1,1,2]`)  - duplicate skips at all three levels.
- Large magnitudes (±10^5): sum of three fits `int`, but say you'd use `long` for ±10^9 inputs.
- Triplets that must be unique in value, not in index  - sorting + skipping is what guarantees this.

**18. Common Mistakes**
1. Using a `Set<List<Integer>>` to deduplicate instead of skipping equal values (works but hides the insight; slower).
2. Skipping duplicates only at `i` (left/right duplicates still produce duplicates).
3. Forgetting to sort (pointers lose their monotone meaning).
4. `while (lo <= hi)`  - the pair (x, x) at crossing indices gets counted wrongly.
5. Not breaking when `nums[i] > 0` - correct but slow (it's an optimization, not a requirement).
6. `int` overflow on the sum with extreme inputs.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why sort at all**  - Sorting gives the monotone property that makes pointer movement safe *and* puts duplicates next to each other so I can skip them instead of using a set.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n²) time: the outer loop is n, the inner scan is linear per outer step. O(log n) space for sorting.
**Q: What if the input had 4 numbers (4Sum)**  - Fix two, run 3Sum's inner logic on the rest - O(n³); or sort and use two pointers with a sum target (same pattern).
**Q: Can you do it without sorting**  - For *a* triplet yes with hashing (Two Sum per element), but for **all unique triplets** without duplicates, sorting is the standard and simplest guarantee.
**Q: Why does skipping duplicates keep completeness**  - Equal values are interchangeable: if a triplet using the first `-1` is valid, one using the second `-1` is the same triplet in value.

**20. Variations**
1. **3Sum Closest (Problem 045)**  - same skeleton, track `|sum - target|` instead of equality, no duplicate skipping needed for the answer value.
2. **4Sum (Problem 054)**  - fix two values, two pointers inside.
3. **3Sum with a target ‰  0**  - identical, `want = target - nums[i]`.
4. **Triplets with sum ‰¤ K (count, not list)**  - count pairs while `lo < hi` (no duplicate concern if you count index triples).

**21. Related Problems** - Problem 001 (Two Sum), 045, 054, 055 (Pair With Given Difference), baseline #26.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I sort first - that does two things: it makes pointer movement monotone, so for a fixed first element I can find the complement in linear time with two pointers, and it groups equal values so I can skip duplicates at each level instead of using a set. For each index i I set lo and hi and move them based on whether the sum is too big or small; on a match I record the triplet and advance both pointers, skipping equal values. Sorting is O(n log n) and the scan is O(n²) overall."

</details>

### Problem 045 - 3Sum Closest

**Category:** Two Pointers | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Sort + fix one + two pointers tracking the best difference

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array `nums` and a `target`, find three integers whose sum is **closest** to `target`, and return that sum. It is guaranteed that exactly one closest sum exists.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums` (length ‰¥ 3), `int target`.
- **Output:** `int` - the achievable triplet sum nearest to target.
- **Constraints:** `2 <= nums.length <= 500` (or up to 10^3), `-1000 <= nums[i], target <= 1000`.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [-1, 2, 1, -4], target = 1
Output: 2
Explanation: (-1) + 2 + 1 = 2, distance 1 - closer than (-4) + 2 + 1 = -1 (distance 2).

Input:  nums = [0, 0, 0], target = 1
Output: 0
Explanation: Only triplet sums to 0; distance 1.
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** identical skeleton to 3Sum, but the inner loop tracks `|sum - target|` instead of waiting for equality.

**Recognition:** "closest / nearest sum to a target" + triplets  - sort + two pointers. Without sorting you'd need O(n³) enumeration; the sorted scan lets you decide direction from one comparison.

<details>
<summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - all O(n³) triplets, keep the best difference.
**9. Why It Fails** - no early exit possible without order; n = 10^3  - 10^9.
**10. Optimal Approach** - sort; for each `i`, set `lo = i+1`, `hi = n-1`; compute `sum = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi]`; update the best if `|sum - target|` is smaller; then move `lo++` if `sum < target` else `hi--`. On an exact match, return `sum` immediately.

**11. Why It Works** - with `i` fixed, the remaining pair-sum must move toward `target - nums[i]`: a too-small sum demands a larger element (only `lo++` can provide one) and vice versa - the same monotone argument as 3Sum. Every candidate sum for this `i` that matters is evaluated as the window narrows; the closest overall is the min across all `i`. No duplicate skipping is needed because duplicates affect *which* triplet you find, not the closest value.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int threeSumClosest(int[] nums, int target) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        int best = nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2];
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length - 2; i++) {
            int lo = i + 1, hi = nums.length - 1;
            while (lo < hi) {
                int sum = nums[i] + nums[lo] + nums[hi];
                if (Math.abs(sum - target) < Math.abs(best - target)) best = sum;
                if (sum == target) return sum;
                else if (sum < target) lo++;
                else hi--;
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `best` initialized from the first triplet avoids assuming any value; the exact-match `return` is just an early exit. The order *update-then-move* ensures every evaluated sum is considered before the pointers change.

**15. Dry Run** - `nums = [-1,2,1,-4]`, `target = 1`  - sorted `[-4,-1,1,2]`

| i | lo | hi | sum | best after | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 3 | -4 + -1 + 2 = -3 | -3 (|ˆ'3ˆ'1| = 4 vs initial 0  - init best = -4+-1+1 = -4, dist 5  - -3 dist 4) | sum < target  - lo++ |
| 0 | 2 | 3 | -4 + 1 + 2 = -1 | -1 (dist 2) | lo++  - lo = hi  - end |
| 1 | 2 | 3 | -1 + 1 + 2 = 2 | 2 (dist 1) | sum > target  - hi--  - lo = hi  - end |
| 2 | 3 | - | loop needs lo < hi  - skipped | - | - |

Result **2** œ" (distance 1, the minimum).

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n²)**: sort O(n log n) + n outer steps - linear inner scan. **Space O(log n)** (sort stack) / O(1) auxiliary.

**17. Edge Cases** - exactly 3 elements; all equal values; target far outside the sum range (the closest is an extreme triplet); duplicates (allowed - they just give equal sums); sums near `Integer.MAX_VALUE` (use `long` for `sum` if values are large).

**18. Common Mistakes** - forgetting to sort (direction logic breaks); updating `best` after moving pointers (skips candidates); comparing `sum - target > best - target` without `abs`; returning the difference instead of the sum.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Difference from 3Sum**  - The stopping condition: 3Sum looks for equality (with duplicate skipping); this one tracks the minimum distance and can stop early on an exact hit.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n²) time, O(1) extra space beyond sorting.
**Q: What if duplicates mattered**  - They don't affect the closest value; skipping them would only save a few comparisons.

**20. Variations** - 3Sum (044); 3Sum with target sum ‰¤ K (counting); closest pair sum in two arrays (one pass with two pointers).

**21. Related Problems** - 044, 054, 055.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Same shape as 3Sum: sort, fix the first element, then use two pointers for the other two. The difference is the stopping rule - instead of waiting for equality I track the best absolute difference seen and move the pointer that reduces the sum when I'm above the target (or increases it when I'm below). On an exact match I return immediately. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space."

</details>
