### Problem 080 - Painter's Partition

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Same as Allocate Books (cap - workers feasibility)

#### 1. Problem Statement
`n` boards with given lengths must be painted by `k` painters working **simultaneously**. A painter paints consecutive boards, one at a time, at unit speed. Minimize the time taken (i.e. minimize the longest total length painted by any single painter).

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] boards`, `int k`, `1 <= n <= 10^5`, `1 <= boards[i] <= 10^4` (or 10^6 in harder versions), `k <= n`.
- **Output:** `int` - minimum possible maximum painter load (= time, since painters work in parallel).

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  boards = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], k = 3
Output: 6
Explanation: [1,2,3]=6, [4]=4, [5]=5  - max 6 (best possible: try to beat it and you can't).

Edge case: k = 1  - sum ; k = n  - max(boards)
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** binary search on answer + greedy partition - **structurally identical to Problem 079**.

**Recognition:** "workers/painters/servers, consecutive items, minimize the maximum load"  - the same template. Recognizing that 076/077/079/080 are *one* pattern is more valuable than solving them as four separate problems.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - enumerate all ways to split into k contiguous groups  - exponential; or probe every cap  - O(range - n).
**9. Why It Fails** - same as 079: the cap range is huge but monotone.
**10. Optimal Approach** - `low = max(boards)`, `high = sum(boards)`; binary search the cap; check = greedily count painters needed (each takes boards while the running total ‰¤ cap). Minimize form: feasible  - `high = mid`, else `low = mid + 1`.

**11. Why It Works** - identical argument to 079: monotone feasibility (bigger cap  - never more painters), greedy check optimal (pack fully before starting a new painter), provable bounds. The only modeling insight: **since painters work in parallel, total time = the slowest painter's load**, so minimizing the maximum load *is* minimizing time.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int minTime(int[] boards, int k) {
        long low = 0, sum = 0;
        for (int b : boards) { low = Math.max(low, b); sum += b; }
        long high = sum;
        while (low < high) {
            long mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            if (paintersNeeded(boards, mid) <= k) high = mid;
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return (int) low;
    }
    private int paintersNeeded(int[] boards, long cap) {
        int painters = 1;
        long load = 0;
        for (int b : boards) {
            if (load + b > cap) { painters++; load = 0; }
            load += b;
            if (painters > k) return painters;
        }
        return painters;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `long` for `cap`/`load` because sums can exceed 2^31 in harder constraints (10^5 - 10^6 = 10^11). The early `if (painters > k) return` keeps checks cheap. Note `paintersNeeded` takes `long cap` - mismatched types here are a common compile-error source.

**15. Dry Run** - `boards = [1,2,3,4,5]`, `k = 3`

| low | high | mid | painters at cap = mid | feasible (‰¤ 3) | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 15 | 10 | [1,2,3,4]=10, [5]  - 2 | œ" | high = 10 |
| 5 | 10 | 7 | [1,2,3]=6, [4]... 6+4=10>7  - [4]=4, [5]  - 3 | œ" | high = 7 |
| 5 | 7 | 6 | [1,2,3]=6, [4], [5]  - 3 | œ" | high = 6 |
| 5 | 6 | 5 | [1,2,3]=6>5  - [1,2]=3, [3,4] 3+4=7>5  - [3]=3, [4,5]=9>5  - [4]=4, [5]=5  - 5 painters | œ- | low = 6 |
| 6 | 6 | - | - | - | stop  - **6** œ" |

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n - log(sum ˆ' max))**, **Space O(1)** - same as 079.

**17. Edge Cases** - `k = 1`, `k = n`; one board; boards of length 1; sums exceeding `int` (use `long`); boards exactly filling a painter's cap.

**18. Common Mistakes** - forgetting that painters run in parallel (the objective is the max, not the sum of loads); using `int` for sums; identical off-by-one issues as 079 (`>` vs `>=` when starting a new painter).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: How many distinct problems share this template**  - Koko (076), Ship (077), Books (079), Painter (080), Smallest Divisor (085), Repair Cars (089) - one template, six framings.
**Q: Why not greedy on the largest board first**  - Greedy without binary search can't prove minimality.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n log S).

**20. Variations** - Allocate Books (079, identical with a different story); minimize maximum subarray sum after k splits; distribute work to minimize completion time (a scheduling model where only contiguous assignment keeps this greedy valid).

**21. Related Problems** - 076, 077, 078, 079, 085, 089.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Since painters work in parallel, the finish time is the load of the slowest painter - so I minimize the maximum load. I binary search that cap between the longest board and the total, and for each cap count how many painters are needed by greedily assigning consecutive boards until the cap would be exceeded. If that fits k painters, search lower; otherwise higher. O(n log total) time, O(1) space - the same template as book allocation and Koko."

</details>

### Problem 081 - Median of Two Sorted Arrays

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Hard (classic; rare for SDE-1 but excellent training) | **Pattern:** Binary search on a **partition** (answer-space idea applied to structure)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given two sorted arrays `nums1` (length m) and `nums2` (length n), return their **combined median** in O(log(m + n)) time. The arrays are individually sorted, may contain duplicates, and need not have equal length.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums1`, `int[] nums2`, both sorted ascending.
- **Output:** `double` - the median of the merged sequence (average of the two middle values for an even total).
- **Constraints:** `0 <= m, n <= 1000`, `1 <= m + n <= 2000` (classic), values up to 10^6.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums1 = [1, 3], nums2 = [2]
Output: 2.0
Explanation: merged = [1, 2, 3], odd length  - middle element 2.

Input:  nums1 = [1, 2], nums2 = [3, 4]
Output: 2.5
Explanation: merged = [1, 2, 3, 4], even  - (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5.

Edge case: nums1 = [], nums2 = [1]  - 1.0 ; nums1 = [2], nums2 = []  - 2.0
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** binary search on **where to cut** the two arrays so the left half holds exactly half the elements and every element on the left ‰¤ every element on the right.

**Recognition:** two sorted arrays + median/mean/k-th element + logarithmic requirement  - **don't merge** (that's O(m+n)); instead binary search the *partition index* of the smaller array. The insight: the median splits the merged array into two equal halves - so find the cut that achieves that.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - merge both arrays and take the middle  - **O(m + n)** time and space. This is correct and often accepted with these constraints - say so first.
**9. Why It Fails** - only the complexity requirement: merging touches every element; O(log(m+n)) demands that most elements are never examined. Also wastes O(m+n) space.
**10. Optimal Approach** - binary search the cut `i` in the **smaller** array (say A has m ‰¤ n elements): `i` elements come from A, `j = (m+n+1)/2 ˆ' i` from B. The cut is correct when:
```
A[i-1] <= B[j]   and   B[j-1] <= A[i]
```
(using sentinels ˆ'ˆž/ˆž when a side is empty). Then:
- odd total  - median = `max(A[i-1], B[j-1])`;
- even  - `(max(left) + min(right)) / 2`.
If `A[i-1] > B[j]` the cut puts too much from A  - move `i` left (`hi = i - 1`); else move right (`lo = i + 1`).

**11. Why It Works** - with `i + j = half`, every element on the left of the cut is ‰¤ every element on the right *iff* the two cross-conditions hold (each array is sorted internally, so only the cross-boundaries matter). If a condition fails, the offending side's cut is wrong by a known direction: `A[i-1] > B[j]` means A contributed too many large elements  - decrease i. Because i ranges over [0, m] and the condition flips exactly once along that range (monotone!), binary search applies - that's the "answer space" idea from P4.4 applied to a *partition index* rather than a value.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public double findMedianSortedArrays(int[] nums1, int[] nums2) {
        if (nums1.length > nums2.length) return findMedianSortedArrays(nums2, nums1);
        int m = nums1.length, n = nums2.length;
        int lo = 0, hi = m, half = (m + n + 1) / 2;
        while (lo <= hi) {
            int i = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;          // elements taken from nums1
            int j = half - i;                     // elements taken from nums2
            int aLeft  = (i == 0)  Integer.MIN_VALUE : nums1[i - 1];
            int aRight = (i == m)  Integer.MAX_VALUE : nums1[i];
            int bLeft  = (j == 0)  Integer.MIN_VALUE : nums2[j - 1];
            int bRight = (j == n)  Integer.MAX_VALUE : nums2[j];
            if (aLeft <= bRight && bLeft <= aRight) {
                if ((m + n) % 2 == 1) return Math.max(aLeft, bLeft);
                return (Math.max(aLeft, bLeft) + Math.min(aRight, bRight)) / 2.0;
            } else if (aLeft > bRight) hi = i - 1;   // too many from nums1
            else lo = i + 1;                         // too few from nums1
        }
        return -1; // unreachable for valid inputs
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - searching the **smaller** array bounds `i` to [0, m] and keeps `j = half - i` in range - always binary search the shorter side. Sentinels handle empty sides (so `j-1` or `i` can legally be out of bounds). `/2.0` (not `/2`) is what returns a `double`.

**15. Dry Run** - `nums1 = [1, 2]`, `nums2 = [3, 4]` (m=2, n=2, half = 2)

| lo | hi | i | j | aLeft | aRight | bLeft | bRight | condition | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | bLeft(3) ‰¤ aRight(2) œ- | lo = 2 |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 | 2 | ˆž | -ˆž | 3 | 2 ‰¤ 3 œ" and -ˆž ‰¤ ˆž œ" | even  - (max(2,ˆ'ˆž) + min(ˆž,3))/2 = (2+3)/2 = **2.5** œ" |

First example `[1,3]` & `[2]`: m=2, n=1  - search `[1,3]` with half = 2: lo=0,hi=2  - i=1, j=1: aLeft=1, aRight=3, bLeft=2, bRight=ˆž  - conditions œ"  - odd  - max(1,2) = **2.0** œ"

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(log(min(m, n))):** each iteration halves the smaller array's search range - we never touch more than log''(min) elements. **Space O(1)** - only indices and sentinel values; the merge approach would be O(m+n).

**17. Edge Cases** - one array empty (median from the other); arrays of very different lengths (search the shorter); all elements of one array smaller than the other; duplicates across arrays; single element total; even vs odd total (`+1` in `half` handles the median-left preference); `Integer.MIN_VALUE`/`MAX_VALUE` as actual data (sentinels could collide - mention using `long` or index-based guards).

**18. Common Mistakes** - searching the longer array (j can go out of range); `return (maxLeft + minRight) / 2` with integer division (loses the .5); forgetting the sentinels; using `while (lo < hi)` with `hi = i - 1` (skips the boundary); merging and calling it O(log n).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why not just merge**  - O(m+n); the constraint asks for O(log(m+n)), which means only the neighbourhood of the median matters.
**Q: What is the invariant**  - "Exactly half of all elements lie to the left of the cut, and the two cross-conditions hold."
**Q: Can this find the k-th element too**  - Yes - the same partition logic with `k` on each side (Problem 065's follow-up).
**Q: Why binary search the smaller array**  - Guarantees `i ˆˆ [0, m]` and `j = half - i` never exceeds n.

**20. Variations** - K-th smallest of two sorted arrays (partition with `k/2`); median of a sliding window (two heaps, Problem 165); median of one sorted array (trivial by comparison).

**21. Related Problems** - 065 (Kth unsorted), 165 (Median from a stream), 013 (Merge Sorted Arrays).

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "The median splits the merged data into two equal halves, so I binary search the cut in the smaller array: i elements from it, and the rest from the other array. The cut is valid when every left element is ‰¤ every right element - which, given both arrays are sorted, reduces to two cross comparisons. If the condition fails I know which side contributed too many and halve accordingly. When it holds, the median reads directly off the four boundary values. O(log(min(m,n))) time, O(1) space."

</details>

### Problem 082 - Minimum Days to Make M Bouquets

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** Binary search on answer (day threshold + greedy count)

#### 1. Problem Statement
A garden has `n` flowers in a row; `bloomDay[i]` is the day flower i blooms. You need `m` bouquets, each made of **exactly k adjacent bloomed flowers**. Return the **minimum day** on which you can make all bouquets, or -1 if impossible.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] bloomDay`, `int k`, `int m`, `1 <= n <= 10^5`, `1 <= bloomDay[i] <= 10^7`, `m`, `k` as given (`m * k <= n` is required for feasibility).
- **Output:** `int` - minimum feasible day, else -1.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  bloomDay = [1, 10, 3, 10, 2], k = 1, m = 3
Output: 3
Explanation: by day 3, flowers 0, 2, 4 have bloomed  - three single-flower bouquets.
             day 2 gives only flowers 0 and 4  - 2 bouquets œ-.

Input:  bloomDay = [7, 7, 7, 7, 12, 7, 7], k = 3, m = 2
Output: 12
Explanation: by day 7 only two runs exist: [0..3] (4 flowers) and [5..6] (2)  - 1 + 0 = 1 bouquet œ-.
             day 12: all bloom  - one run of 7  - ŒŠ7/3Œ‹ = 2 bouquets œ".

Edge case: m * k > n  - -1 (impossible by construction).
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** binary search on answer - the answer is a **day**, and feasibility is monotone (*more days never bloom fewer flowers*  - the bouquet count can only increase).

**Recognition:** "minimum day/time such that¦" + a monotone count  - classic answer-space. The check: walk the row, count consecutive runs of bloomed flowers (‰¥ day threshold), and add `runLength / k` for each run.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - simulate day by day from 1 to max(bloomDay), recounting bouquets each day  - **O(maxDay - n)** ‰ˆ 10^7 - 10^5 - impossible.
**9. Why It Fails** - the day range is up to 10^7 and each simulation is O(n). But feasibility flips only once: before some day it fails, after it succeeds  - binary search.
**10. Optimal Approach** - if `m * k > n` return -1. Search `day` in `[min(bloomDay), max(bloomDay)]`. Check: scan the row; count consecutive flowers with `bloomDay[i] <= day`; on each break, add `run / k` to the bouquet count; at the end add the final run. If `bouquets >= m`  - feasible  - `high = mid`, else `low = mid + 1`. Return `low`.

**11. Why It Works** - monotone: waiting longer can only add bloomed flowers, never remove them, so any bouquet made on day d is still makeable on day d+1  - threshold exists. The greedy count is exact (not an approximation): bouquets need *adjacent* flowers, and the maximal runs of bloomed flowers are precisely where bouquets can be formed - `ŒŠrun/kŒ‹` per run counts disjoint bouquets optimally (they can't overlap anyway since each flower is used once).

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int minDays(int[] bloomDay, int k, int m) {
        if ((long) m * k > bloomDay.length) return -1;
        int low = Integer.MAX_VALUE, high = 0;
        for (int d : bloomDay) { low = Math.min(low, d); high = Math.max(high, d); }
        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            if (bouquets(bloomDay, k, mid) >= m) high = mid;
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return low;
    }
    private int bouquets(int[] bloomDay, int k, int day) {
        int made = 0, run = 0;
        for (int d : bloomDay) {
            if (d <= day) { run++; if (run == k) { made++; run = 0; } }
            else run = 0;
        }
        return made;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `run == k` resets immediately (greedy: form a bouquet as soon as k adjacent flowers are available; forming earlier can never reduce the final count). `(long) m * k` avoids overflow in the feasibility shortcut. The search starts at `min(bloomDay)` - no day earlier than the earliest bloom can work.

**15. Dry Run** - `bloomDay = [1,10,3,10,2]`, `k = 1`, `m = 3`

| low | high | mid | bouquets at day = mid | feasible (‰¥ 3) | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | 5 | bloomed: 0,2,4  - 3 singles | œ" | high = 5 |
| 1 | 5 | 3 | bloomed: 0,2,4  - 3 | œ" | high = 3 |
| 1 | 3 | 2 | bloomed: 0,4  - 2 | œ- | low = 3 |
| 3 | 3 | - | - | - | stop  - **3** œ" |

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n - log(maxDay ˆ' minDay)):** ~24 iterations (range ‰¤ 10^7) - O(n) per check. **Space O(1).**

**17. Edge Cases** - `m * k > n`  - -1; `m = 0` (0 days - state the convention); all flowers bloom the same day; `k = 1` (just count bloomed); `k = n` (needs max bloom day); bloom days out of order in the array.

**18. Common Mistakes** - forgetting the `m*k > n` check; searching from day 1 to 10^7 linearly; overlapping bouquets (must reset `run` after each bouquet); starting `low` at 0 when blooms start at 1 (harmless but wasteful).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why binary search**  - The feasibility predicate is monotone in the day - "can I do it by day d" flips once.
**Q: Why is the greedy count correct**  - Bouquets require adjacency and each flower is used once, so maximal runs partition the garden; taking ŒŠrun/kŒ‹ from each is optimal.
**Q: Complexity**  - O(n log D), D = day range.

**20. Variations** - Koko (076, same shape with a different check); ship capacity (077); "earliest day when all tasks complete" (parallel scheduling - a different greedy).

**21. Related Problems** - 076, 077, 079, 085.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Binary search the day. Feasibility is monotone - waiting longer only blooms more flowers - so I ask 'by day X, can I make m bouquets' by scanning the row and counting complete runs of k adjacent bloomed flowers. If the count reaches m I try an earlier day, otherwise a later one. With an initial m·k ‰¤ n check, that's O(n log dayRange) instead of simulating every day."

</details>

### Problem 083 - Kth Missing Positive Number

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Easy-Medium | **Pattern:** Binary search on "how many missing before index i"

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given a **strictly increasing** array of positive integers, return the k-th positive integer that is **missing** from the array.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] arr` strictly increasing, `int k`, `1 <= n <= 1000` (up to 10^3 classic), `1 <= k <= 500`.
- **Output:** `int` - the k-th missing positive.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  arr = [2, 3, 4, 7, 11], k = 5
Output: 9
Explanation: missing positives = 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, ¦  - the 5th is 9.

Input:  arr = [1, 2, 3, 4], k = 2
Output: 6
Explanation: nothing missing before 4  - the missing run continues 5, 6  - 2nd is 6.

Edge case: arr = [5], k = 1  - 1 (missing start from 1).
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** binary search on a **derived monotone quantity**: *"how many positives are missing before position i"* = `arr[i] - (i + 1)` - a non-decreasing function of i.

**Recognition:** increasing array + "k-th missing/absent element"  - the number of missing values grows monotonically with the index  - binary search the first index where that count reaches k.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - walk the positive integers 1, 2, 3, ¦ and skip values present in a set / pointer scan  - O(max(arr)) or O(n) with two pointers but potentially far past the array.
**9. Why It Fails** - the answer can be far beyond `arr[n-1]` (e.g. `arr = [100]`, `k = 50`  - 50 is fine, but `k` can reach past the last element)  - walking positives one by one is O(answer), unbounded relative to n.
**10. Optimal Approach** - binary search the **answer value** itself (the answer-space form from P4.4).

Define, for any positive integer x:
```
missing(x) = number of positive integers <= x that are absent from arr
           = x - #{ a[i] <= x }
```
`missing(x)` is non-decreasing in x (each step adds one positive number, which is either present or missing - never removes one). So the predicate `missing(x) >= k` flips exactly once  - binary search:

1. `low = 1`, `high = arr[n-1] + k` (an upper bound that is always large enough: at worst all k missing values sit above the last element).
2. `mid = low + (high - low) / 2`.
3. `present = #{ a[i] <= mid }` - one upper-bound search on `arr`.
4. If `mid - present >= k`  - at least k missing values are ‰¤ mid  - the k-th missing is at or below mid  - `high = mid`; else `low = mid + 1`.
5. Return `low` - the smallest x with `missing(x) >= k`, which is exactly the k-th missing positive.

**11. Why It Works** - the k-th missing value `v` satisfies: `missing(v) >= k` (v and k values below it are missing  - ‰¥ k) while `missing(v - 1) < k` (only kˆ'1 missing values below v). That is precisely "the smallest x with missing(x) ‰¥ k" - so the binary search lands exactly on v. Monotonicity holds because `missing(x+1) = missing(x) + 1` if x+1 is absent, or `missing(x)` if present - it never decreases.

**12-13. Steps & Java**

```java
class Solution {
    public int findKthPositive(int[] arr, int k) {
        int low = 1, high = arr[arr.length - 1] + k;
        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            int present = countAtMost(arr, mid);   // #{ a[i] <= mid }
            if (mid - present >= k) high = mid;    // k-th missing is at or below mid
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return low;
    }
    private int countAtMost(int[] a, int x) {      // upper bound: first index with a[i] > x
        int lo = 0, hi = a.length;
        while (lo < hi) {
            int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            if (a[mid] <= x) lo = mid + 1;
            else hi = mid;
        }
        return lo;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `countAtMost` is Problem 069's upper bound (count of elements ‰¤ x); reuse it rather than inventing a scan. The predicate uses `mid - present`, where `present` counts elements **‰¤ mid** - both sides of the subtraction refer to the same inclusive boundary, which is what keeps the off-by-one in check. `high = arr[n-1] + k` is provably sufficient: if every array element ‰¤ `arr[n-1]` were present, the missing values would be `arr[n-1]+1 ¦ arr[n-1]+k`.

**15. Dry Run** - `arr = [2, 3, 4, 7, 11]`, `k = 5` (expected answer 9; missing set = {1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, ¦})

| low | high | mid | #{a[i] ‰¤ mid} | missing(‰¤ mid) = mid ˆ' present | ‰¥ 5 | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 16 | 8 | 4 (2,3,4,7) | 8 ˆ' 4 = 4 | œ- | low = 9 |
| 9 | 16 | 12 | 5 (+11) | 12 ˆ' 5 = 7 | œ" | high = 12 |
| 9 | 12 | 10 | 5 | 10 ˆ' 5 = 5 | œ" | high = 10 |
| 9 | 10 | 9 | 4 | 9 ˆ' 4 = 5 | œ" | high = 9 |
| 9 | 9 | - | - | - | - | stop  - **9** œ" |

Cross-check: missing values ‰¤ 9 are {1, 5, 6, 8, 9} - exactly 5 œ", and missing ‰¤ 8 = {1,5,6,8} = 4 < 5, so 9 is indeed the 5th missing positive.
**16. Complexity** - **Time O(log(maxArr + k) - log n)** (or O(log n) with the index-based variant: `arr[i] - (i+1)` is monotone  - one binary search over indices, then an O(1) formula). **Space O(1).**

**17. Edge Cases** - nothing missing before the array (`[1,2,3,4]`, k=2  - 6); `k` larger than gaps inside the array (answer beyond `arr[n-1]`); single element; `arr[0] > k` (answer may be k itself); very large k (upper bound must be `arr[n-1] + k`).

**18. Common Mistakes** - off-by-one between "missing below" and "missing ‰¤ mid" (as demonstrated above - the predicate must count mid itself); using `while (low <= high)` with `high = mid`; linear scanning from 1 (O(answer)); forgetting that the answer can exceed the array's last element.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: O(log n) without a second search**  - Use the index form: missing before index i = `arr[i] - (i+1)`; binary search the first i where that ‰¥ k, then the answer is `arr[i] + (k - (arr[i] - (i+1)))`¦ which simplifies to `arr[i] - (arr[i] - (i+1) - k)`  - compute directly; walk through it with the example.
**Q: Unsorted input**  - HashSet + scan (O(n)) or sort first (O(n log n)).
**Q: Complexity**  - O(log range) or O(log n).

**20. Variations** - Find missing number in 1..N (baseline #8 - the no-duplicates special case); First Missing Positive (018 - unsorted, O(1) space); k-th smallest in a sorted-but-rotated array.

**21. Related Problems** - 018, baseline #8, 068, 069.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I binary search the *value*, not the index. For any candidate x, the number of missing positives ‰¤ x is x minus how many array elements are ‰¤ x - and that count grows monotonically with x. So I look for the smallest x where at least k positives are missing: that x is the k-th missing value itself. Each step needs one inner lower/upper bound on the array, so it's O(log(max + k) · log n) - or O(log n) using the arr[i] ˆ' (i+1) index identity."

</details>

### Problem 084 - Kth Smallest Pair Distance

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Medium-Hard | **Pattern:** Binary search on answer + two-pointer counting

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array `nums` (not necessarily distinct), define a **pair distance** as `|nums[i] - nums[j]|` with `i < j`. There are `n(n-1)/2` pairs. Return the k-th **smallest** distance among them.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums`, `1 <= n <= 10^4`, `1 <= k <= n(n-1)/2`.
- **Output:** `int` - the k-th smallest distance.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [1, 3, 1], k = 3
Output: 2
Explanation: pairs (1,3)=2, (1,1)=0, (3,1)=2  - sorted distances [0, 2, 2]  - 3rd is 2.

Input:  nums = [1, 6, 1], k = 3
Output: 5
Explanation: distances = |1-6|=5, |1-1|=0, |6-1|=5  - [0, 5, 5]  - 3rd = 5.
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** binary search on the answer (a distance) + an O(n) **counting** routine.

**Recognition:** "k-th smallest/largest of some pair-derived value" + n up to 10^4 (so n² pairs = 10^8, borderline)  - don't materialize the pairs; ask *"how many pairs have distance ‰¤ d"* - a monotone count  - binary search d.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - compute all n(nˆ'1)/2 distances, sort them, pick index kˆ'1  - **O(n² log n)** time, O(n²) space (10^8 distances at n = 10^4 - memory blows up first).
**9. Why It Fails** - storing 10^8 integers is ~400 MB and sorting them is slow; the structure (sorted array + monotone count) lets us avoid generating pairs at all.
**10. Optimal Approach** - sort `nums`. Binary search the distance `d` in `[0, max ˆ' min]`. Count pairs with difference ‰¤ d using **two pointers**: for each `i`, advance `j` while `nums[j] - nums[i] <= d`; pairs contributed by `i` are `j - i - 1`. Then:
- if `count >= k`  - the k-th smallest is ‰¤ d  - minimize: `high = mid`
- else `low = mid + 1`
Return `low`.

**11. Why It Works** - `count(d)` = number of pairs with distance ‰¤ d is non-decreasing in d (bigger d only includes more pairs)  - monotone  - binary search finds the smallest d with `count(d) >= k`, which is by definition the k-th smallest distance (exactly the same "smallest x with ‰¥ k things below/equal it" identity used in Problem 083). The counting routine is O(n) amortized because `j` never moves backwards.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public int smallestDistancePair(int[] nums, int k) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);
        int low = 0, high = nums[nums.length - 1] - nums[0];
        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            if (countWithin(nums, mid) >= k) high = mid;   // k-th smallest ‰¤ mid
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return low;
    }
    private int countWithin(int[] a, int maxDiff) {
        int count = 0, j = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
            while (j < a.length && a[j] - a[i] <= maxDiff) j++;
            count += (j - 1) - i;              // pairs (i, i+1 .. j-1)
        }
        return count;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `j` starts at `max(j, i+1)` implicitly because it only grows across iterations (never reset)  - total inner-loop work ‰¤ n  - O(n) counting. `count += (j-1) - i` counts all partners of `i` whose value stays within `maxDiff`.

**15. Dry Run** - `nums = [1, 3, 1]`  - sorted `[1, 1, 3]`, `k = 3`, `low = 0`, `high = 3 ˆ' 1 = 2`

Counting routine (`countWithin(d)` = pairs with difference ‰¤ d):
- `d = 1`: only the pair (1, 1) qualifies  - **count = 1**
- `d = 2`: (1,1)=0, (1,3)=2, (1,3)=2  - **count = 3**

Binary search:

| low | high | mid | countWithin(mid) | ‰¥ 3 | action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2 | 1 | 1 | œ- | low = 2 |
| 2 | 2 | - | - | - | stop  - **2** œ" |

Distances sorted = [0, 2, 2]  - the 3rd smallest is 2 œ" - the search finds the smallest `d` whose count reaches `k`, which is exactly the k-th smallest value.
**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n log n + n - log(range)):** sorting, then ~31 iterations (range ‰¤ 10^4 for classic constraints, up to 10^9 in variants) - O(n) counting. **Space O(1)** beyond sorting (the brute force would be O(n²)).

**17. Edge Cases** - all elements equal (all distances 0  - answer 0); duplicates (they create distance-0 pairs - the `<=` in counting includes them); k = 1 (0 if any duplicate, else the smallest gap); k = n(nˆ'1)/2 (the maximum distance = span); n = 2 (single pair).

**18. Common Mistakes** - forgetting to sort (counting requires order); resetting `j` to `i+1` every iteration  - O(n²) counting (works but slow - mention the trade-off); using `count >= k` with `low = mid` (minimize form needs `high = mid`); integer overflow in `(long) count` when n reaches 10^5+ (10^10 pairs don't fit `int`).

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why not generate all pairs**  - n² pairs at n = 10^4 = 10^8 - memory and time blow up; the count predicate avoids materializing them.
**Q: Why is counting O(n)**  - `j` only moves forward across the whole loop - the same two-pointer amortization as a window.
**Q: Generalization**  - k-th smallest sum/difference of pairs (LC 373 family - needs a heap instead), k-th smallest in a sorted matrix (binary search on value with a count).

**20. Variations** - K-th smallest pair **sum** (heap + binary search); k-th smallest in a row/column-sorted matrix (same count idea); find the pair with the smallest distance (just scan after sorting).

**21. Related Problems** - 083, 078, 065, 055.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I binary search the distance itself. For a candidate d, counting pairs within distance d on a sorted array is a two-pointer sweep in O(n): for each left index I advance the right pointer while the difference stays within d, and the number of valid partners is the span between them. Since that count only grows with d, the smallest d whose count reaches k is exactly the k-th smallest distance. O(n log n + n log range) time, constant extra space."

</details>

### Problem 085 - Smallest Divisor for a Threshold

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
Given an array of positive integers and a `threshold`, choose the smallest divisor such that the **sum of the element-wise ceiling divisions** is **‰¤ threshold**.

- **Input:** `int[] nums` (positive), `int threshold`, `1 <= n <= 10^4`, `1 <= nums[i] <= 10^4`, `threshold >= n`.
- **Output:** `int` - the minimum divisor.

```
Input:  nums = [1, 2, 5, 9], threshold = 6
Output: 5
Explanation: divisor 5  - Œˆ1/5Œ‰+Œˆ2/5Œ‰+Œˆ5/5Œ‰+Œˆ9/5Œ‰ = 1+1+1+2 = 5 ‰¤ 6 œ"
             divisor 4  - 1+1+2+3 = 7 > 6 œ-
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** minimize a feasible value - binary search on answer with an O(n) sum check (Koko's twin).

```java
class Solution {
    public int smallestDivisor(int[] nums, int threshold) {
        int low = 1, high = 0;
        for (int x : nums) high = Math.max(high, x);
        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            long sum = 0;
            for (int x : nums) sum += (x + (long) mid - 1) / mid;
            if (sum <= threshold) high = mid; else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return low;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(n log maxVal). **Mistakes:** forgetting ceil division (`(x + mid - 1) / mid`); `int` overflow in the sum; starting `high` at `threshold` instead of max value.
**60 seconds:** "Bigger divisors only shrink the ceiling sum, so feasibility is monotone  - binary search the divisor between 1 and max(nums). The check is a linear pass with integer ceiling division."

</details>

### Problem 086 - Minimum Speed to Arrive on Time

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
A train journey has `n` legs with distances `dist[]`. For all legs **except the last**, the arrival time per leg is `ceil(dist[i] / speed)`; the **last** leg's time is exact `dist[n-1] / speed`. Find the minimum integer speed such that the total time is **‰¤ hour**. Return ˆ'1 if impossible (it always exists for speed  - ˆž here, but verify the boundary).

- **Input:** `double hour`, `int[] dist` (positive), `1 <= n <= 10^4`, `1 <= dist[i] <= 10^5`, `1 <= hour <= 10^7`.
- **Output:** `int` - minimum speed (1..10^7), or ˆ'1 if even speed 10^7 can't make it.

```
Input:  dist = [1, 3, 2], hour = 2.7
Output: 3
Explanation: speed 3  - 1 + 1 + 2/3 = 2.667 ‰¤ 2.7 œ" ; speed 2  - 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 > 2.7 œ-
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** minimize a feasible value (binary search on answer) with a **floating-point check** - note the last leg uses exact division (no ceiling), which is the classic trap.

```java
class Solution {
    public int minSpeedOnTime(double hour, int[] dist) {
        if (dist.length - 1 > hour) return -1;        // even infinite speed can't help
        int low = 1, high = 10_000_000;
        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            if (feasible(dist, hour, mid)) high = mid;
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return low;
    }
    private boolean feasible(int[] dist, double hour, int speed) {
        double time = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < dist.length - 1; i++) time += Math.ceil((double) dist[i] / speed);
        time += (double) dist[dist.length - 1] / speed;
        return time <= hour;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(n log 10^7) ‰ˆ 24 passes over n. **Mistakes:** using ceil on the last leg; using `double` comparison without an epsilon (values like 2.7 can be 2.7000000001 - add a tiny tolerance if the judge is strict); forgetting the `dist.length - 1 > hour` impossibility check (each non-last leg takes ‰¥ 1 unit of time at any speed).
**60 seconds:** "Speed only reduces travel time, so feasibility is monotone  - binary search speed from 1 to 10^7, checking in O(n). I split the sum: ceiling division for every leg except the last, exact division for the last leg - that asymmetry is the trap in this problem."

</details>

---

### Problem 087 - Row With Maximum Ones

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Easy-Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
Given an `m - n` matrix where **each row is sorted** (0s then 1s), return the index of the row containing the **most 1s** (and the count). Aim for better than O(m - n).

- **Input:** `int[][] mat`, `1 <= m, n <= 100` (or up to 10^4 in variants).
- **Output:** `int[2]` - {rowIndex, count}.

```
Input:  mat = [[1,0,1],
                [1,1,1],
                [1,0,0]]
Output: [1, 3]
Explanation: row 1 has three 1s - the maximum.
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** binary search per row - count of 1s = `n - lowerBound(row, 1)` (Problem 068 applied m times). A slicker O(m + n) walk also exists (start at the top-right corner and move left/down).

```java
class Solution {
    public int[] rowAndOnes(int[][] mat) {
        int bestRow = 0, bestCount = -1;
        for (int i = 0; i < mat.length; i++) {
            int first = lowerBound(mat[i], 1);
            int count = mat[i].length - first;
            if (count > bestCount) { bestCount = count; bestRow = i; }
        }
        return new int[] {bestRow, bestCount};
    }
    private int lowerBound(int[] row, int x) {
        int lo = 0, hi = row.length;
        while (lo < hi) { int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;
            if (row[mid] < x) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid; }
        return lo;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(m log n) with binary search, or O(m + n) with the corner walk (move left when you see a 1, move down when you see a 0 - never revisits a cell). **Mistakes:** counting linearly per row (O(m·n)); forgetting rows are sorted (the precondition that makes either approach valid).
**60 seconds:** "Each row is sorted, so the number of ones is n minus the index of the first 1 - a lower bound. Doing that per row is O(m log n); alternatively I walk from the top-right corner, moving left on a 1 and down on a 0, which is O(m + n)."

</details>

### Problem 088 - Find the Duplicate Number

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden - two valid approaches)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
An array of `n + 1` integers contains values in `1..n`, so at least one value is repeated. Find the repeated value **without modifying the array** and using only **O(1) extra space**.

- **Input:** `int[] nums`, `2 <= n+1 <= 10^5`, exactly one value may repeat (others appear once).
- **Output:** `int` - the repeated value.

```
Input:  nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2]      - 2
Input:  nums = [3, 1, 3, 4, 2]      - 3
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern A - binary search on value (fits this phase):** count how many array values are ‰¤ mid; if that count > mid, the duplicate is ‰¤ mid (pigeonhole: values in 1..mid number `mid`, but more than `mid` of them are present)  - `high = mid`, else `low = mid + 1`. O(log n) time, O(1) space, no array modification.

```java
class Solution {
    public int findDuplicate(int[] nums) {
        int low = 1, high = nums.length - 1;
        while (low < high) {
            int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            int count = 0;
            for (int x : nums) if (x <= mid) count++;
            if (count > mid) high = mid;    // duplicate lies in [low, mid]
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return low;
    }
}
```
**Why it works:** with values 1..n and n+1 slots, `count(‰¤ mid) > mid` means some value ‰¤ mid occurs twice. The predicate is monotone (the duplicate value always satisfies it; smaller values don't)  - binary search.

**Pattern B - Floyd's tortoise and hare (O(1) space, O(n) time):** treat `nums[i]` as a pointer: `i  - nums[i]`. Because a value repeats, the sequence must enter a cycle; find the cycle entrance (the duplicate) with the standard two-phase algorithm.

**Complexity:** A  - O(n log n) time, O(1) space (read-only œ"). B  - O(n) time, O(1) space (also read-only œ").
**Mistakes:** modifying the array (violates the constraint); XOR tricks (they find a value missing-or-duplicated pattern, not reliable when *multiple* values could repeat); using a HashSet (O(n) space - forbidden).
**60 seconds:** "Binary search the value space: count how many entries are ‰¤ mid. If more than mid entries are ‰¤ mid, pigeonhole says some value in 1..mid repeats, so the duplicate is in the lower half; otherwise it's in the upper half. O(log n) rounds, O(1) space, array untouched - and I'd mention Floyd's cycle detection as the O(n) alternative."

</details>

---

### Problem 089 - Repair Cars

**Category:** Advanced Binary Search | **Difficulty:** Medium | **Pattern:** (hidden)

#### Question - attempt before expanding
A mechanic has `n` cars to repair and `ranks[]` (each mechanic's skill). A mechanic with rank `r` repairs `c` cars in time `r - c²`. Cars may be split arbitrarily among mechanics. Return the **minimum time** needed to repair all cars.

- **Input:** `int[] ranks`, `int cars`, `1 <= ranks.length <= 10^4`, `1 <= ranks[i] <= 100`, `1 <= cars <= 10^6`.
- **Output:** `long` - the minimum achievable time.

```
Input:  ranks = [1, 2, 3], cars = 6
Output: 20
Explanation: give 3, 2, 1 cars to the three mechanics  - 1·9 + 2·4 + 3·1 = 9 + 8 + 3 = 20.
             Equal split (2,2,2)  - 4 + 8 + 12 = 24 - worse.
```

<details><summary>Show Pattern & Solution</summary>

**Pattern:** minimize a feasible value - binary search on answer with a greedy **maximum production** check.

**Feasibility:** given time `T`, mechanic with rank `r` can finish at most `floor(sqrt(T / r))` cars (since `r·c² ‰¤ T`). If the sum over all mechanics ‰¥ `cars`, T is feasible. Monotone: more time  - never fewer cars  - threshold exists.

```java
class Solution {
    public long repairCars(int[] ranks, int cars) {
        long low = 1;
        long high = 0;
        int maxRank = 0;
        for (int r : ranks) maxRank = Math.max(maxRank, r);
        high = (long) maxRank * cars * cars;   // one mechanic does everything - always feasible
        while (low < high) {
            long mid = low + (high - low) / 2;
            long produced = 0;
            for (int r : ranks) {
                produced += (long) Math.sqrt(mid / r);
                if (produced >= cars) break;
            }
            if (produced >= cars) high = mid;
            else low = mid + 1;
        }
        return low;
    }
}
```
**Complexity:** O(ranks - log(maxRank - cars²)) - about 60 iterations - 10^4 = 6-10^5 operations. **Space O(1).**
**Mistakes:** `int` overflow in `rank * cars²` (cars up to 10^6  - 10^12 - must be `long`); using `Math.sqrt` on an already-integer division without care (do `mid / r` in integer/`long` first); non-monotone feasibility (it is monotone - verify before applying binary search); forgetting the single-mechanic upper bound.
**60 seconds:** "Binary search the time. For a candidate T, each mechanic with rank r can repair at most floor(sqrt(T/r)) cars - sum that greedily and compare with the required count. More time never lowers production, so feasibility is monotone. O(m log(range)) with long arithmetic throughout."

</details>

## Common Mistakes From Phase 4

1. **Mixing conventions:** `while (low <= high)` with inclusive bounds vs `while (low < high)` with `high = n` - pick one pair and never split them.
2. **`high = mid - 1` while minimizing**  - discards a feasible answer (the #1 answer-space bug).
3. **Floor mid + `low = mid`** in the maximize form  - infinite loop when `low + 1 == high`. Use the upper mid: `low + (high - low + 1) / 2`.
4. **`(low + high) / 2`**  - use `low + (high - low) / 2` (overflow habit).
5. **Unproven bounds** - always say out loud: "`low` is definitely infeasible, `high` is definitely feasible."
6. **Non-monotone feasibility** - a predicate that flips back and forth silently produces wrong answers. Test it: does improving the candidate ever *hurt*
7. **`int` overflow in the check** (sums of 10^13, squares near 2^31)  - `long`.
8. **Forgetting early exit** in feasibility checks (correct but slow - mention it).
9. **Scanning linearly on sorted data** - always ask "what does sortedness buy me"
10. **Not stating why binary search applies** - answer interviews with *monotonicity*, not "it felt like binary search."
11. **Wrong mid rounding for the objective** - minimize  - floor mid + `high = mid`; maximize  - upper mid + `low = mid`.
12. **Ignoring duplicates** in rotated arrays (the `nums[low] == nums[mid]` ambiguity  - O(n) worst case).

# Phase 5 - Recursion + Backtracking

**Goal:** learn to *design* a recursive process - base case, state, choices, undo - instead of memorizing formulas.

**Prerequisites (your baseline):** #36 Factorial, #37 Fibonacci (naive). You know that a function can call itself; this phase teaches when that's correct and how to make it fast.

## Pattern Chapter - Recursion + Backtracking

### P5.1 Recursion in Two Sentences

A recursive function solves a problem by **expressing it in terms of a smaller instance of itself**, and stops when the instance is small enough to answer directly. Every correct recursion needs:

1. **Base case** - the smallest input, answered without recursing.
2. **Recursive case** - reduce the problem, assume the recursion answers the smaller part, combine.

### P5.2 The Call Stack (why base cases matter)

Each call gets its **own stack frame** with its own local variables. Frames are destroyed on return - that's why a recursive helper's state (like a path list) must be shared *carefully* (reference) or copied deliberately.

```
fib(4)
"œ"" fib(3)
"'   "œ"" fib(2)
"'   "'   "œ"" fib(1)   - 1   (base)
"'   "'   """" fib(0)   - 0   (base)
"'   """" fib(1)       - 1   (base)
"""" fib(2)
    "œ"" fib(1)       - 1
    """" fib(0)       - 0
```

Count the calls: `fib(4)` spawns 9 calls but only 4 *distinct* subproblems (0,1,2,3). **Recomputation is the enemy** - this exact tree is the motivation for DP (Phase 13). Also note depth: `fib(n)` recurses n levels deep; Java's default stack handles ~10^4 frames, not 10^6 - mention depth in interviews.

### P5.3 Recursion vs Backtracking vs Dynamic Programming

| | Recursion | Backtracking | DP |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Question** | "How do I break this down" | "How do I explore all choices and undo" | "How do I stop solving the same subproblem twice" |
| **State** | input parameters | input + a mutable "path/decision" | a table/memo keyed by state |
| **Output** | one answer | **all** valid configurations (or the first) | one optimal value/count |
| **Repeated subproblems** | tolerated | tolerated (but pruned) | forbidden  - memoized |
| **Typical depth** | O(n) | O(n) (depth of the choice tree) | O(1) recursion (or iterative) |
| **Example** | sum of array, power | subsets, permutations, N-Queens | knapsack, LCS |

Rule of thumb: **exploring choices with an undo step  - backtracking; an optimal value over overlapping states  - DP; a single divide-and-conquer reduction  - plain recursion.**

### P5.4 The Backtracking Skeleton (choose  - explore  - undo)

```java
void backtrack(State state, List<Choice> options) {
    if (isGoal(state)) { record(state); return; }   // 1. base / goal
    if (shouldPrune(state)) return;                  // 2. prune (optional but powerful)
    for (Choice c : options) {
        if (!isValid(state, c)) continue;            // 3. filter
        choose(state, c);                            // 4. choose
        backtrack(state, nextOptions);               // 5. explore
        undo(state, c);                              // 6. UNDO - the step people forget
    }
}
```

**Why undo instead of copying state** Copying at every node costs O(state) per branch  - O(state - nodes). Undoing costs O(1) per branch (usually one `add`/`remove` or one swap) - same result, far less memory.

### P5.5 The Decision Tree (what you draw in an interview)

For `subsets([1, 2, 3])`:

```
[]
"œ"" choose 1
"'   "œ"" choose 2
"'   "'   "œ"" choose 3  - [1,2,3]
"'   "'   """" (skip 3)   - [1,2]
"'   """" (skip 2)
"'       "œ"" choose 3  - [1,3]
"'       """" (skip 3)   - [1]
"œ"" choose 2
"'   "œ"" choose 3  - [2,3]
"'   """" (skip 3)   - [2]
"""" choose 3  - [3]
         + the empty set []
```

Every leaf is an answer; every path is a partial configuration. **Draw this** whenever you design a backtracking solution - it makes base cases and duplicates obvious.

### P5.6 State, Choice, Prune - the three design questions

1. **State:** what must the recursion know (index, current path, remaining budget¦). If two branches with the same state would do identical work, that's a memoization signal (DP).
2. **Choice:** which options are available at this level (next element, next digit, next row¦). The loop over choices defines the tree's width.
3. **Prune:** what makes a branch hopeless Any test that kills a branch *early* (sum already too big, a queen already attacked) can cut an exponential tree dramatically - often the difference between passing and timing out.

### P5.7 Common Mistakes

1. Forgetting the `undo` after the recursive call  - the path accumulates garbage.
2. Recording the path *by reference* (`res.add(path)`) - every answer ends up being the same live list  - always `new ArrayList<>(path)`.
3. Base case off-by-one (returning one level too early/late)  - missing or duplicated answers.
4. Not sorting + skipping duplicates (Subsets II / Combination Sum II)  - duplicate outputs.
5. Infinite recursion (state not actually getting smaller).
6. Missing the prune  - exponential blow-up on constraints that were designed for pruning.
7. Deep recursion on n = 10^5 input (stack overflow)  - this phase's problems keep n ‰¤ ~20 for that reason; say so.

### P5.8 Complexity Intuition

| Problem shape | Leaves | Total nodes | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Subsets (n elements, include/skip) | 2¿ | ~2·2¿ | O(n·2¿) |
| Permutations (n!) orderings | n! | Î£ P(n,k) ‰ˆ e·n! | O(n·n!) |
| Combinations of size k | C(n,k) | Î£ C(n,i) = 2¿ | O(n·2¿) |
| N-Queens (n rows) | ~n! pruned | much less with checks | O(n!) with pruning |

When constraints say `n ‰¤ 20`, they're telling you O(2¿) is intended; `n ‰¤ 8` for permutations, `n ‰¤ 9` for N-Queens-like problems.

### Problem 090 - Sum of First N Numbers (Recursion)

**Category:** Recursion | **Difficulty:** Easy | **Pattern:** Linear recursion (warm-up: base case + recursive case)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Compute `1 + 2 + ¦ + n` recursively - without a loop.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int n`, `0 <= n <= 10^4` (recursion depth = n, so bounds are small by design).
- **Output:** `long` - the sum (or int for small n).

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  n = 5    - 15        (5 + sum(4))
Input:  n = 0    - 0         (base case)
Edge case: n = 1  - 1
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** linear recursion - one recursive call per step, depth = n.

**Recognition:** "do it recursively" + a natural 1-based structure  - base case at 0/1, recursive case reduces n by 1. This is the shape you must be able to write *and trace* before Phase 13.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - a for loop (or the closed formula n(n+1)/2)  - O(n) / O(1). Correct, but the exercise is the recursive form.
**9. Why It "Fails"** - it's not about speed here: recursion builds the habit of *stating a base case and trusting a smaller call*, which subsets/permutations require. (Also note the O(n) stack depth - Java's default stack overflows around ~10^4 frames.)
**10. Optimal (recursive) Approach** - `sum(0) = 0`; `sum(n) = n + sum(n-1)`.

**11. Why It Works** - induction in code: assume `sum(n-1)` correctly returns 1+¦+(n-1); adding n makes it correct for n. The base case stops the descent. Every call returns before its parent needs it  - values flow back up the stack.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public long sum(int n) {
        if (n == 0) return 0;              // base case
        return n + sum(n - 1);             // recursive case: smaller instance
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `n == 0` (not `n == 1`) keeps n = 0 correct without a special branch. `n + sum(n-1)`: the `+ n` happens *after* the recursive call returns - that's why calls unwind in reverse order.

**15. Dry Run (call/return flow)**
```
sum(3)
 "œ" 3 + sum(2)
 "'        "œ" 2 + sum(1)
 "'        "'        "œ" 1 + sum(0)
 "'        "'        "'        """ return 0
 "'        "'        """ return 1
 "'        """ return 3
 """ return 6
```
Each frame holds its own `n` while waiting  - no state is lost.

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n)** (n calls, each O(1) work). **Space O(n)** recursion stack - the frames *are* the space cost; mention that a loop would be O(1).

**17. Edge Cases** - n = 0 (base case must handle it); n = 1; large n (stack overflow near 10^4 - the constraints hint at this).

**18. Common Mistakes** - missing base case (StackOverflowError); base case that doesn't match the formula for n = 0/1; making the recursive step not smaller (`sum(n)` calling `sum(n)`); forgetting that the addition happens on the unwind.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Why recursion over a loop**  - Demonstrates the base-case/reduction structure that backtracking and DP build on; I'd also give the O(1) formula as a follow-up.
**Q: Space complexity**  - O(n) stack frames; tail-recursion optimization doesn't exist in Java.
**Q: What's the risk at large n**  - StackOverflowError - recursion depth is bounded by the stack, not the heap.

**20. Variations** - Sum of array (pass an index instead of shrinking n); reverse an array recursively (091); power(x, n) (093 - divide and conquer, O(log n)).

**21. Related Problems** - 091, 092, 093, baseline #36, #37.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Base case: sum of zero is zero. Recursive case: the sum up to n is n plus the sum up to nˆ'1 - assuming that smaller call is correct, the result for n follows immediately. Each call waits on its child and adds its own n on the way back up. That's O(n) calls with O(n) stack space - and I'd mention the closed-form O(1) solution as the pragmatic alternative."

</details>

### Problem 091 - Reverse an Array Recursively

**Category:** Recursion | **Difficulty:** Easy | **Pattern:** Two-pointer recursion (shrink from both ends)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Reverse an array **in place using recursion** (no loops).

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] arr`, `1 <= n <= 10^4`.
- **Output:** `void` - array reversed in place.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]    - [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
Input:  arr = [1, 2]             - [2, 1]
Edge case: arr = [7]             - [7] (base case: single element needs no swap)
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** recursion with **two indices** - the "state" is a pair, not a shrinking single value.

**Recognition:** "recursively" + symmetric operation from both ends  - `reverse(left, right)`: swap, then recurse on `(left+1, right-1)`; stop when `left >= right`.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - iterative two-pointer swap (your baseline #4/#27)  - O(n)/O(1). Or build a reversed copy  - O(n) space.
**9. Why It Differs** - the point here is recursion on *two* indices: the base case must cover two shapes (`left >= right`), which catches the odd/even length distinction.
**10. Approach** - `reverse(l, r)`: if `l >= r` return; swap; `reverse(l+1, r-1)`.

**11. Why It Works** - each call fixes the outermost unfinished pair and reduces the subproblem by two elements; the base case hits the middle element (odd length) or the crossing point (even). Total calls = Œˆn/2Œ‰, each swapping once  - each position touched exactly once.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public void reverse(int[] arr) {
        reverse(arr, 0, arr.length - 1);
    }
    private void reverse(int[] arr, int left, int right) {
        if (left >= right) return;               // base case (handles odd & even)
        int t = arr[left]; arr[left] = arr[right]; arr[right] = t;
        reverse(arr, left + 1, right - 1);        // smaller instance
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `left >= right` (not `==`) is the safe base: with two indices moving toward each other, `==` is only hit for odd lengths; `>=` covers both.

**15. Dry Run** - `arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]`

| frame | left | right | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 4 | swap  - [5,2,3,4,1]  - recurse(1,3) |
| 2 | 1 | 3 | swap  - [5,4,3,2,1]  - recurse(2,2) |
| 3 | 2 | 2 | `left >= right`  - return |
| 2 | - | - | returns (swap already done) |
| 1 | - | - | returns |

Result **[5,4,3,2,1]** œ" (Note: swaps happen *before* the recursive call - nothing to undo here.)

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n):** Œˆn/2Œ‰ calls, O(1) each. **Space O(n)** recursion depth (‰ˆ n/2 frames) - worth stating that the iterative version is O(1) space.

**17. Edge Cases** - single element; two elements; empty array (`length - 1 = -1`  - `0 >= -1`  - returns immediately œ"); even vs odd length.

**18. Common Mistakes** - base case `left == right` only (breaks even lengths  - keeps swapping past the middle); swapping *after* the recursive call (works too, but easy to mis-order); forgetting the swap entirely and just recursing.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Depth**  - Œˆn/2Œ‰ frames - for n = 10^4 that's fine; for 10^6 it would overflow.
**Q: Could I return a new array instead**  - Yes, `out[n-1-i] = arr[i]`, but that's O(n) space and not in-place.
**Q: Recursion or iteration**  - Iteration is the production answer; recursion demonstrates the frame model.

**20. Variations** - Reverse a string recursively; reverse a linked list recursively (Phase 6); rotate array (014, built from reverses).

**21. Related Problems** - 014, 113, baseline #4, #27.

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I recurse on two indices: swap the ends, then solve the same problem for the inner subarray. The base case is `left >= right`, which covers both odd lengths (they meet in the middle) and even lengths (they cross). Each call shrinks the range by two, so it's n/2 calls with constant work each - in-place, O(n) time."

</details>

### Problem 092 - Check Palindrome Recursively

**Category:** Recursion | **Difficulty:** Easy | **Pattern:** Two-pointer recursion with a boolean AND

#### 1. Problem Statement
Determine whether a string is a palindrome **using recursion**.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `String s`, `0 <= n <= 10^4` (letters only, or ignore case/symbols - state the convention).
- **Output:** `boolean`.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  s = "racecar"   - true   (r==r, a==a, c==c, middle e)
Input:  s = "hello"     - false  (h vs o differ)
Edge case: s = ""  - true ; s = "a"  - true ; s = "ab"  - false
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** two-pointer recursion with **short-circuit** - first mismatch propagates `false` all the way up.

**Recognition:** recursive palindrome check  - compare ends; if equal, recurse inward; if not, stop immediately. Same shape as Problem 091 but returning a value instead of mutating.

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - reverse the string and compare (baseline #12)  - O(n) time, O(n) space; or iterate with two pointers  - O(n)/O(1).
**9. Why It Differs** - recursion here shows **value propagation**: a `false` found deep must not be overwritten by later `true` returns - that's what `&&` handles.
**10. Approach** - `isPalindrome(l, r)`: if `l >= r`  - true; if `s[l] != s[r]`  - false; else  - `isPalindrome(l+1, r-1)`.

**11. Why It Works** - induction: if the inner substring is a palindrome and the outer pair matches, the whole is; one mismatch anywhere returns false for its frame, and every parent ANDs that false upward. Short-circuiting `&&` means we stop recursing the moment a mismatch is found.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
        return check(s, 0, s.length() - 1);
    }
    private boolean check(String s, int l, int r) {
        if (l >= r) return true;                    // empty or single char
        if (s.charAt(l) != s.charAt(r)) return false;
        return check(s, l + 1, r - 1);
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - the mismatch check **returns before recursing**, so the call depth equals the number of *matching* pairs, not the full length (a short-circuit benefit worth mentioning).

**15. Dry Run** - `s = "abca"`

| frame | l | r | chars | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 3 | a == a |  - check(1,2) |
| 2 | 1 | 2 | b != c | **false** |
| 1 | - | - | - | false (propagated) |

Result **false** œ" (`"abca"` is not a palindrome - this is the input from Problem 050's branch case.)

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n/2) = O(n):** each matching pair is one frame. **Space O(n/2) = O(n)** stack depth (worst case: a palindrome, since a non-palindrome stops early).

**17. Edge Cases** - empty string; single character; two characters (equal or not); even/odd length; string with spaces/case (define normalization first).

**18. Common Mistakes** - `if (l == r)` base case only (breaks even lengths); reversing the whole string as "the recursive solution"; ignoring normalization (case/punctuation) when the problem mentions it.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: Base case for odd vs even**  - `l >= r` covers both: odd lengths meet in the middle; even lengths cross.
**Q: Space complexity**  - O(n) stack in the worst case (a palindrome) - an iterative version is O(1).
**Q: Follow-up - at most one mismatch allowed**  - Problem 050 (Valid Palindrome II).

**20. Variations** - Recursive substring checks; valid palindrome with one deletion (050); longest palindromic substring (expanding around centers - Phase 13 preview).

**21. Related Problems** - 050, 091, 282 (LPS, DP).

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Compare the two ends: if they differ, the string isn't a palindrome - return false immediately. If they match, recurse on the inner substring. The base case `left >= right` handles both even and odd lengths, and because `&&` short-circuits, the first mismatch stops the whole chain. O(n) time, O(n) stack in the worst case."

</details>

### Problem 093 - Power (x, n)

**Category:** Recursion | **Difficulty:** Easy-Medium | **Pattern:** Divide and conquer (exponentiation by squaring)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Compute `x^n` (x raised to integer power n) recursively, without using `Math.pow`.

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `double x`, `int n` where `-2^31 <= n <= 2^31 - 1`.
- **Output:** `double`.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  x = 2.0, n = 10    - 1024.0
Input:  x = 2.0, n = -2    - 0.25       (1 / 2^2)
Edge case: n = 0  - 1.0 (even for x = 0  - 1 by convention)
           n = Integer.MIN_VALUE  - handle: negate in long to avoid overflow
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** divide & conquer - **exponentiation by squaring**: `x^n = (x²)^(n/2)` for even n, `x · x^(n-1)` for odd n.

**Recognition:** "power/exponent quickly" + recursion  - halving the exponent gives **O(log n)** instead of O(n) multiplications. This is the canonical "make the recursive step *bigger*" example (you reduce n by *half*, not by 1).

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - multiply x by itself n times  - O(n) multiplications (n up to 2^31  - ~2 billion - too slow).
**9. Why It Fails** - linear in the exponent; the constraints are literally telling you to use log time. Negative n also needs explicit handling in any version.
**10. Optimal Approach** - `myPow(x, n)`: if n < 0  - `1 / myPow(x, -(long) n)`; recursive: even  - `half * half`; odd  - `x * pow(x, n-1)` (or the cleaner `half * half * x` form).

**11. Why It Works** - `x^2k = (x^k)²` and `x^(2k+1) = x · (x^k)²` - both identities mean each recursion **halves the exponent**  - depth ‰ˆ log''(n) ‰¤ 31 for a 32-bit exponent. Correctness follows by induction on those identities.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public double myPow(double x, int n) {
        if (n == 0) return 1.0;
        long exp = n;                          // long: MIN_VALUE cannot be negated as int
        if (exp < 0) { x = 1 / x; exp = -exp; }
        double half = myPow(x, (int) (exp / 2));
        double result = half * half;
        return (exp % 2 == 1)  result * x : result;
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - converting to `long` first is essential: `-Integer.MIN_VALUE` overflows back to itself. Flipping `x = 1/x` up front turns the negative case into a positive one (only once), keeping the recursion clean. `exp / 2` with integer division truncates correctly for positive `exp`.

**15. Dry Run** - `x = 2.0`, `n = 10`

| frame | exp | even | computes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | œ" | half = pow(2,5)  - result = half² |
| 2 | 5 | œ- | half = pow(2,2)  - result = half² - 2 |
| 3 | 2 | œ" | half = pow(2,1)  - result = half² |
| 4 | 1 | œ- | half = pow(2,0) = 1  - result = 1 - 2 = 2 |
| 3 | - | - | 2² = 4 |
| 2 | - | - | 4² - 2 = 32 |
| 1 | - | - | 32² = **1024** œ" |

Depth = Œˆlog''(10)Œ‰ + 1 ‰ˆ 4 frames instead of 10 multiplications.

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(log n):** the exponent halves each call (‰¤ 31 levels for any int exponent). **Space O(log n)** recursion depth (an iterative version using a running base is O(1)).

**17. Edge Cases** - `n = 0` (1.0); negative n (invert x); `n = Integer.MIN_VALUE` (long cast - the classic trap); `x = 0` with `n < 0` (divide by zero  - infinity; state the convention); `x = 1` or `-1`.

**18. Common Mistakes** - O(n) linear recursion (times out); negating `Integer.MIN_VALUE` as an int (overflow  - wrong huge positive); recursion on `n-1` for negative n (infinite loop); returning 1 for `0^0` without noting the convention.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: How many multiplications**  - ‰¤ 2·log''(n) (one per level, sometimes two).
**Q: Iterative version**  - Running product: square the base while halving the exponent, multiply in when the bit is set - O(log n)/O(1).
**Q: Why use long for n**  - `Integer.MIN_VALUE` has no positive int counterpart.

**20. Variations** - Fibonacci in O(log n) (matrix exponentiation, advanced); modular exponentiation (keep the modulus in every multiply); sqrt via binary search (075).

**21. Related Problems** - 075, baseline #37, 273 (climbing stairs - the DP contrast).

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "Instead of multiplying n times, I square and halve: for an even exponent, x^n = (x^(n/2))²; for an odd one, one extra factor of x. Each call halves the exponent, so depth is log n - about 31 multiplications for any 32-bit exponent. I cast n to long first because Integer.MIN_VALUE can't be safely negated, and I handle the sign by inverting x once at the start."

</details>

### Problem 094 - Generate All Subsequences

**Category:** Recursion | **Difficulty:** Easy-Medium | **Pattern:** Include/exclude recursion (the subsets engine)

#### 1. Problem Statement
Given an array of **distinct** integers, generate **all possible subsequences** (any subset of elements in their original order, including the empty subsequence).

#### 2. Input - 3. Output - 4. Constraints
- **Input:** `int[] nums`, `0 <= n <= 12` (2¿ outputs - the constraint is really saying "small n").
- **Output:** `List<List<Integer>>` - all 2¿ subsequences.

#### 5. Examples
```
Input:  nums = [1, 2, 3]
Output: [[], [1], [2], [1,2], [3], [1,3], [2,3], [1,2,3]]     (8 = 2³ subsequences)

Edge case: nums = []  - [[]]  (only the empty subsequence)
Input:  nums = [1]  - [[], [1]]
```

#### 6. Pattern - 7. How to Recognize
**Pattern:** include/exclude recursion - at each index, branch into "take it" and "skip it".

**Recognition:** "all subsequences/subsets/combinations"  - at element i you have exactly two choices  - binary decision tree with depth n  - 2¿ leaves. This is the foundation for Subsets (095), Combination Sum (099), and much of DP (a subsequence is a DP state in disguise).

<details><summary>Show Brute Force  - Solution (attempt first)</summary>

**8. Brute Force** - "generate everything then filter" - for subsequences there's nothing to filter, so the brute force *is* the answer; the alternative brute force is bit manipulation: for mask in `0..2¿-1`, include element i if bit i is set  - O(n · 2¿).
**9. Why It's Still Worth Doing Recursively** - bit masks are fine but don't teach the decision-tree shape that harder problems (with pruning) require. Also, with constraints ("no two adjacent", "sum = target") the recursive version prunes; the mask version cannot.
**10. Approach** - `gen(i, path)`: if `i == n`  - record a copy of `path`  - return. Otherwise: (a) **skip** `nums[i]`  - `gen(i+1, path)`; (b) **take** it  - `path.add(nums[i])`, `gen(i+1, path)`, `path.remove(last)` (undo).

**11. Why It Works** - every subsequence is uniquely determined by a sequence of take/skip decisions, so every leaf of the decision tree corresponds to exactly one subsequence, and every subsequence corresponds to exactly one root-to-leaf path  - no duplicates, none missing. The `i == n` base fires once per path  - exactly 2¿ recordings.

**12-13. Steps & Java**
```java
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> subsequences(int[] nums) {
        List<List<Integer>> res = new ArrayList<>();
        build(nums, 0, new ArrayList<>(), res);
        return res;
    }
    private void build(int[] nums, int i, List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> res) {
        if (i == nums.length) {                  // base: decided on every element
            res.add(new ArrayList<>(path));      // COPY - see the common-mistakes note
            return;
        }
        build(nums, i + 1, path, res);           // skip nums[i]
        path.add(nums[i]);                       // choose
        build(nums, i + 1, path, res);           // explore
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);            // UNDO
    }
}
```

**14. Code Explanation** - `new ArrayList<>(path)` is mandatory: `res.add(path)` would store the *same live list* n times, and every "answer" would end up as the final state. The undo (`remove(size-1)`) restores the state for the sibling branch - this is the backtracking contract.

**15. Dry Run (decision tree)** - `nums = [1, 2]`
```
gen(i=0, path=[])
"œ"" skip 1  - gen(1, [])
"'      "œ"" skip 2  - gen(2, [])    - record []
"'      """" take 2  - gen(2, [2])   - record [2]   - undo
"""" take 1  - gen(1, [1])
       "œ"" skip 2  - gen(2, [1])   - record [1]   - (undo of take 2)
       """" take 2  - gen(2, [1,2]) - record [1,2] - undo
```
Recording order: `[], [2], [1], [1,2]` (order varies with branch order - the set is what matters). **4 = 2²** subsequences œ"

**16. Complexity** - **Time O(n · 2¿):** 2¿ leaves, each copying a path of up to n elements. **Space O(n)** recursion depth + path (plus the output itself, which is inherently O(n·2¿)).

**17. Edge Cases** - empty array (one empty subsequence); n = 1; duplicates (this version assumes distinct - see 096 for the deduplicated form); n up to 12 (2¹² = 4096 - beyond ~24, 2¿ blows memory).

**18. Common Mistakes** - storing `path` without copying; forgetting the undo (the take-branch contaminates the skip-branch); base case at the wrong index; recording inside the loop instead of at the leaf.

**19. Interview Questions**
**Q: How many subsequences**  - 2¿ (each element independently in or out).
**Q: Could I do it iteratively**  - Yes: start with `[[]]`, and for each element, append it to every existing list - O(n·2¿) with no recursion.
**Q: Follow-up - only those with sum = target**  - Prune when the running sum exceeds target (Combination Sum family, 099).

**20. Variations** - Subsets (095 - same tree, usually with a one-direction loop); subsequences with a constraint (prune); bitmask generation (iterative alternative).

**21. Related Problems** - 095, 096, 099, 102 (Generate Parentheses - a constrained version of the same tree).

**22. Interview Explanation - 60 Seconds**
> "I build a decision tree over the elements: at index i I either skip the element or take it, then recurse to i+1. When I reach the end, I record a copy of the current path - that's one complete subsequence. Take branches undo their choice afterwards so the sibling branch starts clean. Every subsequence maps to exactly one path, so I get all 2¿ of them with no duplicates: O(n·2¿) time."

</details>
